lawyer:
Md Imam Hasan, Advocate-For the Petitioner. 
Md Ehsanul Haque, with Md Zobaidur Rahman, Advocates-For the Respondent Nos. 2-5 & 8-9.
parties:
Al-Mamun Mridha ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Land Survey Tribunal, Dhaka Metropolitan Dhaka ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Md Akram Hossain Chowdhury J : On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution this Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the  respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 28-11-2011 passed by the respondent No. 1, the Land Survey Tribunal, Dhaka in Land Survey Tribunal Case No. 22 of 2008 (Annexure-D) allowing the application of the respondent Nos. 2-5 and 8-9 for appointment of an Advocate Commissioner under Order XXVI, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. At the time of issuance of the rule this Court, pending hearing of rule, stayed the proceedings of Land Survey Tribunal case Nos. 22 of 2008 by an ad-interim order and also passed an order for hearing this rule along with Writ Petition No. 9911 of 2011. But the learned Advocate of the petitioner informed this Court that the rule issued in Writ Petition No. 9911 of 2011 has already been discharged for non-prosecution. In such a position we have taken up this rule for disposal on its own merit.

3. The facts leading to the rule, in brief, are that the respondent Nos. 2-7 being plaintiffs filed Land Survey Tribunal Case No. 22 of 2008 before the Land Survey Tribunal, Dhaka under section 145A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 contending inter-alia that an area of 0.0476 acres of land was wrongly recorded in the City Survey Plot No. 3758/3897 instead of 0.0760 acres in the name of respondent No. 2-5 and therefore they filed the above noted Tribunal Case for correction of the record.

4. The present petitioner and others being defendants contested the case by filing written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and contending inter-alia that the petitioner and respondent No. 15 has been owning and possessing the land in dispute by way of purchase and after scrutinizing the papers and possession the Settlement Officer recorded the land in the name of the petitioner and other respondent in the respective khatian in the last Dhaka City Survey operation.

5. During pendency of the Land Survey Tribunal Case No. 22 of 2008 the respondent No. 2-5 and 8-9 being applicants filed an application under Order XXVI, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure for appointment of an Advocate Commissioner for holding a local investigation on the land in dispute.

6. The said application was opposed by the present petitioner by filing written objection. The learned Judge of the Land Survey Tribunal after hearing the said application by his order dated 28-11-2011 allowing the respondents' application for appointment of Advocate Commissioner for holding local investigation under Order XXVI, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure and fixed the next date on 8-2-2012 for depositing Advocate Commissioner's fees.

7. Since there is no appellate authority appointed as yet under section 145B of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 to challenge any order of the Land Survey Tribunal, the petitioner being aggrieved by the order dated 28-11-2011 by filing this writ petition obtained the present rule along with an ad-interim order staying the proceedings of aforesaid Land Survey Case.

8. The respondent Nos. 2-5 and 8-9 by filing an affidavit-in-opposition controverted the allegations made in the writ petition and con-tending inter-alia that the learned Judge of the Tribunal rightly and properly passed the impugned order and the impugned order is not contrary to the provisions of 145D of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950; since the tribunal did not yet issue any writ for holding local investigation, it could not be said that the order was passed for accommodating all the prayers of these respondents.

9. Mr Md Immam Hasan, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that under section 145D of the statute i.e. the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, empowered the Land Survey Tribunal to exercise its powers following the procedure under the Code of Civil Procedure in certain matters, so far as not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act for the purpose of disposal of the land survey case. Though the sub-section (i) (e) of section 145D of the Act, empowered the tribunal for issuing commission but that is to the extent of examination of the witnesses or documents only; other than that particular purpose the tribunal has/had no authority to pass an order for local investigation. The learned Advocate for the petitioner referring to the above section 145D of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 behestly submits that the learned Judge of the Tribunal without applying his judicial mind passed the impugned order in a slipshod manner without assigning any reason thereto. As such, the impugned order dated 28-11-2011 passed in Land Survey Tribunal Case No. 22 of 2008 is liable to be declared without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

10. On the other hand Mr Md Ehsanul Haque, with Mr Md Zobaidur Rahman, the learned Advocates appearing for the respondent Nos. 2-5 and 8-9 opposing the rule submits that the learned Judge of the Tribunal maintaining all procedure of the Act passed the impugned order; as because in section 145D of the SAT Act it has been categorically mentioned the tribunal shall exercise the powers and follow the procedure under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, so far as not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act. He therefore submits that in the present case the learned Judge of the tribunal as yet not issued any writ for holding the local investigation by an Advocate Commissioner, as such, it could not be said that the tribunal below has ordered for holding local investigation on all the prayers as they sought for. The petitioner by filing this writ petition stayed the whole proceedings of the case for an uncertain period which encouraged the prolongation of the legal process of justice; as such, he urges for discharging the rule.

11. Heard the learned Advocates, perused the writ petition, affidavit-in-opposition and the annexures annexed thereto. It appears from the record that the respondents, who are the plaintiff Nos. 1-4 and 7-8 in the land survey case has filed an application before the Land Survey Tribunal on 19-7-2009 under Order XXVI, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure for holding a local investigation by an Advocate Commissioner and in the said application they have categorically mentioned in the prayer as to which subjects are to be investigated by an Advocate commissioner in the local investigation; those subjects as mentioned in the application are as follows:

(ক) সিটি জরিপ খতিয়ান নং-২৬৩৭, দাগ নং৩৭৫৮/৩৮৯৭ ও সিটি জরিপ খতিয়ান নং ৮৮৭, দাগ নং ৩৭৫৮/৩৮৯৭ এর জমি আর, এস, খতিয়ান নং-১৪৫৮, দাগ নং ৬৬৫ এর ৮.২৫ শতাংশ জমির অন্তর্গত ভূমি কিনা ৷

(খ) নালিশী সম্পত্তি অর্থাৎ সিটি জরিপ খতিয়ান নং ২৬৩৭, দাগ নং-৩৭৫৮/৩৮৯৭ ও সিটি জরিপ খতিয়ান নং ৮৮৭, দাগ

নং ৩৭৫৮/৩৮৯৭ ও কতগুলি ঘর আছে, কে কে বসবাস করে ৷ উক্ত ঘরের মধ্যে কোন দোকান পাঠ আছে কিনা, দোকান থাকিলে দোকান গুলি কোন মালিকের নিকট হইতে চুক্তিপত্র বলে ভাড়াটিয়া হিসাবে ব্যবসা করে কিনা, কোন লোক ভাড়াটিয়া হিসাবে বসবাস করে কিনা করিলে কত টাকা দেন এবং কাকে মালিক হিসাবে ভাড়া প্রদান করেন ৷ সিটি জরিপ খতিয়ান নং-২৬৩৭, দাগ নং ৩৭৫৮/৩৮৯৭ ও সিটি জরিপ খতিয়ান নং ৮৮৭, দাগ নং-৩৭৫৮/৩৮৯৭ এর ভূমির চৌহদ্দি কি/চতৃর্দিকে কে কে আছেন ৷

12. It further appears from the impugnedorder dated 28-11-26পুঁ1 that the learned Judge of the tribunal passed the impugned order in the following manner-

“অদ্য মোকদ্দমা দরখাস্ত শুনানীর জন্য দিন ধার্য্য আছে। বাদীপক্ষ হাজিরা দিয়াছে ৷ বিবাদী পক্ষ হাজিরা দিয়াছে ৬- ৭ নং বিবাদী পক্ষ হলফ নামা যুক্ত এক দরখাস্ত দাখিল করিয়া স্থানীয় তদন্তের দরখাস্তের বিরুদ্ধে লিখিত আপত্তি দাখিল করিয়াছে। শুনিলাম । ৬০০০ টাকা কমিশন ফি দাখিল অন্তে মঞ্জুর। (ডি, ও, পি) ৬-৭ নং বিবাদী পক্ষ এক দরখাস্ত দাখিল করিয়া সংশোধনী দরখাস্তের আপত্তি দাখিলের জন্য সময়ের প্রার্থনা করিয়াছে। প্রার্থনা মঞ্জুর করা হইল, আগামী ৮/২/৯২ ইং তারিখ সংশোধনী দরখাস্ত শুনানী ও কমিশন ফি দাখিল।”

13. We find nothing in the four corners of the aforesaid order in what context the application for local investigation was allowed. Thus, it is presumed that the learned Judge of the Tribunal allowed the application as a whole as the respondents sought for local investigation. Though the learned Advocate for the respondents submits that the local investigation was sought for examining certain documents and to that regard the impugned order was passed but the impugned order does not say so.

14. For proper disposal of the rule we may quote here the section 145D of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, which runs as follows:

145D. Power and Procedure of Tribunals—(i) For the purposes of the disposal of suits or appeals, a Land Survey Tribunal or a Land Survey Appellate Tribunal, as the case may be, shall exercise the powers and follow the procedure under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, so far as not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act or the rules made there under, in respect of the following matters, namely;

(a) summoning and enforcing the attendance of any person and examining him;

(b) requiring the discovery and production of any document;

(c) requiring evidence on affidavit;

(d) requisitioning any public record or a copy thereof from any office;

(e) issuing commissions for the examination of witnesses or documents.

And

(f) such other matters as may be prescribed by rules.

(2) Any proceeding before a Land Survey Tribunal or a Land Survey Appellate Tribunal shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of section 193 of the Penal Code.

(3) A Land Survey Tribunal or a Land Survey Appellate Tribunal shall sit at such place or places as the Government may fix.

(4) The judge of the Land Survey Tribunal or Land Survey Appellate Tribunal may make such administrative arrangements as he considers necessary for the performance of the functions of the Land Survey Tribunal or Land Survey Appellate Tribunal, as the case may be.

(5) The Land Survey appellate Tribunal may, of its own motion or upon an application made to it, by order in writing, transfer, at any stage of the proceedings, any suit from the Land Survey Tribunal to another Land Survey Tribunal within the territorial limits of its jurisdiction.

15. In the aforesaid sub-section-(i) (e) of section 145D shows, this particular section is only relating to issue a commission for examination of witnesses or documents. Though the statute provides that the Code of Civil procedure may be followed in certain matters, so far it is not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act or rule made there under. One of those matters is to issue commission as provided under sub-section- (i) (e) of section 145D; wherein it is specifically mentioned that to issue a commission for the purpose of examination of witnesses or documents only.

<u>16. In the present case we find that the respondents in their application prayed for holding a local investigation by an Advocate Commissioner to investigate the possession of the property in question and also to investigate who are possessing thereon and further who are residing or enjoying the shops stands thereon and are getting rents from the shop keepers. Such prayer of the respondents are totally based on an application as generally filed in a civil suit for deciding the title and possession of the land in dispute but it does not attract the provisions of section 145D of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950.</u>

17. Thus, we find that the learned Judge of the tribunal upon misconception of law and misreading the materials on record passed a non-speaking order in a slipshod manner which is not maintainable in the eye of law. As such, we are in a considered view that the impugned order dated 28-11-2011 passed by the learned Judge of the Land Survey Tribunal, Dhaka in holding a local investigation in the Land Survey Tribunal Case No. 22 of 2008 was passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

18. In the result, the rule is made absolute.

19. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court is recalled and vacated.

20. The learned Judge of the Tribunal is directed to proceed with the case in accordance with the law from its position as it was, other than the local investigation.

Communicate this judgment and order at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mahbubey Alam, Senior Advocate, instructed by Firoz Shah, Advocate-on-Record—For the Appellant.

Not represented—Respondent Nos. 2-4.
parties:
Md. Badsha Miah ------ Appellant
Vs.
Sonali Bank and others ------ Respondents.
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 14-8-2002 passed by this Division in Civil Petition for leave to Appeal No. 1290 of 2000)
full_judgment:
Syed JR Mudassir Husain CJ: This appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 22-11-2000 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in Tribunal Case No.108 of 1999 allowing the same upon setting aside the judgment and order dated 20-11-1997 passed by the Administrative Tribunal, Dhaka in Tribunal Case No. 228 of 1997 allowing the same.

<u>2. The relevant facts are that the appellant filed the above case before the Administrative Tribunal, Dhaka for declaration that he is entitled to get all the financial benefits for the period from the date of his retirement up to the joining his duties.</u>

<u>3. The appellant's case was that while serving as Deputy General Manager of Sonali Bank, he was retired from service by an order dated 13-12-1993 under section 9(2) of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act, 1974 along with 4 others of the same Bank and 9 others of some other nationalised Banks including Agrani Bank; that one Mr Kobad Ali, Deputy General Manager of the Agrani Bank, who was also one of those so retired by the Government, instituted Administrative Tribunal Case No. 168 of 1994 before the Administrative Tribunal, Dhaka challenging his order of retirement; that during the pendency of the said Tribunal Case, the present appellant Md. Badsha Miah of Sonali Bank submitted representation to the Hon'ble President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh on 20-8-1996 for his reinstatement in service whereupon a notification was issued on 15-1-1997 whereby the appellant was reinstated in service but without any arrear salary and allowances for the period he was out of service treating the said period as an extraordinary leave. Thereafter, the appellant joined his duties; that in the meantime the Administrative Tribunal case filed by Mr Kobad Ali was heard and upon hearing the parties, the Administrative Tribunal allowed the said case upon setting aside the order of his retirement and directing his reinstatement in service with all financial benefits. Accordingly, said Kobad Ali was reinstated in service on 23-4-1997 with all benefits for the period he was out of service.</u>

4. The appellant, being encouraged by the aforesaid order allowing the financial benefits to Mr Kobad Ali  submitted an application before the Hon'ble President for review of his order dated 15-1-1997 by which the appellant was reinstated but the President rejected the prayer for review for granting the appellant the service benefits on 13-8-1997. The appellant thereafter filed the aforesaid Administrative Tribunal Case on the ground that he stands on the same footing with the case of Mr Kobad Ali and also alleged that the appellant was denied the equal treatment violating Article 27 of the Constitution.

5. The respondents contested the case by taking a plea of limitation and principle of estoppel.

6. The Administrative Tribunal upon hearing the parties allowed the case of the appellant by its judgment and order dated 20-11-1997 holding that the appellant (applicant) filed the case within the prescribed period of 6 (six) months from the date of rejection of the review application of the appellant on 13-8-1997 and, as such, the appellant's Tribunal Case is not barred by limitation and the order refusing to grant financial beriefit4 to the appellant is violative of Note 4 of Rule 72 of Bangladesh Service Rules (BSR) Part 1 and also in violation of Article 27 of the Constitution. And thereby the Administrative Tribunal came to the finding that the present appellant (applicant) was entitled to get the financial benefit for the period of his unemployment by judgment and order of the Administrative Tribunal as aforesaid.

7. The respondent employer of the appellant being thus aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment of the Administrative Tribunal dated 20-11-1997 preferred appeal before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal being Administrative Appeal No. 108 of 1999 who after hearing the parties allowed the appeal by its, judgment and order dated 22-11-2000 reversing the judgment and order of the Administrative Tribunal on the ground that period of limitation should run from the notification dated 15-1-1997.

8. The appellant, being aggrieved by the above judgment of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal dated 22-11-2000 moved this Division and obtained leave to consider as to whether the Administrative Appellate Tribunal committed an error of law in, holding the view that without challenging the notification dated 15-1-1997 the appellant cannot challenge the order rejecting the review of the appellant by the Hon'ble President of Bangladesh on 13-8-1997 and also to consider as to whether the appellant's Tribunal Case having been filed on 20-11-1997 after rejection of the aforesaid order of review was time barred or not.

9. Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Counsel, appearing for the appellant, contended that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal committed an error of law in holding the view that without challenging the notification dated 15-1-1997, the appellant cannot challenge order rejecting his review petition by the President passed on 13-8-1997 inasmuch as the President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, being the highest Constitutional functionary and there being no appellate Authority above him, since the aforesaid order being reviewable only by the President, the appellant was entitled to challenge the order of review before the Administrative Tribunal and, as such, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal wrongly held that the petition before the Tribunal by the appellant is barred and in such view of the matter, the findings and, decisions of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal are wrong and cannot sustain in law.

10. Mr. Alam next contended that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal while dismissing the appeal misread and misconstrued the second proviso of sub-section 2 of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 and therefore, committed illegality in dismissing the appeal without considering that the word review has been included in the aforesaid provision of law and, as such, the findings and decisions arrived at by the Administrative Tribunal being erroneous are liable to be set aside. He further contended that the High Court Division having misdirected itself in considering the aforesaid provision of law came to an erroneous finding which cannot be sustained in law.

11. Mr Abdur Razaque Khan, the learned Additional Attorney-General, contended that the appellant did not file any review petition before the President of the Republic and the copy of the same has not been filed before the Administrative Tribunal nor even to this Division. But the appellant actually filed incompetent representation under the garb of review before the Secretary, Ministry of Finance, Banking Division and the same was rejected on 3-8-1997 and in such view of the matter the question of filing review petition before the President did not arise. He, therefore, argued that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal rightly considered the provision of section 9(2) of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 and other attending facts and circumstances of the case.

12. We have heard the learned Counsels of both sides and considered their submissions. On perusal of the impugned judgment, we find that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal meticulously considered the case of both the parties, the provision of section 912) of the Public Servant (Retirement) Act, 1974 and also the provision of Rule 3(2)(d) of the Administrative Tribunal Rules 1992.

<u>13. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the ease and in view of the submissions made by the learned Counsels of both sides, we find that the learned Administrative Appellate Tribunal upon meticulous consideration of the materials on record rightly came to the findings which are as follows:</u>

<u>"Section 4(2) of the Administrative Tribunals Act says that a person may make an application to the Tribunal if he is aggrieved by any order, decision or action of the authority, and the second proviso thereto prescribes a period of 6 months from the date of such order, decision or action to file such an application. The respondent's learned lawyer referring to the cause title to the application at one stage submits that for the purpose of this case, he has been aggrieved by the review order of rejection dated 13-8-1997. It will be noted that the review itself was not maintainable under any law and, as such, the maintainability of a case challenging an order passed in such a view is out of the question. It may be mentioned, however that the original order in the notification dated 15-1-1997 has not merged in the review order dated 13-8-1997 and, as such, the applicant has not got any relief without assailing the original order itself. We do therefore, hold that if it is a case challenging the notification dated 15-1-1997, it is barred by limitation and on the contrary, if it is a case against the review order dated 13-8-1997 claiming declaration as to entitlement to service benefits it is not maintainable."</u>

14. We are fully in agreement with the above findings and decisions arrived at by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal and, as such, we find no substance in this appeal.

In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Md. Mizanul Haq Chowdhury, Advocate with Hasan Mohammed Riyed, Advocates-For the Plaintiff.

parties:
Hasan Vegetable Oil Mills Ltd. ----- Plaintiff 
Vs
MT Sceptre and 6 others ----- Defendant
full_judgment:
AFM Abdur Rahman J : The instant Admiralty Suit filed by the plaintiff Messrs Hasan Vegetable Oil Mills Limited, on 13-05-2001 against the vessel MT Sceptre and others has been heard on contest by the defendants now disposed of by this judgment.

2. The facts leading to initiation of the instant Admiralty Suit is that the plaintiff is a private limited company having industrial undertaking for refining and production of Edible Oil which are imported from abroad and in course of the business the plaintiff intended to import Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO) from Argentina and accordingly opened Letter of Credit bearing No. 03990112-C, dated 12-05-1999, through the City Bank Limited, Principal Office, Dilkusha C/A, Dhaka, for import of 10,000 MT (CDSO) from Andre (Cayman Islands) Trading Co. Ltd. at a price of US $ 445,000. The Plaintiff obtained marine Insurance Cover Note No. CGICBBA/ MC-112 / OS/99(CO-INS) dated 12-05-1999 from the City General Insurance Company Limited, Dhaka. The Shipper-seller Andre (Cayman Islands) Trading Co. Ltd., shipped the said cargo in full quantity and in good order and condition through the defendant No. 1 vessel MT Sceptre flying Panama Flag. The Master of the vessel issued Tanker bill of lading in favour of the shipper and the plaintiff received the shipping documents including the invoice and bill of lading in time through the bank channel. The defendant No. 1 vessel MT Sceptre arrived at Chittagong Port on 22-06-1999 and the cargo (CDSO) was delivered to Tank Terminal, namely Messrs Van Ommeren Tank Terminal (Bangladesh) Limited, Chittagong and survey was conducted by the surveyor who issued report which shows that out of total 10,000 MT the vessel effected delivery of 9923.924 MT CDSO resulting short landing of 76.076 MT of CDSO. The said short landing was endorsed by the customs authority at Chittagong port. The plaintiff submitted bills of entry for taking delivery of the entire quantity of CDSO as imported by it but the plaintiff was given delivery of 9923.924 MT of CDSO having 76.076 MT short. The plaintiff suffered loss for the said short landing and accordingly submitted a claim bill to the defendant No. 4, Messrs Rainbow Shipping Lines, the local agent of the defendant No. 1 vessel MT Sceptre and demanded immediate arrangement for settlement of the cargo claim. Although the plaintiff only claimed in the said claim letter the C&F value of the short cargo, yet the same was not resolved by the defendants. Despite the fact the defendant No. 4 supplied a copy of the guarantee letter, issued by the P&I Club of the vessel, London Steamship Owners Mutual Insurance Association Limited assuring that the claim would be settled through agreement by the parties, yet as the said agreement was not reached and therefore the defendant No. 1 vessel MT Sceptre is liable to compensate the plaintiff which runs as follows:—

I. C&F value of the short landed 76.076 MT cargo of CDSO @US$ 445.00 per Ton. US$33853.82

II. Insurance 1% charge US$338.53

III. Loss and Compensation Total US$ 34192.35

Equivalent to BD Tk. 18,80,579.25 @ US $ = BD Taka 55

3. The claim of the plaintiff not being satisfied, the plaintiff instituted the instant Admiralty Suit for realization of the claim from the defendants to the extent of an amount of US$ 34192.35 equivalent to BD. Tk. 18,80,579.25 along with an interest @ of Tk. 18% per annum from the date of filing of the suit till realization. The defendant No. 1 vessel MT Sceptre at that time left Chittagong Port without settling the dispute with the plaintiff, but as it again came to Chittagong on 10-05-2001, the plaintiff obtained an order of arrest of the said vessel from this court detaining the defendant No.1 vessel. But later it was released upon furnishing bank guarantee protecting the plain-tiff's interest for an amount covering the full claim of the plaintiff in the instant suit.

4. The defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 entered appearance and contested the suit by filing joint written statement by denying all the material allegations in the plaint. It has been stated inter-alia that the Tanker vessel MT  Sceptre arrived at Chittagong Port on 22-6-1999 with cargo of Crude Degummed Soyabean Oil (CDSO) against the bill of lading estimated quantity of 17,000 MT. A Ullage survey was conducted at Chittagong Port on 22-6-1999 in order to ascertain the exact quantity of the cargo prior to commencing the discharge of the same and it was found that the tanker holds of the vessel contain 16,951.331 MT of CDSO. The surveyor issued report on 11-7-1999 which was signed by tile surveyor of the consignee and the carrier. Therefore, there may be short landing of 48.669 MT of CDSO out of bills of lading quantity 17,000 MT. But as per the ships figure at the load port, there was only 16,923.643 MT CDSO loaded in the vessel and therefore the vessel cannot be held liable for any alleged claim of the plaintiff. The vessel delivered 16,951.331 MT of CDSO and on completion of the discharge of the entire cargo from the vessels tank it was jointly inspected and checked by the chief officer of the vessel and the surveyor of the consignee and the tanks of the vessel MT Sceptre was found to be totally empty and drained upon which a dry tank certificate was issued on 7-7-1999. The load port of the cargo was San Lorenzo, Argentina. The plaintiff served a claim letter through the defendant No. 4 Messrs Rainbow Shipping Lines Limited on 11-10-1999 claiming US$ 33,853.82 compensation against the alleged short landing quantity of 76.076 MT of CDSO and since these defendants are not liable for any alleged claim of the plaintiff, the same has not been responded to. The defendant carried the supplier-shippers cargo with all due care and diligence and delivered the same as was loaded at the port of loading San Lorenzo, Argentina and if there is any short landing of cargo than the quantity of load at the load port the same may be due to inherent nature of cargo of oil and, as such, this defendants are not liable for alleged any short landing of cargo. The short landing of 48,669 MT is well covered within the extent of 1% ocean allowance and, as such, the plaintiff cannot claim any compensation for such short landing. The defendant in order to avoid litigation and to minimize losses under compelling circumstances obtained P&I Club guarantee in favour of the plaintiff for an amount of US$ 93,849.20 dated 6-7-1999 on condition that the plaintiff would refrain from arresting or otherwise detaining the vessel MT Sceptre for which the vessel left Bangladesh without any objection from the defendant. But later when it came again to Bangladesh with cargo the plaintiff effected a illegal arrest of the vessel and compelled the carrier to furnish bank guarantee for an amount of Bangladesh Tk. 18,80,579.25 and accordingly got release of the vessel from arrest. The alleged claim of the plaintiff as stated in break down in Paragraph No. 11 of the plaint is exorbitant one and the defendants are not liable to comply the said claim. The plaintiff having no cause of action against the contesting defendants instituted the instant Admiralty suit on false pretext which is liable to be dismissed and the bank guarantee to be returned.

5. Upon the aforesaid pleadings of the parties this court framed issue of the suit as under;

1. Is the suit maintainable under Admiralty Jurisdiction?

2. Does the plaintiff have any cause of action against the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 for filing the instant Admiralty Suit?

3. Is the suit barred by limitation?

4. Is the suit barred under the principles of estoppels, waiver and acquiescence?

5. Whether the defendant No. 1 has received 17,000 MT of CDSO and issued Bill of Lading certifying receipt of the same?

6. Whether the defendant No. 1 has made a short delivery of 76,076 MT of CDSO?

7. Whether the defendants are under legal obligation to effect delivery of the Bill of Lading's quantity cargo?

8. Has the plaintiff suffered any losses and damages?

Upon such issue as framed by this Court the plaintiff led evidence of PW 1 Biswajit Saha and PW 2 Abu Jafar. The plaintiff Exhibited various documents which are as follows:—

Exhibit No. Identity of the document

1 Special power-of-attorney

2 Letter of Credit dated 12-5-1999

3 (series) 3(1) - 3(a) Commercial Invoice No. N0002143/4-A to N0002143/4-3

4 (series) 4(1) - 4(a) Tanker bill of lading dated 18-5-1999 No. 10-No.19

5 Certificate dated 14-7-1999

6 Claim Bill dated 11-10-1999

7 Letter to the commissioner of customs dated 6-7-1999

8 Certificate dated 7-7-1999 from consignee, carrier and terminal surveyor.

6. The defendant Nos. examined MHM Mahfuzur Captain M. Altafur Rahman as 2. The defendants exhibited documents:— 1, 2 and 3 Rahman and DW 1 and DW the following documents:-

Exhibit No. Identity of the document

A, B Two letters of authority

B(1) Signature

C, C(1), C(2) Joint ullage survey report dated 17-5-1999 and 21-5-1999

D, D(1) Letter of discrepancy

E Oil densities of the vessel

F, F(1) -F(3) Joint ullage survey report

F(4) - F(6) Signatures of captain SA Khan

F(7) - G(1), H(3) - H(5) Signatures of the surveyor Capt. M. Altafur Rahman

G Joint dry tank inspection certificate

H, H(1)-H(2) Joint survey reports

7. Upon hearing the evidence and reconciling the pleadings of the parties this court finds that the issues are required to be recasted and accordingly the same is recast.

1. Is the suit maintainable under the admiralty jurisdiction?

2. Is the suit barred by limitation?

3. Has suit suffers from defect of parties?

4. Is their any cause of action against the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3?

5. Is their any short landing of the cargo at the discharge port?

6. Is the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 are liable to compensate the plaintiff for the short landing cargo?

8. In the instant suit the learned Advocate Mr. Mizanul Haq Chowdhury along with Mr. Hasan Mohammed Riyed represented the plaintiff while the learned Advocate Mr. M. Hafizullah and the learned Advocate Mr. Muhammad Ohiullah appeared on behalf of the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 and conducted the hearing of the suit on behalf of the said defendants.

9. Now we will dispose of the issues in the light of the evidence led by the parties.

Issue No. 1: The maintainability aspect of the suit.

10. Although the issue has not been pressed by the parties so seriously, yet as the same involves question of law, it requires decision. To maintain such suits under Admiralty jurisdiction Section 3(2)(ja) of the Admiralty court Ain 2000 provides as follows:

এ্যাডমিরাল্টি কোর্ট আইন, ২০০০

ধারা ৩(২); এ্যাডমিরাল্টি কোর্ট নিম্নবর্ণিত যে কোন প্রশ্ন বা দাবী সম্পর্কে শুনানী এবং সিদ্ধান্ত গ্রহণ করিবার এখতিয়ার থাকিবে। যথা:

(ক)

(খ)

(গ)

(ঘ)

(ঙ)

(চ)

(ছ)

(জ) কোন জাহাজে পণ্য পরিবহন বা কোন জাহাজের ব্যবহার বা ভাড়া সংক্রান্ত চুক্তি হইতে উদ্ভুত কোন দাবী;

English version of the law:

Admiralty Court Act 2000

Section 3(2); The Admiralty Court shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine any questions or claims of the following; namely.

(a)

(b)

(c)

(d)

(e)

(f)

(g)

(h) any claim arising out of any agreement relating to the carriage of goods in a ship or to the use or hire of a ship;

11. The plaintiff in the instant suit claimed that it suffered loss due to 76.076 MT short landing of cargo CDSO. The plaintiff being the importer of CDSO steeped into the shoe of the shipper-supplier as notifying party in the Bill of Lading and the claim having been against the sea carrier of the cargo, the cause as alleged in the plaint combs well within the purview of Section 3(2)(ja) of the Admiralty Court Act, 2000 and as such the instant suit is maintainable under the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court. Therefore, the issue No. 1 is disposed of in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendants.

Issue No. 3, 4, 5 and 6 merit of the dispute aspect.

12. All these issues being inter related and required to be considered first, the same are taken together for disposal.

13. The plaintiff claims in the plaint that it has imported 10,000 MT of CDSO from the supplier and carrier Andre (Cayman Islands) Trading Co. Ltd. of Monte Video, of Uruguay under two letter of Credit (L/C) each having 445 MT which has been loaded in the defendant No. 1 vessel. MV Sceptre at the port San Lorenzo, Argentina for carriage to Chittagong Port which arrived the discharge Port on 22-6-1999. The plaintiffs claimed that 76.076 MT of CDSO out of his imported 10,000 MT of CDSO was short landed. The defendant No. 1 through the written statement claims that although the Bill of Lading mentioned quantity of CDSO was 17000 MT yet a short quantity of 16,923.643 MT measured in Ullage survey at the load port was loaded in the defendant No. 1 vessel MT Sceptre at the load port and it discharged that exact quantity of 16,951.331 MT of CDSO at Chittagong Port as received by the shore tank terminal and the said quantity was measured in a Ullage survey conducted before the discharge of the cargo at Chittagong Port attended by the surveyor on behalf of the consignee and the carrier.

14. The DW 1 MHM Mahfuzur Rahman in his examination-in-chief stated that after arrival of the vessel a Ullage survey was carried out on board and the surveyor found total quantity of CDSO as 16,951.331 MT on board the vessel MT Sceptre and accordingly issued joint survey report dated 22-6-1999 and 3-7-1999. Those certificates were exhibited as Exhibit-F series and G which upon perusal shows that 16,951.331 MT of CDSO was discharged from the vessel MT Sceptre indicating that the defendant No. 1 admitted that there was a short landing of 48.669 MT of CDSO. But admittedly the Bill of Lading quantity of CDSO being, 17,000 MT loaded at the load port of San Lorenzo, Argentina, the deposition of PW 1 Mr. Biswajit Saha revels that there are other four importers who also imported the CDSO cargo by the defendant No. 1 vessel MT Sceptre along with the plaintiff jointly who are (1) KSA Oil refinery and vegetable products limited, (2) Shah Amanat Edible Oil Company Limited, (3) Md. Elias Brother Private Limited and (4) Mostafa Vegetable Oil Industries Limited. It was further disclosed by the PW 1 that they have effected a rateable distribution of landed quantity duly approved and certified by the customs bond officer and surveyor of the consignee as well as the shipping agent which was marked as Exhibit-5. These facts have not been stated in the plaint and in contrary the plaintiff claimed that the customs certificate shows that out of 10000 MT of CDSO carried by the defendant No. 1 vessel MT Sceptre the plaintiff received 9,923.924 MT and, as such, the plaintiff received a short of 76.076 MT of CDSO.

15. So far the claim that the defendant No. 1. vessel loaded 16,923.643 MT of CDSO at the load port, the DW 1 in his examination-in-chief stated that there was a Ullage survey conducted at the load port whereupon the surveyor issued the Ullage survey report which has been marked as Exhibit-C series where from it revealed that the vessel loaded 16,923.643 MT of CDSO.

16. The learned Advocate Mr. Mizanul Haq Chowdhury, appearing on behalf of the plaintiff argued that the defendant vessel is bound to deliver the quantity of the CDSO stated in the bills of lading which appears to be 17,000 MT out of which the plaintiff is entitled to 10,000 MT of CDSO and as such the defendant No. 1 vessel is liable to compensate the plaintiff for the short fall of 76.076 MT of CDSO.

17. On the other hand, the learned Advocate Mr. Muhammad Ohiullah argued that the Ullage survey report at the load port clearly shows that the defendant No. 1 vessel MT Sceptre received a less quantity of cargo than mentioned in the Bill of Lading, which was issued prior to loading of the cargo and accordingly the master of the vessel, upon satisfaction that the shipper has failed to load the bills of lading mentioned quantity of CDSO, issued a discrepancy certificate which has been marked as Exhibit-D, D(1) stating that it loaded 16,923.643 MT of CDSO at the load port. In this respect the defendant No. 1 mainly took two plea, one being that the shipper failed to load the exact quantity of CDSO as mentioned in the bills of lading and the second that the short landed quantity of CDSO is covered by 1% Ocean allowance and therefore, the defendant No. 1 is not liable to compensate the plaintiff.

18. In this suit the crux point to be decided is the quantity of the CDSO which has been delivered from the defendant No. 1 vessel MT Sceptre. The defendant No. 1 is claiming that it had loaded a less quantity of CDSO at the load port since the shipper has 'failed to load the exact quantity of CDSO as mentioned in the bills of lading which has been issued on 18-3-1999, much earlier than the loading of the cargo on 17-5-1999 on board the vessel. These two dates have been proved from exhibit No. 4 (series) and C (series).

19. On the other hand, the plaintiff is claiming that the defendant No. 1 vessel had loaded the bills of lading mentioned quantity 10,000 MT of the CDSO on board the vessel at the load port. Therefore in order to resolve this discrepancy in quantity at the load port, it involves another party in the whole dispute i.e. shipper-supplier of the cargo, to prove what was the exact quantity of CDSO loaded. But surprisingly the plaintiff opted for not to made the shipper supplier a party in the instant suit. Admittedly the defendant has unloaded a cargo, a less quantity of 48.669 MT of CDSO out of the total quantity it carried i.e. 17,000 MT of CDSO. But who is liable for this short quantity ought to be adjudicated by the court and accordingly relief is to be awarded against the defaulting party upon decreeing the suit against the said liable party. But the vital party, who loaded the cargo on board is absent before this court. Therefore, this court finds that this suit has a lacuna of defect of parties rendering the suit liable to be dismissed.

20. It appears that the plaintiff has obtained less quantity of the cargo from the quantity it imported and certified by the customs authority as appears from Exhibit-5. But as the liability of the short fall cannot be decided in the absence of the shipper-supplier this suit must fail for the lacuna of defect of parties and therefore, these issues are disposed of in favour of the contesting defendants and against the plaintiff.

Issue No. 2; Limitation aspect.

21. The learned Advocate Mr. Muhammad Ohiullah, appearing on behalf of the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 argued that the instant suit is hopelessly barred by the principal of limitation since the Provisions of Article 3, Rules 6 of the Carriage of goods by Sea Act, 1925 provides for filing the suit within one year after delivery of the goods and since the instant cargo was delivered on 22-6-1999 and suit filed on 13-5-2001 the same is barred on the point of limitation and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

22. The learned Advocate Mr. Ohiullah in this context, relied on the decision reported in 61 DLR 463 and 10 DLR 307.

23. Article 3 of Rule 6 of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 provides as follows;

"The shipper shall not be responsible for loss or damage sustained by the carrier or the ship arising or resulting from any cause without the act, fault or neglect of the shipper, his agents or his servants.

This rule cannot be contracted out of where the Rules are incorporated into the bill of lading by section 1 of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, because Art. V allows the carrier only to contract out of his rights and immunities under the Rules. But where the Rules are incorporated only by contract an express provision in the bill of lading conflicting with Art. IV, r. 3, would probably be given effect to, particularly as there is no rule in Art. IV equivalent to Art. 111, r. 8".

24. The learned Advocate Mr. Mizanul Haq Chowdhury, attempted to impress this court that as the negotiation was going on in between the parties the question of the date of delivery when the good ought to have been delivered will be calculated from the date of failure of the negotiation. We are unable to accept the argument since it appears that the suit for any short landed cargo is to be brought within one year after delivery of the goods.

25. Article 3, 'Rules 6 of the carriage of goods by Sea Act 1925 deals with the limitation in filing suit on the claim of short landing providing 1(one) year period from the date of delivery which also described when the delivery of the cargo shall be constituted in the following language;

Unless notice of loss or damage and the general nature of such loss or damage be given in writing to the carrier or his agent at the port of discharge before or at the time of the removal of the goods into the custody of the person entitled to delivery thereof under the contract of carriage, or, if the loss or damage be not apparent, within three days, such removal shall be prima facie evidence of the delivery by the carrier of the goods as described in the bill of lading.

The notice in writing need not be given if the state of the goods has at the time of their receipt been the subject of joint survey or inspection. In any event the carrier and the ship shall be discharged from all liability in respect of loss or damage unless suit is brought within one year after delivery of the goods or the date when the goods should have been delivered.

26. In the case of any actual or apprehended loss or damage, the carrier and the receiver shall give all reasonable facilities to each other for inspecting and tallying the goods.

27. But it appears that the Provisions of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925 (Act No. XXVI of 1925) is applicable in the instant case and the Provisions of Section 4 of the Act Provides as follows;

"Statement as to application of Rules to be included in bills of lading.—Every bill of lading, or similar document of title, issued in Bangladesh which contains or is evidence of any contract to which the Rules apply, shall contain an express statement that it is to have effect subject to the provisions of the said Rules as applied by this Act.

28. It appears that the Provision of Section 4 of the said Act limited the applicability of the Rules relating to Bills of Lading set out in the schedule of the Act, upon statement to be made in the body of the bills of lading rendering it applicable which prompt us to examine the sets of bills of lading as exhibited by the plaintiff marked as Exhibit 4(series), wherefrom it appears that the language it used apparently made the said rules applicable when it reads as follows;

"If this Bill of Lading is a document of title two which the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act of the United States, approved April 16, 1936, or similar legislation giving statutory effect to the International Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules relating to Bills of Lading at Brussels of August 25, 1924 applies by reason of the port of leading or discharge being in territory in which the world Act or other similar legislation is in force, this Bill of Lading shall have effect subject to the provision of the said Act or other similar legislation, as the case may be, which shall deemed incorporated herein, and nothing herein contained shall he deemed a surrender by the carrier if any of this rights or ammunition or an increase of any of its responsibilities or liabilities under said Act or the similar legislation. If any tern of this Bill of Lading is repugnant to the said Act or other similar legislation as to incorporate such terms shall be void to that extent but no further. "

29. In the case of Eximpo Trading Ltd vs MV Banglar Kakoli reported in 61 DLR 463 this bench, differently constituted, on the similar point decided as under:

Clause 4 contained on the reverse side of the bill of lading relates to the question of jurisdiction and reads as follows;

"4. Jurisdiction. The contract evidenced by this Bill of Lading shall be governed by the law of the place where the Carrier has his principal place of business and disputes determined at that place (or at the option of the Carrier, at the port of destination) according to that law to the exclusion of the jurisdiction of the Courts of any other country" From the jurisdiction clause in the bills of lading it is clear that the contract would be governed by the law of the place where the carrier has his principal place of business. Hence the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, 1925 would be the law applicable to the instant voyage and accordingly, the Courts in Bangladesh would have exclusive jurisdiction over any dispute arising out of the carriage of goods. However; this did not prevent the plaintiff from litigating in Singapore.

30. As the Bill of Lading, as aforesaid, being a contract of carriage stipulated for the application of the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925 as applicable the instant dispute shall come within its purview.

31. The plaintiff filed the suit on 13-5-2001 and apparently delivery of the cargo CDSO was made on 22-6-1999 which allowed the learned Advocate Mr. Ohiullah to argue that the suit is barred by limitation against which the learned Advocate Mr. Mizanul Haq Chowdhury replied that as the settlement negotiation was going on the point of limitation commence from the date of failure of the negotiation talk and , as the defendants refused to settle the matter only on April 2001 the plaintiff has filed this suit well within the time of 1(one) year.

32. In this context the learned Advocate Mr. Mizanul Haq Chowdhury relied on the case reported in 10 DLR 242 which was confirmed in the case reported in 11 DLR 520.

33. We have examined both the decision as referred by the learned Advocate Mr. Mizanul Haq Chowdhury. The case of Dada Ltd. vs RSN Company Ltd. reported in 10 DLR 242 is a suit for realization of compensation for non-delivery of goods which was carried from the Port of Chittagong to Khulna Port by an Inland Vessel. It was contended on behalf of the defendant of that suit that article 30 and 31 of Limitation Act 1908 was applicable which barred the filing of suit beyond one year from the date of delivery or from the date when the delivery was ought to be made. That dispute being a dispute upon inland carriage of good the municipal law applicable and, as such, his lordship justice Asir decided the dispute on the context of the Limitation Act. In the case of River Steam Navigation Co. Ltd. and India General Navigation and Rly Co. Ltd. vs Messers Dada Ltd. a division bench of the Dhaka High Court constituted by their lordship Amin Ahmed CJ and Chakrabarty I affirmed the judgment reported in 10 DLR 242 treating the dispute in the same context.

<u>34. But in the instant case the dispute of short delivery involves carriage of goods through the high seas under the Provision of Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1925 and the Bill of Lading Act 1865. Therefore the decision made in the light of Section 30 and 31 of the Limitation Act, 1908 is not attracted to this case since the Provision of Limitation Act, 1908 is not applicable as the Bill of Lading which acts in one aspect as contract of Carriage stipulated the applicability of the aforesaid Act which is a special substantive law of Limitation as it provided for extinguishment of the liability of the Carrier for short delivery due to failure of non-service of notice within, three days. Therefore, this court notes that the alleged negotiation for compensation by the plaintiff with the defendant No. 4 does not enable the plaintiff to rely upon the decision as made by their lordship in the 11 DLR 520 case that "the expression" "When the goods ought to be delivered in the third column of article 31 of the Limitation Act must be construed to mean when the plaintiff realized that the defendant by their conduct meant to convey that the goods could not be delivered". This not being attracted in the instant case, this court finds no merit in the argument of the learned Advocate Mr. Mizanul Haq Chowdhury.</u>

35. Further a division Bench of this court in the case of Continental Traders vs Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation reported in 10 DLR 307 = PLD 1957 Karachi 315 decided the point of Limitation for filing suit for short delivery in the following language;

"The carrier and the ship shall be discharged from all liabilities in respect of loss or damage unless suit is brought within one year after delivery of the goods or the date when the goods should have been delivered".

36. In the case of Gladstone Wyllie and Co. Ltd. vs Shahidi Trading Corporation Ltd. reported in 10 DLR 307 it has been decided that:

"A ship is discharged from all liabilities under rule 6 of Article 3 of the schedule to the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act in respect of loss or damage of the goods unless the suit is brought within one year after the delivery of the goods or the date when the goods should have been delivered."

37. The Rule is very much clear in this respect as it also defined what is the point of delivery stating that unless notice of grievance as to short delivery is given within 3(three) days of the removal of the cargo, the argument as advanced by Mr. Mizanul Haq Chowdhury appears to have no merit. Therefore, this court finds that the suit is also barred by limitation and, as such, the same is liable to be dismissed.

38. As this court has found that this suit is barred tinder the principal of defect of parties and also on the point of limitation, the shot is liable to be dismissed.

39. The Court fee paid is sufficient.

40. Hence, ordered.

41. The suit be and hereby dismissed against the defendant Nos. 1-5 on contest and ex-parte against the non-contesting pro-forma defendants. However, there shall be no order as to costs.

42. The Bank Guarantee submitted by the defendants earlier be returned immediately to the filing Advocate on behalf of defendant Nos. I and 3.

End.

AF Hassan Ariff with TM Shakil Hasan, Abdur Rahman, Advocates-For the appellants in both the above-mentioned.

full_judgment:
Md Nuruzzaman J: The two First Appeals are directed against the judgment and decree dated 7-6-2008 (decree signed on 14-8-2008) passed by the Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Money Suit No. 2 of 2006 decreeing the suit.

2. The plaintiff as appellant filed Cross-Objection (appeal) No. 1 of 2010 against the said judgment and decree, so far it relates to non granting the interest as per section 47B of the Insurance Act 1938.

3. We are disposing the above-mentioned two First Appeals and a Cross-Objection (appeal) by this single judgment as those arisen out of the same judgment and decree passed in the same Money Suit.

4. The material facts relevant for disposal of the instant appeals as have been derived from the plaint of the suit, in short, are that the respondent M/s. Maq Enterprise Ltd as plaintiff instituted a Suit being Money Suit No. 53 of 2005 in the court of Joint District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka against the defendants for recovery of a sum of Taka 7,68,72,540 from them. Eventually, the said Money Suit was transferred in the court of Joint District Judge, 3rd Court Dhaka and on transfer the suit was renumbered as Money Suit No. 2 of 2006.

5. The plaint case, in short, are that the plaintiff as a public limited company incorporated under the Companies Act having it's registered office at 141/1, Segunbagicha, Dhaka-1000 and has been manufacturing cartoons, back board, neck board and other related products for over two decades. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are the companies registered under the Companies Act, 1994 and have been conducting general insurance business (Marine, Fire Miscellaneous) since its inception. The plaintiff has a factory at Kadamtali, Faridabad, Shyampur, Dhaka wherein cartoons, back board and neck board and other related products are being manufactured. There are number of godowns in the factory premises for storage of raw materials used in the factory. The plaintiff has taken cash credit (Loan) facility from Sonali Bank, Bangabandhu Avenue Corporate Branch, Dhaka for financing procurement of raw materials and their storage in the godowns in the factory premises against pledge and hypothecation. The Prime Insurance Company Limited, the defendant No. 1 (leader) and Standard Insurance Limited, defendant No. 2, having received premium, issued on co-insurance basis, the Fire Insurance Policy No. 1-02-0010-0002-524-12-2001 (Co-insurance) dated 27-12-2001 in favour of Sonali Bank BB Avenue, Corporate Branch, as mortgagee and M/s Maq Enterprises Limited (the plaintiff) as mortgagor covering fire, lighting, R and SD and malicious damage risk of the items listed in the schedule to the aforesaid Insurance Policy for a total sum of Taka 14 crores. Thereafter on 12-12-2002, at night, a devastating fire broke out in the godown at the factory premises of the plaintiff; wherein 1992 MT. of insured duplex board was in godown No. 32 belonging to the insured/ plaintiff M/s. Maq Enterprises Ltd. was totally burnt. The plaintiff lodged a GD entry No. 900 dated 13-1412-2002 with Shyampur Police Station, Dhaka on the fire incident for further necessary action by them as per law. The plaintiff has informed the defendant No. 1 M/s Prime Insurance Company Ltd. On 13-12-2002 (Friday) over telephone and on 14-12-2002 in writing about the incident of fire on 12-12-2002. It caused a damage to the stock of duplex board in the godown No. 32 pledged with the bank and covered by the Fire Policy No. 1-02-0010-0002-524-12-2001 (Co-insurance) in favour of Sonali Bank, BB Avenue, Corporate Branch, Dhaka and A/C M/s Maq Enterprises Ltd. Issued by defendant No. 1 Prime Insurance Company Ltd. The defendant No. 1 has also been requested to take further necessary action as per law and usage in the matter and process payment of compensation to the plaintiff. On 14-12-2002 defendant No. 1, Prime Insurance Company Limited has appointed 2 (two) surveyors, namely, M/s. Rupali Surveyors, 19/E, Sheikh Shaheb Bazar Road, Dhaka and M/s. Jorip O-Paridarshan Co. Islam Chamber (13 floor), 125/A, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka-1000 to conduct joint survey and assess the extent of loss of the insured stores. The plaintiff has supplied all papers and documents as asked for and/ or as required by the surveyors in terms of the Insurance Policy directly and where necessary, through Sonali Bank, BB Avenue, Corporate Branch, Dhaka to facilitate speedy survey and assessment of loss. Thereafter on 14-12-2002 the surveyors appointed by the defendant No. 1, have visited the godowns in the premises of the factory of the plaintiff and on 21-12-2002 submitted a preliminary survey report to Prime Insurance Company Limited indicating huge loss due to fire and also resulting from use of water for extinguishing fire by the Fire Brigade and others in the midnight of 12-12-2002 pending further in-depth investigation of the cause and determination of the quantum of loss as well salvage. Then the plaintiff has formally lodged insurance claim for Taka 8,16,72,000 against Fire Policy No. 1-02-0010-0002-524-12-2001 (Co. Ins.) issued by Prime Insurance Company Limited, defendant No. 1 through Sonali Bank, BB Avenue, Corporate Branch, Dhaka, the Mortgagee, for the loss of insured stores in godown No. 32 as per requirement under the Insurance Policy, resulting from damage in the fire on 12-12-2002. The claim lodged under the joint signature of the plaintiff and the Sonali Bank, BB Avenue, Corporate Branch, Dhaka has been sent to the Prime Insurance Company Ltd., defendant No. 1, vide Letter No. BBA/ GAD-1/ MAQ BIMA dated 26-12-2002 of Sonali Bank, BB Avenue, Corporate Branch, Dhaka. The Officer-in-Charge of Shyampur Police Station, Dhaka investigated the fire incident as a follow up action of GD entry No. 900 dated 13-14.12.2002 and on 28-12-2002 submitted a report on the fire incident. A huge loss of stores in the fire has been reported by the police in their report. On 9-2-2003, Bangladesh Fire Service and Civil Defense, too have submitted a report on the relevant fire incident. They have stated in their report that fire has been caused by electric short circuit. They have assessed and valued the loss of stores in the fire in godown No. 32 at Taka 8 crores. The plaintiff as well their banker, the Sonali Bank, BB Avenue, Corporate Branch, Dhaka have almost continuously and diligently endeavoured by letters, telephones and through meeting at personal level with the ranking officers including the Managing Director to impress defendant No. 1, the Prime Insurance Company Ltd for expeditious settlement of the plaintiff's insurance claim. Defendant No. 1 has made promises several times but has miserably failed to act in the manner expected to them. They have attributed delay in payment of the claim during the period ending in May, 2004 non-receipt of Survey Reports from the Surveyors deployed by them, finally, after months of persuasion by the plaintiff. The Surveyors fielded by defendant No. 1 have submitted their Survey Reports on 29-5-2004 wherein loss has been assessed as follows:

6. Insured claimed fire loss of Taka 8,16,72,000 against 1,992 metric tons of duplex board stored in the above-mentioned godown. We have examined the entire stock of duplex board inside the above-mentioned godown carefully and scrutinised the related papers/ receipts, etc. made available.

7. As per records maintained by the insured and the Sonali Bank, BB Avenue, Corporate Branch, Dhaka, the stock of duplex board of different sizes/ weights were found as under in Godown No. 32 at the time of occurrence of fire 1,992 metric tons valued at 1,992 metric tons x Taka 41,000 = Taka 8,16,72,000 (Taka Eight Crores Sixteen Lac Seventy-two Thousand) only.

8. We have thoroughly investigated the loss and arrived at the following assessment on "Declaration basis" as contained in the relevant insurance policy. The prevailing market price of per metric ton of duplex board is more or less Taka 41,000 tallying with the declared price mentioned in the relevant insurance policy, hence, we have assessed the loss accordingly.

9. Value of stock as per Bank statement: Taka 8,16,72,000 (per ton Taka 41,000) Less 10% deterioration of quality for 2½ years long storage in the godown (—) Taka 81,67,200 = Taka 7,35,04,800. Less: 12% salvage value on Taka 3,99,95,500 against 975.50 metric tons fire and water affected duplex board found physically (—) Taka 47,99,450. Net assessed loss = Taka 6,87,05,340 (Taka six crores eighty seven lakh five thousand three hundred forty) only.

10. The surveyors were appointed by defendant No. 1, the Prime Insurance Company Ltd deducted 10% (Taka 81,67,200) only from the payable amount of the plaintiff's claim for so-called deterioration of quality of duplex board due to 2½ years long storage in the godown. This finding (determination of quality due to long storage) of the surveyors were vehemently objected to by the plaintiff vide letter dated 21-7-2004. The surveyors on reassessment in the light of the plaintiff's representations of their previous finding on deterioration of quality have on 1-12-2004 submitted a corrigendum to their joint final Survey Report eliminating deductions (of 10%) from the total assessed loss.
