Mr Hossain referreing section 23A of the Insurance Company Act, 1973 has submitted that in that section there is no such provision that re-insurer is the necessary party in the suit. He has further added that the plaintiff has no claim except the loss assessed by the surveyors. Therefore, there is no necessity of schedule in the plaint of the suit because the plaintiff in the plaint incorporated the whole survey report. He has further added that the suit is not bad for defect of party as claimed by the Appellant because against the re-insurer the plaintiff has no claim nor sought any reliefs and, as such, the re-insurer is not necessary party. He has categorically pointed out that the non examination of the makers of survey report has not made nugatory the result of the same and the suit, because the defendants in the written statement and through exhibit 5 and Uma admitted the claim of the plaintiff. He has further submitted that the Arbitration clause of the policy has become nugatory because defendants admitted plaintiff's claim vide their letter dated 17, July 2004 claiming the re-insurance claim to the Shadaran Bima Corporation.

41. He further reiterating the submissions of Mr Abdur Rahman submitted that the application for additional evidence cannot be entertained by this Court because the appellant of the First Appeal No. 82 of 2012 as defendant contested the suit by filing joint written statement along with defendant No. 1 and in the trial Court he did not raise any objection as to the grounds stated in the application for additional evidence and, as such, the same can't be accepted in the appellate stage. He has further added that in the Court below the defendant Appellants neither adduced any witness nor objected the plaintiff’s claim raising the point of contributory negligence. Rather, they admitted the claim of plaintiffs and, as such, they cannot raise said objection in the appellate Court. He further replied to the submissions of Mr Abdur Rahman that the plaintiff neither violated any clause of the Insurance policy nor negligent in respect of maintenance of the insured godown. More-so, the clauses and conditions of Insurance Policies as referred by Mr Abdur Rahman there was no complain by the insurer at the tenure of policy nor at the time of the trial before the court below. Furthermore till to day the appellants have failed to give any specific point of violation of the terms and condition of policy. Therefore, he argued that the submissions advanced by the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants do not bear any substance.

42. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of the respective parties. We are of the view that in respect of the submission of the learned Advocate for the appellant Mr Ariff that filing of the suit by the plaintiff instead of the Sonali Bank is not maintainable. In this regard to address the legal issue we can place reliance upon the principles enunciated by the Apex Court to the case of Janata Insurance Company Ltd. vs M/s Islam Steel Mills Limited reported in 15 MLR (AD) 478 = 63 DLR (AD) 5, wherein their Lordships held that:

"The general rule as regards an agent is that where person contracts as agent for a principal the contract is the contract of the principal and not that of agent; prima-facie as common law the person who may be sued is the principal and the only person who can be sued is the principal. Therefore, there is no legal bar that the contracts entered by the agent can be enforced by the principal in the same manner the agent can enforce the same of the obligations arising from the contract. Therefore, we find no substance in the objection raised by the learned Counsel that the suits at the instance of the plaintiffs are not maintainable."

43. On perusal of the said decision of our Apex Court, we are of the view that the principal or agent or of the party can file the suit for policy benefit, here the plaintiff Maq Enterprise is the principal and the Sonali Bank Limited, BB Avenue, Corporate Branch, Dhaka is the agent. So, according to us if the principal filed the suit there is no reason to deny the claim by the agent.

44. Furthermore, the agent has also no right or supervisory power over the principal. Herein the instant suit the Sonali Bank Limited as the pro-forma defendant did not speak so, as urged by the Appellant Counsel. So, we find substance in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1.

45. Next Mr AF Hassan Ariff, raised a question according to section 23A of the Insurance Corporation Act, 1973 claiming that the Sadharan Bima Corporation is the necessary party in the suit as required by statutory provision of law.

46. However, we have gone through the section 23A of the said Act which has already been quoted elsewhere in the judgment and wherefrom it is clear that it is the pre-condition upon every insurer that 50% of the re-insurable general insurance business shall be re-insured with Sadharan Bima Corporation. This provision of law is binding upon the Insurance Company in default every insurer would be penalised. On perusal of the provision of law of section 23A we find no direction or pre-condition that the re-insurer must be made party in claiming the insurance benefit under the agreement to contacting company. It is the cardinal principle of section 23A of the Insurance Corporation Act 1973 that all the insurer's must be re-ensured its 50% of insurance business to the Shadharan Bima Corporation which is the pre-condition as per the said section, however, nowhere in the language of the provisions of the section expressly indicate that re-insurer Shadharan Bima Corporation is the necessary party in the suit.

47. It would be noteworthy for convenience of the discussions and address the legal issues to decide whether the Shadharan Bima Corporation is the necessary or proper party in the suit. It is our considered view that:

A party may be considered as necessary party when two conditions must be satisfied, first, there must be a right to some relief against him in respect of the matter involved in the suit and, second, that his presence should be necessary in order to enable the court effectively and completely to adjudicate upon and settle the question involved in the suit."

48. More-so, in support of our view we are getting support from the principles enunciated by the Apex Court to the case of Mt. Jahan Ara Begum vs A. L. Md. Shamsul Hoque, reported in 27 DLR (AD) 129, wherein it has been held that: "Necessary party in a suit without whom an effective decree cannot be passed: Test as to who is a necessary party.

49. In the absence of a necessary party a decree cannot be made in favour of the plaintiff. The question as to what parties are necessary is often not easy to determine. One test which has been recognised as of great importance is that when in the absence of a party the court cannot give an effective remedy, that party is a necessary party.

50. From the above discussions it is depicted that the instant suit was filed against the insurer defendant appellants to realise the insurance claim money under agreement which was executed between plaintiff and defendants. Admittedly Shadharan Bima Corporation is a re-insurer of the insurer the plaintiff has no nexus with Shadharan Bima Corporation and, as such, the said Corporation not a necessary party to adjudicate the controversy in between plaintiff and defendants.

51. So, we are of the view that the argument launched by Mr AF Hassan Ariff, the learned Counsel for the appellant that the suit is bad for defect of party for non-impleading Sadharan Bima Corporation as defendant and the suit is not maintainable is not tenable in the eye of law.

52. In reply to the submission of Mr Ariff that Final Joint Survery Report material Exts. I-III was submitted before the trial Court but none was deposed in support of the report. Mr Mohammed Motahar Hossain, the learned Advocate for the respondent took us through Exhibit-5 dated 21-12-2002 the preliminary survey report which is in the paper book at page 87 wherefrom it appears that the defendants admitted the claim of the plaintiff sending a letter to the Sadharan Bima Corporation claiming 50% of the re-insurance money from them. He pointing out that since Exhibit-5 and material Exts. I-Ill are admitted facts and it was also not denied by the defendants in the trial Court. Now they cannot raise any objection denying the materials on record.

53. Now to substaint the admitted facts he referred to the case of Official Receiver of the High Court of Dacca and Official Liquidator of the Dass Bank Ltd vs Nabadwip Chandra Podder, reported in 27 DLR (AD) 133.

54. According to section 58 of the Evidence Act the admitted facts need not be proved. Herein according to Exthibit-5 and Uma are the two preliminary Survey Reports which have by both the parties been admitted in trial in presence of both the parties. Furthermore, material exhibits were not denied by the defendants in the trial Court.

55. So, we are of the view that non-examination of the maker of the reports, i.e. the surveyor does not made nugatory the contents of the report. So, in this regard we are of the further view that the argument launched by the learned Counsel of the appellant is not tenable in the eye of law as they did not raise any objection before the Court below.

56. In this regard reliance may be placed to the case of Joynal Abedin vs Mafizur Rahman reported in 44 DLR (AD) 162, wherein it has been held that:

"Secondary evidence, admissibility of certified copies of certain kabuliyats were filed without calling for the original copies. Learned Judge of the High Court Division on a wrong consideration of section 66 Evidence Act left those out of consideration treating them as inadmissible as the originals were not called for. But the documents having been filed and marked exhibits without any objection the question of inadmissibility of those documents cannot be raised at a subsequent point of time. The Court below acted wrongly in not considering the Kabuliyats Exhibit-D series and failed to consider the effect thereof and this has materially affected the decision in this case."

57. Mr AF Hassan Ariff and Mr Abdur Rahman, learned Advocates raised a question in respect of non-mentioning the schedule in the plaint at the time of their argument. They have pointed out that without mentioning claim in the schedule of the plaint they cannot claim the fire benefit. However, in reply of submission above Mr Hossain, argued that the plaintiffs has no claim for himself, but he has only claim as per preliminary report and final joint report of the surveyors. Therefore, he incorporated the whole survey report in the plaint as claimed and, as such, there is no necessity to mention the claim showing separate schedule in the schedule of the plaint.

58. We have gone through the plaint as well as the joint survey report incorporated in the plaint. Wherefrom it appears that the surveyors and the experts jointly prepared the report and submitted the same to the concerned authority i.e., the defendants insurers and to the plaintiff, none of them raised any objection against the said report to the Court below. So, it is apparent from the face of the record that the proposed claim of the plaintiff should not be scheduled in the plaint as he has no claim except the statements of reports as claimed and stated in the joint survey report. Therefore, we are of the view that in exceptional case like insurance claim when surveyors report not denied either of the parties in the suit there is no necessity to attach the schedule in the plaint when the joint survery report has been incorporated in the plaint claiming the said money in prayer portion. So, submission advanced that there is no schedule in the plaint, i.e. there is no statement of materials which is not fatal for this suit. Such an argument can be made on as usual case but not for exceptional case like insurance claim.

59. It further appears that in the present case fire broke out in the godown, all the godowns were under the Fire Policy. Out of which PW 1 categorically stated that godown No. 32 has been gutted by fire. So, they did not claim the total properties which were mortgaged to the Insurance Company, rather they claimed specifically which has been ascertained by jointly experts and surveyors without any objection from defendants. Therefore, we are of the view that the report submitted by the expert neither vague nor require any formal proof by examining any of the makers.

60. Mr Ariff and Mr Abdur Rahman, the learned Advocates jointly took us accordingly to them to actual position of godown of 32 stating that fire has been broken out for the contributory negligence. They argued that the expert does not clarify the actual cause of fire, rather they opined that the fire has been broken out due to short circuit wherein in the report there are some signs of smoking and there was an uninterrupted light in the godown and there also shortage of maintenance of the godown and electrical wiring.

61. In this regard in reply Mr Mohammed Mutahar Hossain and Mr Shah Mohd Ahsanur Rahman, the learned Advocates for the respondent strongly opposed the submissions of the Appellants Counsels and submitted that it is the duty of the insurer to make out the cause/ causes as to whether all the parts and parcel of the godowns were in a good condition or not.However, if there is any contributory negligence not on the part of the plaintiff but obviously it is a negligence of the insurer. They do not rebut the same neither in the written statement nor before the Court below in deposition and now, at the stage of appeal they cannot raise such a question which is a question of facts not of law.

62. From the arguments of both the parties it seems to us that either of the parties did not adduce any specific witness in the Court below to establish the case of contributory negligence. Moreover, no specific point has been argued before us. The defendants without raising the question of contributory negligence in written statement and without adducing any evidence on that plea in the Court below cannot be permitted to agitate before the appellate Court as it is a disputed question of facts not of law. We have gone through the materials on record but we find no reason in records to opine that there is any contributory negligence on behalf of the plaintiff. So, we are unable to accept the submissions of the learned Advocates for the appellants.

63. Mr Abdur Rahman the learned Advocate appearing in Fist Appeal No. 82 of 2012 on behalf of the Appellant has referred clause 18 of the contract wherein both the parties to the contract agreed that any dispute arises in between the parties regarding claim of benefit of insurance, in that case they should referred the matter to the Arbitration to settle the same, and, as such, the suit is not maintainable but the Court below without considering this aspect of the case passed the impugned judgment and decree and, as such, the same is liable to be discharged.

64. On the other hand Mr Hossain replied the submission of Mr Abdur Rahman stating that before filing the suit there was an appointment of surveyors by the appellant who submitted the report to the Appellants and Respondent in that time defendant appellants did not refer the matter in Arbitration as per claim of the plaintiff respondent. Even, at the time of trial the defendant Appellant did not file any application for Arbitration, even, did not raise any objection in the trial, therefore, the defendants Appellant waived the provision of Arbitration by implication and accepted the process of civil jurisdiction and, as such, after the judgment and decree they are not entitled to raise the question of Arbitration in this court in appellate forum.

65. We have perused the clause 18 of the Insurance Policy from which it appears that there is a provision for Arbitration however, on considering the materials on record it seems to us that the provision of Arbitration has become nugatory by implication and acceptance of the Civil Court process and, as such, the same is waived by the defendants because the defendant neither in the written statement nor at the trial raised the question of Arbitration. More specifically we are observing that the defendant after obtaining the Joint survey report did not take any step for Arbitration. Even, at the time of trial they did not file any application under section 10 of the Arbitration Act before the court below to stop the proceeding of this suit and refer the dispute in Arbitration which is permissible under the provision of section 10 of the Arbitration Act, 2001. Therefore, raising the said question after conclusion of trial and passing judgment and decree no legal scope to decide that the suit was not maintainable as argued by the learned Advocate for the Appellants, thus, we find no substance in the submission of the learned Advocates for the appellant.

66. Mr Abdur Rahman next raised the question of violation of the provision of clause of the insurance contract referring some sections of the said Act which have been mentioned elsewhere in the judgment. In this score on meticulous scrutiny the provision of the insurance agreement we find nothing specifically from the written statement, deposition of the DW 1. Moreso, it appears from the exhibits 1, 5 and Umma that contents of those exhibits were not denied by the defendants by implication of any provision of agreement as well as statutory provision of law as referred to us, therefore, we are of the view that there is no specific allegation for violation of any clause of insurance agreement which makes the claim of insurance benefit nugatory.

<u>67. The appellants of the First Appeal No. 82 of 2012 by filing an application sought for adducing additional evidence we have considered the submissions of Mr Abdur Rahman the learned Advocate for the appellant and gone through the application on perusing the same it appears that both the appellants contested the suit by filing joint written statement. In the Court below DW No. 1 deposed on behalf of the defendant No. 1 as well as defendant No. 2. The defendant No. 2 did not raise any objection nor filed any application for adducing further evidence. Rather, accepted all the activities of the DW 1 and defendant No. 1. So, according to the provision of Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure without raising any objection or filing any application regarding same subject which has not been rejected by the trial Court so, there is no scope to allow the application for additional evidence in the appellate Court. Moreso, when the judgment and decree was passed as admitted position of the surveyors report we do not find any reason for additional evidence to enable the Court to dispose of the appeal.</u>

68. Now we shall discuss regarding the Cross-Objection. The plaintiff filed a Cross-Objection being objection No. 1 of 2010 claiming interest from the date of fire and in support of the Cross objection Mr Shah Mohd Ahsanur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the respondent has referred section 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure vis-a-vis section 47B of the Insurance Act, 1938.

69. We feel it would be noteworthy and better for reference and discussions to quote the same herein below:

"S.34. Interest-(1) Where and in so far as a decree is for the payment of money, the Court may, in the decree, order interest at such rate as the Court deems reasonable to be paid on the principal sum adjudged, from the date of the suit to the date of the decree, in addition to any interest adjudged on such principal sum for any period prior to the institution of the suit, with further interest at such rate as the Court deems reasonable on the aggregate sum so adjudged, from the date of the decree to the date of payment, or to such earlier date as the Court thinks fit.

(2) Where such a decree is silent with respect to the payment of further interest on such aggregate sum as aforesaid from the date of the decree to the date of payment or other earlier date, the Court shall be deemed to have refused such interest, and a separate suit therefore shall not lie."

"S. 27B: Restriction on Certain Investments.-Except with the prior approval of the Board of Directors at a regularly convened meeting by the vote of not less than two-thirds of total number of directors and also upon a reference by the Board, of the Government, no insurer shall invest in, or hold any shares of debentures of any company, firm or other business concern in which any of its directors, or any member of the family of such director, has any interest as proprietor, partner, director, manager or managing agent:

Provided that no investment shall be permissible in the first issue of capital by a company, firm or other business concern in which any of the directors of the insurer or any member of the family of such director has any interest as proprietor, partner, director, manager or managing agent."

"S.47B: Interest on Late Settlement of Claims.-(1) Where payment on a policy issued by an insurer becomes due and the person entitled thereto has complied with all the requirements, including the filing of complete papers, for claiming the payment, the insurer shall, if he fails to make the payment within a period of ninety days from the date on which the payment becomes due or the claimant complies with the requirements, whichever is later, pay interest as specified in sub-section (2) on the amount so payable unless he proves that such failure was due to circumstances beyond his control."

(2)The interest under sub-section (1) shall be payable for the period during which the failure continues and shall be calculated at monthly rates at the rate of five per cent higher than the prevailing bank rate.

<u>70. The Insurance Act, 1938 as amended by Insurance (Amendment) Ordinance, 1970 inserting section 47B to 47L by section 27 of the said Ordinance. The sub-section (2) of section 47B provides the provisions of granting interest of claim amount. On perusal of sub-section (2) of section 47B of the Act it divulged that the granting of interest is mandatory not discretionary of the court. Hence, the statutory interest under section 47B of the said Act, the Court has no discretion in the matter.</u>

<u>71. We have gone through section 47B of the Insurance Act, 1938 as well as section 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure, wherefrom it appears that the Insurance Act is a special law which override the general law of Civil Procedure Code. More-so, in support of our view we can place reliance to the case of Chalna Marine Products Ltd. vs Reliance Insurance Ltd. reported in 50 DLR (AD) 100, wherein their lordships have held that-</u>

<u>"The plaintiff-appellant is entitled to the statutory interest under section 476 of the Insurance Act, 1938. The learned Judges failed to notice that the appellant is entitled to this statutory interest under the law and the court has no discretion in the matter. So, the Court below did not apply its mind in granting the interest which is not in accordance with law."</u>

72. Therefore, we find merit in the Cross Objection and, as such, the same is allowed. Therefore, it is hereby ordered that the plaintiff objector will be entitled to get interest from the date of occurrence i.e. fire took place on 12-12-2002 as per provision of section 476 of the Insurance (amendment by ordinance 1970) Act 1938.

73. Upon foregoing narrations and discussions, we are of the view that both the First Appeals having no merit, those failed.

74. In the result, both the First Appeals are dismissed without any order as to costs.

75. The impugned judgment and decree passed by the Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka on 7-6-2008 challenged in both the First Appeals are hereby affirmed.

The office is directed to send down the lower Court records with copy of this judgment at once.

End.

lawyer:
Sharif Bhuiyan with Moin Ghani and Tanim Hossain Shawon, Advocates ------ For the Plaintiff. 
Kamal-ul-Alam, Senior Advocate with Omar Sadat, Advocates ------ For the Defendant No. 9.
parties:
Asset Wonder Limited ------ Plaintiff
Vs
MV Athens (formerly MV Hansa) and others ------ Defendants.
full_judgment:
This is an application filed by the defendant No. 9 for vacating the order of arrest of the vessel MV Athens dated 24-11-2013.

2. Plaintiff filed the present Admiralty Suit against the defendants for recovery of its claim for a sum of USS 5,17,000 equivalent to Taka 4,01,96,750 from the defendants as damages and compensation for loss and damage suffered by the plaintiff resulting from collision between the plaintiff's vessel Ruby Star with the defendant No. 1 vessel MV Athens (formerly MV Hansa) IMO No. 8913667 occurred on 25-10-2013, now lying in the Jahanarabad Yard, Kadamrasul, Sitakunda, Chittagong. Upon an application filed by the plaintiff for arrest of the vessel MV Athens (ex MV Hansa) this court ordered for arrest of the said vessel on 24-11-2013.

3. Defendant No. 9 Arefin Enterprise, appeared in the suit on 13-1-2014 and filed the present application for vacating the order of arrest of the vessel MV Athens stating that this defendant opened Letter of Credit No. 1472-1302-0045 dated 7-11-2013 for importing the vessel namely MV Athens for scrapping the same as per Memorandum of Agreement dated 2-11-2013; that thereafter the defendant-applicant submitted Bill of Entry No. C-1407000 dated 10-11-2013 before the Customs Authority for releasing the same and after completion of all legal formalities got release order from Custom Authority started scrapping the vessel and as such it ceased to be vessel and lost its legal character to navigate; that the aforesaid vessel has been delisted from the shipping registry and the Government of Bangladesh has given all necessary permissions to beach and cut the same and when the vessel was beached it had lost its power to navigate on water and hence cannot be treated as a ship under the definition of a 'ship' as per section 2(b) of the Admiralty Court Act, 2000; that the plaintiff in its plaint clearly admitted that the plaintiff's claim in the present suit is for recovery of the alleged damages done by the defendant No. 1 vessel MV Athens on 25-10-2013 outside the territorial jurisdiction of Bangladesh and the defendants No. 3, 4 and 5 were the former owners on the date of occurrence of collision and the defendant No. 9 is the current owner of defendant No. 1 MV Athens and the vessel was purchased for the purpose of scrapping and at present lying at the beaching yard at Jahanarabad Yard, Kadam Rasul, Sitakunda, Chittagong. It was further stated that the said vessel arrived at Chittagong Port on 14-11-2013 and the said vessel was ready for scrapping on 16-11-2014. Thus it is apparent that at the date of filing of the present suit on 24-11-2014 the defendant Nos. 3, 4 and 5 are the previous owners of the defendant No. 1 vessel had no beneficial interest in the defendant No. 1 vessel and as such the suit is not maintainable within the jurisdiction of this Hon'ble Court. It was also stated that since the applicant has already started scrapping the vessel and as such the said vessel has become scrapped goods which lost the legal character to navigate either mechanically or legally as such the order of arrest cannot be sustained in the eye of law. It was also alleged that on the date of filing of the present suit and the order of arrest was made, the defendant No. 1 vessel was not a ship in the eye of law against which an action in rem could be initiated. With these averments, the plaintiff prayed for vacating the order of arrest on the ground of lack of jurisdiction and not maintainable in the eye of law and the order of arrest is liable to be vacated.

4. Against the application for vacating the order of arrest, plaintiff-opposite-party filed written objection dated 22-1-2014 stating, inter-alia, that the statement made in paragraph Nos. 5, 7 and 10 of the vessel are incorrect and not based on record. It appears from the documents filed by the defendant-applicant that the applicant did not obtain necessary permission for cutting the vessel on 10-11-2013 and 16-11-2013 when the vessel was released from the Customs Authority and all the aforesaid statements made with a view to mislead the court in order to avoid liability and the jurisdiction of the Hon'ble Court. The vessel MV Athens did not lose the nature and legal characteristic of a 'ship' as defined in section 2(b) of the Admiralty Court Act, 2000 when the order of arrest of the vessel was passed on 24-11-2013 or served on 25-11-2013. From the documents filed by the applicant, it transpires that defendant No. 9 did not obtain necessary permission for scrapping of the vessel MV Athens when the order of arrest of the vessel was passed on 24-11-2013. The said vessel was still afloat near the mouth of the beaching yard and had not been beached or scrapped on 25-11-2013, when service of the order of arrest was effected by the Marshall of this court on the vessel MV Athens. During the service, a staff of the plaintiff's counsel was also present and at the time of service the order of arrest by the Marshall, the vessel was afloat. It also appears that when the order of arrest was passed, necessary permissions for the scrapping of the vessel were not obtained as per the Ship Breaking and Recycling Rules, 2011. Particularly, the defendant No. 9 failed to produce the necessary environment clearance certificate from the Department of Environment and Treasury Challan in favour of the Ship Building and Ship Recycling Board ("SBSRB"), certificate from the Department of Explosives, Ship Recycling Plan (SRP) approved by the SBSRB and necessary cutting permission from the SBSRB which are all required before scrapping process can be started. The statement that the vessel MV Athens ceased to be a 'ship' as defined under section 2(b) of the Act, 2000 as soon as the ship entered the territorial water of Bangladesh, beached and lost its power to navigate on water is clearly misstatement of fact aimed at misleading this Hon'ble Court. It is a settled principle of law that the Admiralty Court has jurisdiction over any claim for damage done by any ship without any distinction as to whether the ship is a sea going ship or an inland ship. The expression 'ship' as defined in section 2(kha) of the Ain that is “জাহাজ” অর্থ নৌ পরিবহনে ব্যবহৃত হয় এমন যে কোন জলযান (vessel) অন্তর্ভূক্ত হইবে। In addition the Ship Breaking and Recycling Rules, 2011 in Rule 2 clearly defines a 'ship' means vessels and floating structures of any type operated in the marine environment and shall include submersibles, floating crafts, floating platforms, self-elevating platforms, floating Storage Unit, floating production storage units and offloading units, a vessel stripped of equipment or being towed destined for breaking purpose. Till 25-11-2013 the vessel was in a navigable condition as it was afloat near the beaching yard after being taken there by navigation. Since the necessary permissions for the scrapping of the vessel were not in place at the time of arrest of the vessel and the vessel was afloat at the time of the order of arrest, the vessel MV Athens did not cease to be a 'ship' within the meaning of law.

5. It further stated that damage caused by the defendant No. 1 vessel MV Athens was due to a collision outside the territory of Bangladesh does not deprive the Hon'ble Court of its jurisdiction over the claim for damage done by MV Athens. This court has jurisdiction over claim for damage which arises from collisions within or outside the country. The Admiralty Court has jurisdiction over ships lying within the territory of Bangladesh. Furthermore; the jurisdiction of this court is exercised in personam (against parties responsible for the ship) or in rem (against the ship) and in suits for damage done due to a collision, which gives rise to a maritime lien, the admiralty action in rem directed against the ship itself.

6. Mr Kamal-ul-Alam, Senior Advocate with Mr Omar Sadat, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant No. 9 firstly, submits that the plaintiff suit in action in rem is not entertainable within the jurisdiction of this court for non-fulfillment of the requirement of the provisions of section 4 (4) (ka) of the Admiralty Court Ain, 2000 (shortly, the Ain) as would be apparent from the provisions of law and the facts stated as admitted in the plaint of the present suit.

7. Secondly, he submits that the plaintiff has also brought the present Admiralty Suit in action in personam against the owners of the defendant No. 1 vessel disclosing the cause of action as arising out of a collision between the plaintiff's vessel RUBY STAR with the defendant No. 1 vessel MV Athens occurred in Hong Kong on 25-10-2013 beyond the territorial waters of Bangladesh as such the plaintiff suit in action in personam is not entertainable and maintainable within the jurisdiction of this Hon'ble Court for non-fulfillment of the provisions of section 5(1) (kha) and 5(5) of the said Ain.

8. He finally submits that the defendant No. 1 vessel MV Athens having had ceased to be a ship before the issuance and the service of order of arrest on 24-11-2013 within the meaning of ship as defined in section 2(kha) of the said Ain, the plaintiffs suit in action in rem against the defendant No. 1 vessel is not entertainable and amenable within the jurisdiction of this court under sections 2, 3 and 4 of the said Ain. In this connection Mr Alam has referred the case of Poplen Shipping Company Ltd. vs Commercial Union Assurance Company Ltd. (1943) 1 KB 161, Steed Man vs Scofield (1992) Lloyd's Law Reports, Vol-2163.

9. On the other hand, Dr Sharif Bhuiyan, with Mr Moin Ghani, and Mr Tanim Hussain Shawon, the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party. Dr. Sharif Bhuiyan, learned Advocate submits that the plaintiff invoked the Admiralty Jurisdiction of the Hon'ble High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh under sub-section (3) of section 4 of the Admiralty Court Act, 2000 in action in rem to enforce a maritime lien arising from the damages caused by the defendant No. 1-vessel MV Athens during a collision with the plaintiff's vessel Ruby Star on 25-10-2013.

10. He further submits that the opposite party has a maritime lien over the defendant No. 1 vessel and maritime lien under sub-section (3) of section 4 is independent of other sub-section of section 4 of the Admiralty Court Ain, 2000 and the claim does not arise from an action in personam as specified in section 5 of the Admiralty Court Ain, 2000. As such neither section 5 nor the sub-sections (1), (2), (4) or (5) of section 4 of the Ain have any manner of application to the invocation of the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court under sub-section (3) of section 4 of the Ain, 2000.

11. He next submits that in the present case the vessel (res) has been impleaded as defendant No. 1 and the defendant No. 2 has been described as "owners and parties interested in the defendant No. 1 vessel. The present owner of the res, the defendant No. 9 has been identified and impleaded in the suit does not mean that the suit ceases to be an action in rem.

12. He also submits that when the cause of action arose on 25-10-2013 and the relevant collision took place both the vessels involved in the collision were ships. Thus when the maritime lien arose the defendant No. 1 vessel was clearly a 'ship' and hence this court has jurisdiction under section 3(2) of the Admiralty Court Ain, 2000 and maritime lien attaches to every part of the ship and subsists till the lien is satisfied. In this respect learned Advocate refers to a decision reported in PLD 1986 Quetta 54.

13. Learned Advocate by referring the documents filed by the defendant No. 9 submits that the ship could not have been partially destroyed at the time of order of arrest which was issued on 24-11-2013 and on the same day the defendant No. 9 received a cutting permission from the Ministry of Industries and the order of arrest was served on 25-11-2013. Thus it is clear from the documents submitted by the defendant No. 9 that the vessel could not have destroyed to such an extent that it would ceased to be a ship.

14. Learned Advocate further referring Rule 1.4 of the Ship Breaking and Recycling Rule, 2011 which states that a ship delivered physically for recycling shall not be subject to any claim or maritime lien arising against any former owner of ship cannot affect the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court as stated in sub-section (3) of section 4 of the Ain.

15. He finally submits that the maritime lien could not have elapsed due to latches. In the present the cause of action arose on 25-10-2013 in Hong Kong and the plaintiff instituted the present suit on 25-11-2013 and on the same day order of arrest was issued, which clearly shows that there was no latches as submitted by the learned Advocate for the defendants. In support of his submissions he referred to the decisions reported in 20 BLD (AD) 230 = 5 BLC (AD) 169, 34 DLR (AD) 110. He also relied British Shipping Laws, Volume 14 the Book Maritime Liens by Dr. Thomas.

16. The prime question to be decided in this suit as raised by the learned Advocate for both the parties that whether the plaintiff has a maritime lien over the defendant No. 1 vessel arising out of the damage caused during the collusion between the vessel Ruby Star and MV Athens in Hong Kong and whether the plaintiff is entitled to invoked the Admiralty Jurisdiction of this court to enforce action in rem to enforce maritime lien under section 4(3) of the Admiralty Court Ain, 2000 arising from damages caused by the MV Athens formerly MV Hansa during a collision with the plaintiff's vessel Ruby Star on 25-10-2013 in Hong Kong.

18. On plain reading of the plaint, it appears, that the vessel has been impleaded as defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 2 has been described as "owners and parties interest in" the defendant No. 1 vessel and the defendant No. 9 is the current owner of the ship, who purchased the defendant No. 1 vessel for scrapping. It may be stated that clause (kha) of section 2 of the Ain defines the 'ship' which has been defined in the same and identical language in section 24(1) of the Supreme Court Act, 1981 and British Administration Justice Act, 1956 and said provision has been laid down in Admiralty Jurisdiction High Courts Ordinance No. (XLIII of 1980) Pakistan wherein the "ship includes any description of vessel used in navigation." It may be also be pointed out that in clause (56) of section 3 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 also defined as 'vessel', shall include any ship or boat or any other description of vessel used' in navigation.

19. Mr Kamal-ul-Alam, learned Senior Advocate for the defendant No. 9 submits that MV Athens is not 'ship' as defined in section 2(kha) of the Ain and section 2(47) of the Merchant Shipping Ordinance 1983, since the vessel has been beached in the beaching yard for scrapping, the vessel will cease to have its mechanised navigability and as such will cease to be a 'ship' to be used in navigation within the ambit of clause (kha) of section 2 of the Ain. In support of this submission Mr Kamal-ul-Alam, learned Senior Advocate cited the case of Polen Shipping Company Limited vs Commercial Union Assurance Company Limited, 1 KB (1942) 161. The facts and circumstances of the case reported in 1 KB (1942) 161 are however, quite different. In the cited case the question before a learned Single Judge of the Kings Bench was whether a floating boat was a ship or vessel within the meaning of insurance policy under which the plaintiff was claiming on account of collision between the vessel and the above floating boat. It was held that a ship or a vessel is a hollow structure intended to be used in navigation, that is, to do its real work on the seas or other waters and capable of free and ordered movement thereon from one place to another. It was further held that floating boat did not fit in within the definition of ship and vessel and, therefore, there was no collision between the two vessels in terms of the insurance policy.

20. It may be pointed out that the arrest of a ship in an action in rem under Admiralty Jurisdiction is not an interlocutory order, the very jurisdiction of the Admiralty court is founded on the arrest of the vessel this is the essence of the procedure of action in rem. The arrest of the defendant vessel, on the filing the plaint and the application for arrest is the assumption of jurisdiction by court. The jurisdiction is founded on the presence of the vessel in the territorial waters of Bangladesh and the arrest of the vessel to answer to the claim of the plaintiff and providing security for such claim.

21. It may be stated that the Ain is more or less reproduction of the Supreme Court Act, 1981 with certain additions and modifications, in which, in sub-section (1) of section 24, the word 'ship' has been defined in identical language as has been employed in clause (kha) of section 2 of the Ain i.e. 'ship' includes, any description of vessel used in navigation'. It may also be pointed out that in clause (56) of section 3 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, the word 'vessel has been defined as 'vessel shall include any ship or boat or any other description of vessel used in navigation.'

22. From the definition of the word 'ship' given in the Admiralty Court Act, 1981, definition of the 'vessel' given in the General Clauses Act, 1897 and the case cited by the learned Advocate for the defendant it is evident that every floating structure in the water cannot be considered as a ship or vessel, but in order to bring a floating structure within the ambit of the definition of the 'ship' in the Ain or the aforesaid Act, or within the purview of clause (56) of section 3 of the General Clauses Act, it is necessary that the floating structure should be navigable. In other words the floating structure should be capable of encountering perils of sea and should have characteristic of a vessel.

23. In the present case, as the vessel was already beached in the beaching yard at the time of filing of the above suit, the contention of Mr Kamal-ul-Alam, learned counsel for the defendants, that the vessel ceased to be navigable within the purview of clause (kha) of section 2 of the Ain, is not devoid of force. However, this does not necessarily lead to the conclusion that the above suit under the admiralty jurisdiction in terms of the Ain are not competent, if the plaintiffs had maritime lien over the vessel, the above suits are competent.

24. It appears that the plaintiff in their plaint averred that on the filing of the suit and on the date of service of notice of arrest upon the defendant vessel was afloat in the Jahanabad beaching yard. Thus the submission made by the learned Senior Advocate Mr Kamal-ul-Alam within the purview of clause (kha) of section 2 of the Ain is not devoid of force.

25.
