full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, C.J: I have had the advantage of going through the judgments proposed to be delivered by my learned brothers, A.T.M. Afzal and Latifur Rahman, JJ; I concur with the judgment of A.T.M. Afzal, J.

M.H. Rahman, J: I have gone through the judgments written by learned brothers, A.T.M. Afzal and Latifur Rahman, JJ .; I concur with the judgment of A.T.M. Aizal, J.

A.T.M. Afzal, J: This appeal by the plaintiff-appellants following leave is from Judgment and Order dated 12 August. 1985 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court Division (at Comilla) in revision, Civil Revision No. 1807 of 1981 discharging the Rule and upholding the concurrent decision of the courts below dismissing the suit being Title Suit No.4 of 1975 of the Second Court of Assistant Judge, Brahmanbaria.

4. Plaintiffs instituted the aforesaid suit for a declaration that the declaration of the suit property as enemy property under Memo No. 1587(29)E.P. dated 27.3.1967 of defendant no.1 and lease order in favour of defendant no.3 under Memo no.1141 E.P. dated 29.8.74 of defendant no.2 are illegal, ultravires, without jurisdiction etc and further for permanent injunction against the said defendants restraining them from interfering with the suit property.

5. The suit was in respect of two schedules of property, 'A' and 'IV'. The total area of A schedule land is 2.31 dec. out of which 1.01 dec. was declared as enemy property. The total land in B schedule is .22 dec. out of which .06 d was declared as enemy property. Plaintiffs case is that A schedule land belonged to 3 brothers in ejmali, namely, Shashi Kumar Paul, Jagneswar Paul and Harimohan Paul. Shashi Kumar Paul gifted his 1/3 share in favour of his two sons, Sudhir Chandra Paul, proforma defendant no.4, Trailakya Nath Paul and wife Shantimayee Paul. Jagneswar Paul gifted his 1/3rd share to his wife Muktakeshi Paul. Harimohan Paul gifted his 1 share to his wife Barada Sundari Paul, plaintiff no.1. All the three gifts were by registered instruments. All the three brothers thereafter died. Muktakeshi Paul then died leaving three Sons, plaintiff no. 4 Ahindra Chandra Paul, proforma-defendant no.5, Surendra Chandra Paul and the predecessor of proforma defendant nos.6-9 Rebati Mohan Paul. Plaintiff no.1 verbally gifted her -/14/- annas share to her two Sons, Plaintiff nos.2 and 3 in equal shares and she herself retained -/2/- annas share therein.

6. Harimohan Paul was the absolute owner in possession of B schedule Land. He was survived by his four sons i.e. plaintiffs nos.2 and 3 and Himangshu Bhushan Paul and Arunangshu Bhushan Paul and wife plaintiff no. Plaintiffs case is that Harimohan Paul gifted some portion of B schedule land to his wife, plaintiff no.1 and on Harimohan Paul's death there was amicable partition among his heirs in consequence of which the remaining portion of B schedule land fell in the exclusive share of plaintiff nos. 2 and 3. Trailakya Nath Paul and Shantimayee Paul sold their share to defendant no.3 who again sold the same to plaintiff nos.I-3 and proforma-defendant nos. 4 and 5. Since defendant no.3 failed to execute a kabala, plaintiffs no.1-3 and pro-defendant nos.4 and 5 filed Title Suit no.207 of 1974 in the Second Court of the Subordinate Judge, Comilla for specific performance of contract.

7. The plaintiffs leased out 'A' schedule property to Alizan Jute Mill and 'B' schedule property to C.I. Jute who paid rent to the plaintiffs. Plaintiffs nos. 1-3 are absolute owners in exclusive possession of the entire B schedule land. The properties of both the schedules have not been divided by metes an bounds among the respective co-sharers and they are all possessing and enjoying the property in question together jointly. Plaintiffs further case is that the defendants in collusion with each other declared the suit properties as enemy property as stated above and defendant no.3 was granted lease of the said enemy property in E.P.L. Case no. 10 of 1974-75 under Memo no.1141 E.P. on 29.08.1974. Hence the suit.

8. Defendants no.2 and 3 filed separate written statements but taking almost the same grounds. Besides denying the claim of the plaintiffs, the defendants raised several objections including that of maintainability of the suit, limitation etc. Defendants main case was that the real owners of the disputed property had left for India for good and have been residing there permanently. The suit property became enemy property by operation of law and was declared as such by the impugned memo dated 27.3.1967 and lease was validly granted to defendant no.3 who has been possessing the suit land.

9. The trial court found that the suit was barred by limitation, that it was not maintainable in its present from, that the deed of gift Ext. 1(a) created no interest in favour of plaintiff no.1 and so her subsequent transfer by alleged oral gift created no interest in favour of plaintiffs no. 2 and 3 and that the plaintiffs failed to prove their case. It was also found that "As Himangshu. Arunangshu will equally get the properties of the L. Hari Mohan they are necessary parties but the plaintiffs have not made them party in this suit. So the Suit is bad for defect of parties also."With these findings the suit was dismissed by judgment and decree dated 31 July, 1976.

10. On appeal by the plaintiffs. Title Appeal no.133 of 1976 the learned Subordinate Judge, Brahmanbaria reversed the findings of the trial court as to limitation etc. but agreed only with the finding that the suit was bad for defect of parties saying "As the plaintiffs could not produce sufficient evidence to show that there was any amicable partition. Himangshu and Arunangshu have left their shares. They have not been added as parties in the suit".

11. The learned Subordinate Judge, however, held that since the plaintiffs are co-sharers of the suit property, the defendants cannot take over possession of the land and lease out the same without a partition of the shares of Himangshu and Arunangshu and that the alleged declaration of the suit property as enemy property and the lease order in favour of defendant no.3 are illegal. But the appeal was ultimately dismissed by judgment and decree dated 29 July, 1981 holding that the plaintiffs are not entitled to get any decree.

12. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree, the plaintiffs took a revision to the High Court Division as stated above in which the impugned judgment and order were passed. The defendants, however, did not move against the judgment of the learned Subordinate, Judge and thereby accepted the findings made against them.

13. It appears from the impugned Judgment that the only issue raised before and considered by the High Court Division was whether the learned Subordinate Judge erred in holding that the suit was bad for defect of parties. On behalf of the appellants it was urged that since they were admittedly co-sharers in possession of the disputed property and were not claiming anything adverse to the interest of Himangshu and Arunangsu they were not necessary parties in the suit. On the other hand, the learned Advocate for the Government argued that since the alleged amicable partition among the co-sharers was not accepted by the court below Himangshu and Arunangshu were necessary parties and their absence caused an incurable defect of party in the suit.

14. The learned Judge of the High Court Division observed that when the plaintiffs want a declaration in respect of the entire unpartitioned suit land, all the co-sharers thereof ought to have been made parties in the suit because no declaration can be given in respect of the entire suit land even if one co-sharer is left out. Being of such view the learned Judge agreed with the finding of the Courts below as to defect of party and accordingly discharged the Rule.

15. It will be evident from the above narration that the plaintiffs were non-suited only on the ground that Himangshu and Arunangshu, their co-sharers in the suit land, were not made parties to the suit. Leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division was right in holding in the circumstances of the case that the suit was bad for defect of party and was liable to be dismissed altogether on that ground.

It has already been notice that the suit involved two schedules of property A and B. A schedule comprised of 2.31 dec. of land out of which 1.01 dec. was declared as enemy property and leased out to defendant no.3. B schedule land comprised of .22 dec. out of which .06 dec was similarly leased out to defendant no.3 as enemy property has also been noticed that the plaintiffs are the only co sharers in A schedule land and Himangshu and Arunangshu have no share therein. It is only in B schedule land that Himangshu and Arunangshu are admittedly co-sharers of the Plaintiff's. The plaintiffs setup a case of amicable partition in B schedule land pursuant to which plaintiffs no.2 and 3 claimed to have obtained the shares of Himangshu and Arunangshu. The case of amicable partition was not however, accepted by the court of appeal below and therefore, the question of defect of party arose in the absence of Himangshu and Arunaugshu who were not made parties to the suit.

16. The plaintiffs have been found to be co sharers in the suit property by the learned Subordinate Judge. There is no finding by any of the courts that any co-sharer in A schedule land has been left out and not made a party in the suit. There is no finding by any of the courts that the suit property became enemy property under the law and vested in the Government subsequently, rather the learned Subordinate Judge has categorically found that the declaration of the suit property as enemy property and the lease order in favour of defendant no.3 are illegal. This finding has not been challenged by the respondents at any stage thereafter. Mr. Moksudur Rahman, learned Advocate, entered appearance for respondents no.1 and 2 in this appeal without filing any concise statement and therefore be was not entitled to be heard at all under the Rules of this. Court. This, however, does not matter much because the, respondents never challenged the said finding in the High Court Division but concentrated only on the ground of defect of party. In such circumstances we do not see how the courts could refuse a decree in favour of the plaintiff at least in respect of A schedule land in which Himangshu and Arunangshu are not co-sharers. We are of the view that having regard to the facts of the case and the findings made by the learned Subordinate Judge himself the dismissal of the suit altogether was clearly illegal.

17. As regard B schedule land it appears that there is some confusion in the findings of the learned Subordinate Judge with regard to the non-inctusion of Himangshu and Arunangshu in the suit and its effect thereon. Plaintiff no.2 deposing as P.W.1 in 1976 admitted that Himangshu and Arunangshu are staying in India but it is nobody's case that they were enemy within the meaning of rule 161 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules 1965 and their shares in B schedule land became enemy property within the meaning of rule 169(4) of the said Rules. The learned Subordinate Judge himself noticed that the defendants have not specifically stated in their written statement as to who were the persons who having left for India became Indian Nationals and their shares became enemy property. In one place of the Judgment the learned Subordinate Judge has expressed the view that since amicable partition was not proved and there being no evidence that Himangshu and Arunangshu have left their shares, non-inclusion of them in the suit, who were admittedly co-sharers, rendered the suit bad for defect of parties. It appears however, from his ultimate finding that he has treated the shares of Himangshu and Arunangshu as enemy property (without any basis) as they are living in India and held that without a partition of the suit property in respect of their sheres the defendants cannot take over possession of the suit land and lease out the same. If Himangshu and Arunangshus share is treated as enemy share then there is no question of defect of parties because the enemy will he taken to be represented by the Assistant Custodian, Enemy Property (Land and Building) respondent no. 1. The view taken by the learned Subordinate Judge that the defendants cannot take over possession without a partition of the suit land in respect of the shares of Himangshu and Arunangshu (if they are enemy) is fully in accord with the law laid down in the case of Benoy Bhushan Vs. S.D.O. Brahmanharia, 30 DLR(SC)(1978) 139, We do not, therefore, see how the plaintiffs could be refused the relief of injunction at least even in respect of B schedule land after having made the finding as aforesaid.

18. These aspects of the matter have not been considered at all by the learned Judge of the High Court Division.

19. The question whether in a suit like this all the co-sharers of a joint land must be made patties may now be examined. Can one or more co-sharer in exclusive possession of a joint property maintain a suit against a third party for protecting the interest of the said co-sharers without making the entire body of co-sharers as parties in the suit is the question.

20. Mr. S.S. Haider, learned Advocate for the appellants, has submitted that the plaintiffs being admittedly co-sharers in possession of the entire land and the suit being for the benefit of all the co-sharers and there being no possibility of any decree which is likely to be prejudicial to the interest of other co-sharers only, the suit cannot fail on the ground of alleged defect of party. Mr. Haider has referred to Order I Rule of 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure and argued that in any case the suit could not be defeated because nonjoinder of Himangshu and Arunangstu as the Court could decide the matter in controversy so far as regards the rights and interests of the parties actually before it. He drew our attention to Abdul Rahman Vs. Abdul Jabbar, 13 D.L.R. 576 in which a Division Bench held that a suit can proceed when the rights of an absent party are not affected by the decision.

<u>21. In immovable properties owned jointly each co-owner has the Tight irrespective of the quantum of his share, to be in possession of every part and parcel of the properties jointly with the other and possession of one co-sharer is in law possession of others as well. Plaintiffs no.1-3 being co-sharers had the right to be in possession of the entire undivided B schedule land and their possession was also the possession of their co-sharers, i.e., Himangshu and Arunangshu. It is a settled law and there is a catena of decisions in support that one of the co-owners can bring a suit for ejecting a trespasser from the property owned by him and others either jointly or as co-owners, the basis being that he has a right to hold every inch of the joint property until a partition takes place. There has been a controversy, however, as to whether a co-sharer can by himself recover possession of the entire joint land or is entitled to joint possession only with the trespasser. In Joygopal Vs. Prabodh, 40 C.W.N 81 Nasim Ali, J. sitting in a Division Bench said that the practice in Calcutta High Court has been all along to give the co-sharer a decree for joint possession with the trespasser, leaving the plaintiff to work out his further rights by a separate suit for partition. Similar view was taken by Chowdhury, J in Hassain Ali Vs. Khoka Mulla, 16 D.L.R(Dhaka) 355. It was, however, observed by Chowdhury J that if the plaintiffs would have been in possession of the (entire) land, they would be entitled to retain the whole of it irrespective of the share held by them. As to the main question whether the suit was bad for defect of party it was held with reference to several decisions or other High Courts that it is a well-settled principle of law that a suit against a trespasser is maintain able by one of the co-sharers. In the case of Abdur Rahman Vs. Prafulla Chandra, 13 D.LR. 865 Sattar J. took the same view that the suit at the instance of some co-sharers who were in exclusive possession of a joint property for recovery of possession against a trespasser is maintainable and therefore the failure to implead the other co-sharers as parties to the suit will not affect the plaintiffs' right to recover possession from the defendant who was trespasser having no title to the property.</u>

<u>22. The question in the present case is not of recovery of possession from a trespasser but one of maintaining possession against a third party (would be trespasser) having no title by some co-sharers who are in exclusive possession of the joint land. In our view, in view of the uniform judicial opinion as to the maintainability of a suit by one co-sharer only against a trespasser, a suit by some of the co sharers in exclusive possession for warding off an invasion to the rights of the said co-sharers of a join property, as in the present case, stands in principle and jurisprudence on a firmer ground and is clearly maintainable. Further, Mr. Haider rightly contended that there was no occasion for affecting the interest of Himangshu and Arunangshu in any way in this suit and as such the Court could proceed to decide the rights of the parties actually before it.</u>

23. The position in law undoubtedly is that in the absence of necessary parties a decree will not be passed in favour of the plaintiff. As to who is a necessary party in a suit one test which has all along been recognized as of great importance is that when in the absence of a party the Court cannot give an effective remedy that party is a necessary party. There is, however, always a distinction between a necessary party and a proper party. A suit will inevitably fail in the absence of a necessary party but it may not be always so in the case of a proper party. In the present case Himangshu and Arunangshu are not necessary parties because the Court can give an effective remedy as prayed for in the suit in their absence. They may be made defendants in the suit as proper parties being co-sharers but the suit cannot fail in their absence because their rights as co sharers are not at all affected by the decree to be passed in the suit and further, as already stated, the settled law is that a co-sharer in exclusive possession is alone entitled to maintain a suit against an intruder without joining other co sharers.

24. In view of the discussion above, we are clearly of the opinion that the learned Judge of the High Court Division without properly considering the scope of the suit and the legal position as to maintainability of a suit of this nature by one or more co-owners of a joint property took a wrong view in the matter causing a failure of justice. It has been wrongly held that the suit is bad for defect of party. The judgment and decree of the Courts below are liable to he set aside.

25. In the result, therefore, this appeal is allowed without any order as to cost. The Judgment and decree of the courts below are set aside and the suit is decreed. It is hereby declared that the declaration of the suit property as enemy properly under Memo No.1587(29) E.P. dated 27.3.67 of defendant No.1 and lease order in favour of defendant No.3 under Memo No.1141 E.P. dated 29.8.74 of defendant No.2 are illegal. inoperative a with out Jurisdiction. The defendants are restrained by permanent injunction from interfering in any manner with the suit land.

Latifur Rahman, J.- Upon reading , the Judgment of my learned brother A.T.M. Afzal, J. I find it difficult to agree with the same. Hence I am writing a separate Judgment in this Case.

27. The plaintiff-appellants filed the instant suit for declaration that the suit property is not an enemy property and for permanent injunction. In the suit, the reliefs sought for in prayer No.1, is for a declaration that treating of the suit property as enemy property by defendant No.1 and the lease order granted by defendant No.2 in favour of defendant No. 3, be declared illegal, ultravires, without Jurisdiction, inoperative, void abinitio and are of no effect in the eye of law. In prayer No.5 the prayer is for granting permanent injunction on hearing the suit on merit and further defendant Nos. 1-2 be restrained from inducting defendant No.3 in the suit property and also for an injunction restraining defendant No.3 by way of a temporary injunction pending hearing of the Suit on merit.

28. All the courts below including the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division found the suit not maintainable for defect of parties as necessary parties were not impleaded in spite of objection raised at the trial.

29. Thus the main question is, whether the suit has been rightly dismissed for non impleading necessary parties which is a pre requisite in law for proper constitution of the suit.

30. In order to appreciate the case of the plaintiff it will be necessary to refer to the plaint case and the averments made therein. The suit land consists of two schedules, schedule 'A' consists of 2.31 decimals of which 1.01 was declared as enemy property and schedule 'El' property comprises .22 acres of land of which .06 was taken over as enemy property. The plaint case is that, Shashi Kumar Paul. Jagneswar Paul and Hori Mohan Paul were 3 brothers and they have equal shares in schedule 'A' Property. Shashi Kumar Paul made a gift by registered deed of his 1/3rd share of 'A' schedule properties in favour of his 2 sons, Sudhir Chandra Paul (proforma-defendant No.4), Sri Lakkhinath Paul and wife Santimayee Paul. Another brother Jugneswar Paul made a gift by registered deed of his 1/3rd share of 'A' schedule properties in favour of his wife Mukta Kashi Paul. Hari Mohan Paul also made a gift by registered deed of his 1/3rd share of 'A' schedule property in favour of his wife plaintiff No.1, Barada Sundari Paul. Thereafter all the 3 brothers died and the afore-mentioned persons got the land of 'A' schedule property and owing and possessing the same in "ejmali" to the extent of their respective shares. Mukta Kashi Paul died leaving 3 sons plaintiff No. 4, Ahindra Chandra Paul, proforma defendant No.5, Srendra Chandra Paul and Rebati Mohan Paul, the, predecessor of proforma defendant Nos.6-9 and they inherited their share in the 'A' schedule properties and amongst other properties. Plaintiff No.1 wife of Hari Mohan Paul verbally gifted 14 annas thares out of her 1 shares in the 'A' schedule properties to her 2 sons i.e. plaintiff Nos.2-3 in equal share and she herself retained 2 annas shares therein. In this way plaintiff Nos.2 and 3 are also cosharers in the 'A' schedule properties. Harimohan Paul died leaving behind 4 sons, plaintiff Nos. 2, 3 and Himangshu Bhusan Paul and Arunangshu Bhusan Paul and wife plaintiff No.1 as his heirs. Hari Mohan Paul was also the absolute owner in possession of the 'B' schedule properties. While alive Hari Mohan Paul made a gift of some portion of the 'B' schedule properties in favour of his wife plaintiff No.1. After his death his 4 sons and wife inherited the remaining portion of B schedule properties among other properties. According to the plaint case amicable partition took place among the co-sharers heirs whereupon the remaining portion of 'B' schedule properties fell in the exclusive saham of plaintiff Nos.2 and 3 and in this way plaintiff Nos. 1, 2 and 3 are the absolute owners in exclusive possession of the entire 'B' properties. It was further averred that the right, title and interest of Plaintiff Nos. 1-3 and their co-sharers Himangshu Bhusan Paul and Arunangshu Bhusan Paul were established in Title Suit No.69 of 1948 of the Court of 2nd Sub-Judge. Comilla. Further, the properties of both the schedules have never been divided by metes and bounds amongst the respective 'C' sharer-owners and they are all jointly possessing and enjoying the suit properties. It is further stated that some of the co-sharers in 'A' schedule properties sold their shares in the said properties to defendant No. 3. Thus, defendant No. 3 also became a co-sharer in the 'A' schedule properties and remained there for a very short period of time without exercising any right of ownership and possessed therein. Immediately thereafter defendant No.3 sold his purchased share in the 'A' schedule properties to plaintiff Nos.1-3 and proforma defendant Nos.4 and 5. Defendant No.3 is a stranger in the 'A' schedule properties after the aforesaid sale. Defendant No.3 even after receiving the consideration money did not execute any document and hence plaintiff No 1-3 and proforma defendant Nos.4 and 5 filed Title Suit No. 207 of 1974 in the Court of 2nd Subordinate Judge, Comilla against the principal defendant No.3 for specific performance of contract and the suit is now pending. It is further stated that principal defendant No.3 by influencing the other principal defendants illegally declared the aforesaid portion of schedules 'A' and 'B' property as enemy property. Having learnt that plaintiff Nos. 1, 2 and 3 have brought Title Suit No.124 of 1974 in the Court 2nd Munsif, Brahmanbaria covering 1/3rd share of 'A' schedule properties and the entire 'B' schedule properties for a declaration that the same cannot be legally declared and taken over as enemy property. After institution of that suit, the plaintiffs and their co-sharers came to know that some unspecified share of 'A' and 'B' schedule properties have been declared as enemy properties under memo No.1587(29) E.P. Dated 27.3.67. Hence the suit.

31. In this case two set of written statements have been filed, one by defendant No. 2 Sub-Divisional Officer, Brahmanbania wherein it was specifically stated that the suit was bad for defect of parties amongst other averments supporting the treating of the property as enemy property by Memo No. 1587(29) B. P. dated 23.6.67. Another written statement was tiled on behalf of defendant No.3 Haji Abdul Jalil wherein question of defect of parties was specifically raised along with challenging the gift made by Harimohan Paul in favour of his wife plaintiff No.1 and also the case of the plaintiff that by amicable partition the, remaining portion of 'B' schedule properties went to plaintiff Nos.2 and 3.

32. In the plaint it has been specifically averred that the properties of both the schedules had never been divided by metes and bounds among the co-sharers and by amicable partition amongst the co-sharers the remaining portion of 'B' schedule properties fell in the exclusive saham of plaintiff Nos. 1 and 3 and thereby plaintiff Nos. 1, 2 and 3 are absolute owners in exclusive possession of the entire 'B' schedule properties. It is also admitted in the plaint that Harimohan Paul did leaving behind wife, plaintiff No. 1.4 sons plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 and Himangshu Bhusaan Paul and Arunangshu Bhusan Paul (not impleaded as parties in the suit). Further, paragraph 16 of the plaint reads as follows:-

"That the petition of the principal defdt. No.3 submitted in the E.P.Case No.10/74-75 on which the principal defdt. No.2 passed an order on 27.8.74 specifically speaks that the suit properties belong to the plff. Nos.1,4 and others. So the plff. have come up with this suit and their co-sharers have been made proforma defdts. If any of the proforma defdt. contests the suit he may be treated as a principal defdt." Admittedly these two Sons of Harimohan Paul were not made parties in the suit and hence the pertinent question for consideration in this appeal is, whether for non inclusion of these two co-sharers as parties any incurable defect has arisen for which the suit must fail.

33. In the back ground of the plaint case, it will be worth while to refer to the material findings of all the courts below touching on the legal question of maintainability of the suit for to impleading necessary parties. The trial Judge held in his judgment as follows:-

"The plaintiffs admitted in para-4 of the plaint that Hari Mohan survived by 4 Sons plaintiffs 2 and 3. Himasngshu Bhusan and Arunangshu Bhusan Paul and plaintiff No.1. As Himangshu. Arunangshu will equally get the properties of the L. Hari Mohan they are necessary parties but the plaintiffs have not made them party in this party. So the suit is had for defect of parties also."

The lower appellate court while agreeing with the finding of the trial court on this material question observed as follows:-

"Admittedly the two Sons of Harimohan Paul Himangshu and Arunangshu are in India. As the plaintiffs could not produce sufficient evidence to show that there was any amicable partition. Himangshu and Arunangshu have left their shares. They have not been added as parties in the suit. So there arises the question whether the suit is bad for defect of parties. The learned Advocate for the appellants submitted that Himangshu and Arunangshu are not necessary parties. In the suit. land in this connection the learned Advocate referred to the case of Abdur Rahman Vs. Profulla Chandra, reported in 13 D.L.R. at page 865. The cited case refers to a suit at the instance of some co-sharers who were in exclusive possession of a joint property for recovery of possession against the trespasser and I do not find any substance in the argument of the learned Advocate to apply the cited case in the instant case. The learned Advocate also referred to another case reported in 22 D.L.R (Dac) page 269 only to argue that the benamdars are not necessary parties in a suit. I do not find any reason as to why Himangshu and Arunangshu being co-sharers in the suit land have not been made parties and I hold that the suit is bad for defect of parties. Point No.2 is accordingly disposed of."

The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division found that partition of 'A' and 'B' schedule properties have not taken place by metes and bounds and that the story of amicable partition of 'B' schedule property has not been proved in this case and in that view both Himangshu and Arunangshu were necessary parties as found by both the courts below. The learned Single Judge further found as follows:-

"It is not known what the left-out co-sharers would say if they are given an opportunity to contest the suit. They may not support the story of amicable partition or they may not support the title and ownership of plaintiff Nos. 1-3 in 'B' schedule properties at all. As such Himangshu and Arunangshu are necessary parties in this suit and their exclusion has caused an incurable defect of party in the suit itself. I find it difficult to see how the plaintiffs can say that they have filed this suit for and on behalf of the left-out co-sharers. when they want a declaration in respect of the entire unpartitioned suit land, all the co-sharers of the unpartitioned land must be made parties thereto. No declaration can be given in respect of the entire suit land even if one co sharer is left out. It cannot be assumed that the left-out co-sharers would have supported the plaintiffs, had they been joined. They might have challenged the title of the plaintiffs themselves".

The learned Single Judge also repelled the contention of the appellants that the admitted co-sharers, plaintiffs are not claiming anything adverse to the interest of the left out co-sharers. From the averments in the plaint, the learned Single Judge correctly found that the plaintiffs agitated the same issue of defect of party from two contradictory stand points, viz. at one breath it is asserted that no partition has taken place by metes and bounds in 'A' and 'B' schedule properties and in another breath the plaintiffs are claiming absolute ownership and exclusive possession by amicable partition of 'B' schedule property. The learned Single Judge further found that "in their memorandum of appeal before the appellate Court below they stated in ground No.5, that Himangshu and Arunangshu had no interest whatsoever in the suit properties as they inherited nothing from their father. This ground contradicts the averments in the plaint wherein Himangshu and Arunangshu were accepted as heirs of Harimohan Paul in respect of that portion of schedule "B" properties which was not gifted away to plaintiff No. 1 ."

<u>34. At the out set it must be stated that the present suit, is in substance, a suit for declaration and permanent injunction against the enemy property authorities to restrain them and or, in any way interfere with the plaintiffs right to property and for injunction. The order of declaring the property as an enemy property was challenged in the plaint as illegal, invalid and void along with the prayer for permanent injunction. Section 53 of the Specific Relief Act reads as follows:-</u>

<u>"A perpetual injunction can only be granted by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits of the suit, the defendant is thereby perpetually enjoined from the assertion of a right, or from the commission of an act, which would be contrary to the rights of the plaintiff."</u>

<u>Section 54 of the Specific Relief Act speaks as follows".</u>

<u>"Subject to the other provisions, contained in, or, referred to by, this Chapter, a perpetual injunction may be granted to prevent the breach of an obligation, existing in favour of the applicant, whether expressly or by implication."</u>

<u>Reading these two sections together it is apparent that a suit for permanent injunction is contemplated under the above two sections and the same can be obtained by a decree made at the hearing and upon the merits of the suit. By the terms merits of the suit would obviously mean determination of the plaintiffs alleged right or alleged commission of act by the defendant which would be contrary to or violative of the rights of the plaintiffs. Therefore, for the grant of perpetual or permanent injunction the existence of a right in the plaintiffs and its threatened violation to the plaintiffs right would have to be found. It is therefore, clear that every suit for a permanent injunction must involve a determination or a declaration to the above effect, or in other words, such a declaration would be necessarily involved or implied in the case of every decree for permanent injunction. It is true that in this case the plaintiffs right was affected by the impugned order of treating the property as a enemy property and so a declaration is sought for in prayer No.1 of the plaint. But we are to keep in mind that this prayer is merely ancillary prayer to the main relief of permanent Injunction. From the averments made in the plaint one is to determine the basic question raised in the case for ultimate decree for permanent injunction at the hearing upon the merit of the suit. In this back ground we are to see whether all the courts below were legally justified in holding that the suit was not properly constituted for not impleading necessary parties in the case.</u>

<u>35. We must bear in mind the distinction between a "necessary" and "proper" party as contemplated under Order 1, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. A necessary party is one whose presence on the record is enjoined by law or in whose absence no effective decision can at all be given and without that person suit cannot be properly constituted and liable to be dismissed. A "proper" party, on the other hand, is one whose presence is not essential in the constitution of the suit but whose presence is desirable in order to properly or completely adjudicate on the matter involved, if omission to implead necessary party is not corrected by the person bringing the suit, the suit is liable to be dismissed. A reference to Order 1, Rule 9 of the Code provides that no suit shall fail for non-joinder of parties. But this rule cannot be applied in a case where the proper constitution of the suit requires a necessary party to be on record.</u>

<u>Hence, I am to see whether the left out co sharers are necessary parties in this suit for declaration and permanent injunction. As per the averments of the plaint all the co-sharers including the left out co-sharers have subsisting interest in the property. If for any reason the plaintiffs could not implead Himangshu and Arunangshu in the category of plaintiffs. I cannot understand why the plaintiffs could not implead these co-sharers as defendants when the objection was raised at the earliest point of time by the contesting defendants. In this suit it is not possible to split up the joint interest of the parties in the land. It is further found that the plaintiffs are not suing in their personal capacity but suing as co-sharers in possession of the suit land. It is quite clear that the plaintiffs filed the suit on specific averments of joint interest in an unpartitioned land and having sued in that capacity all must be brought on record. It cannot be said that the left out co-sharers are not jointly interested in the immovable property and that being the position they must be brought on record as they have direct interest in the suit property. In a suit for declaration and permanent injunction if the plaintiffs get a decree then the same conclusively binds all the parties and in that event it is undisputed that the suit ought to have been heard in presence of all the co-sharers for an effective decree within the frame of the suit. The main averments is that, all the co-sharers are interested in all the lands but the plaintiffs are in possession as co-owners and in that view a cosharer in possession is certainly entitled under the law to maintain a suit for declaration and permanent injunction to protect his proprietary right in it but all joint owners must be on record for proper constitution of the suit as they are jointly interested in the subject matter of the suit. Thus, I find that the plaintiffs suit is in fact defective for want of necessary parties and it cannot proceed. This being a case of declaration of title and permanent injunction the plaintiff is oblige to make out a case of good title for all the co-sharers and this issue of title could not be decided leaving these two admitted co-sharers. Section 53 of the Specific Relief Act says that a decree for permanent injunction can only be granted upon the merits of the suit. The plaintiffs story of amicable partition of "B' schedule properties and acquisition of absolute ownership by the plaintiffs was not accepted by the courts below. Further, the division of 'A' schedule properties by metes and bounds was also not accepted by the courts below. Hence, right, title and interest cannot be finally concluded without the necessary parties. In a suit for declaration and perpetual injunction the plaintiff must first establish his legal right. After the plaintiff succeeds in establishing his legal right and its violation he is granted a permanent injunction. Permanent injunction can be granted by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits of a suit which concludes a right for ever. Thus, unless the rights of all persons who have joint right, title and interest are brought on record, no violation of right of all persons can be determined. Thus it is very simple that all joint owners must be on record. Where there is a joint right it may be necessary for all persons jointly interested to be joined as parties, and if they are not joined the suit will be bad for misjoinder. The immovable property being jointly owned each co-owner is in theory Interested in every portion of the suit land and each has a right, irrespective of the quantity of his share. Due to the conflicting averments and adverse claim which was not accepted by the courts blow, the co-owners ought to have been made parties. In paragraph 16 of the plaint it has been stated that all the co-sharers have been made proforma defendants. This factual assertion is also not correct as admittedly two of the co-sharers are left out. Further, there is averments that if any of the proforma defendant contests the suit he may be treated as a principal defendant. Hence it is palpable to say that the plaintiffs have got no consent to file the suit on behalf of these left out co sharers and that their interest is also adverse to be plaintiffs interest. From the very beginning of the suit the objection as to non-joinder of necessary parties was raised specifically in the written statement, even then the plaintiff did not care to implead these two admitted co-sharers namely. Himangshu and Arunangshu as parties. This is one of the circumstances also which lends support to the fact that the plaintiffs are claiming as if they are only heirs of Harimohan Paul.</u>

36. I will refer hereinbelow some of the decisions of proper appreciation of the issue in controvercy in this case. In a case reported in A.I.R. 1927 Madras 984. (Kaliapa Nadar and others Vs. Muthu Vijaya Thambayasami Chunnichi Naickar Avergal) a Division Bench observed as follows:-

"It is an elementary principle of law that persons who have got joint right should join in an action to assert that right and it is not open to one or two persons who have a joint right along with others to bring a suit for the assertion of that right on behalf of ail without joining them as defendants. The judgment of the learned District Judge is correct on this point."

In the case of Allam Gangadhara Rao V. Gollapalli Gangarao, AIR 1968 Andhpra 291 it has been held that even in the case of persons jointly entitled to any relief, the language of R. I of O.1 C.P.C. says that all such persons may be joined in one suit, either as plaintiffs or defendants. The reason is that such persons together represent a single and indivisible right which cannot be adjudicated upon and no effective decree can be passed by the Court in absence of such persons. In Aswini Kumar V. Kshitish Chandra, AIR 1971 Cal 252, which was a case for declaration of title and recovery of possession, it was held that the suit becomes incompetent if some of the co-owners are not impleaded as parties. In the case of Kanakaranthanamaly Vs. Loganath Mudaliar, AIR 1965 SC 271, a dispute arose relating to the property purchased by the wife with money gifted by the husband in a suit by daughter to recover property from beneficiary under will of father. The brothers were not impleaded as parties. It was held that the suit was incompetent for non-joinder of necessary parties. In the case of Kanakarathanammal Vs. VS. Loganatha Mudaliar and another reported in A.I.R. 1965 SC-271, it has been observed as follows:-

"It is true that under O. 1, R. 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure no suit shall be defeated by reason of the misjoinder or non-joinder of the parties, but there can be no doubt that if the parties who are not joined are not only proper but also necessary parties to it, the infirmity in the suit is bound to be fatal. Even in such cases; the Court can under O. 1, R. 10, sub-rule 2 direct the necessary parties to be joined, but all this can and should be done at the stage of trial and that too without prejudice to the said parties plea of limitation.

In the case of Aswini Kumar Roy and another Vs. Kahitish Chandra Sen Gupta and others, reported in AIR 1971 Calcutta-252, it has been observed that the suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession becomes in competent if some of the co-sharers are not impleaded as parties as in a suit of this kind all the co-sharers are necessary parties.

37. Before parting with the case it may be stated that there are uniform judicial decisions of this sub-continent that one co-owner can sue to eject a trespasser from the suit property without impleading in the case other co owners. The basis being that a co-owner has a right to hold every inch of the joint property until a division takes place. The present case being not one of dispossession by a trespasser the principle enunciated in those decisions has no manner of application in the fact of the present case.

38. Accordingly the appeal is dismissed without costs. The judgment and decree of the High Court Division is maintained.

ORDER OF THE COURT

39. By majority decision: the appeal is allowed without any order as to cost. The judgment and decree of the Courts below are set aside and the suit is decreed. It is hereby declared That the declaration of the suit property as enemy property under Memo no.1587(29) E.P. dated 27.3.67 of defendant no.1 and lease order in favour of defendant no. 3 under Memo no. 1141 E.P dated 29 of defendant no. 2 are illegal, inoperative and without jurisdiction. The defendants are restrained by permanent injunction from interfering in any manner with the suit land.

End.

case_source: Arising out of Judgment and order dated 12.1.90 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Chandpur, in Miscellaneous Case No.19 of 1987
full_judgment:
Syed Fazle Ahmed, J.: This rule calls in question the legality and propriety of the judgment and order dated 12.2.90 passed by Subordinate Judge, Chandpur, in Miscellaneous Case No. 91 of 1987.

2. Facts giving rise to this Rule may briefly be put thus:

Pre opposite parties filed Misc. Case No. 70 of 1979 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Chandpur under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, contending inter alia that the pre-emptor was the sharer in the disputed holding along with opposite party Nos. 2-4 Pre-emptee petitioners are not the co-sharer of the disputed holding. Pre-emptee petitioners purchased 30 decimals of land from seller opposite party No. 2 to 4 by registered sale deed dated 2.8.76 for a consideration of Tk. 2000/-. No notice of the sale was served upon the pre opposite party as per provision of law. Subsequently pre-emptor opposite party came to know of the alleged sale from Md. Fazar Ali on 8th Chaitra, 1385 B. S. and thereafter obtained certified copy of the sale deed from Hajiganj S.R. Office and became fully aware of the sale on 1.4.79. Pre-emptor opposite parry made the deposit with compensation and filed the case seeking pre-emtion of the disputed transfer.

3. Pre-emptee petitioner contested the case by filing written objection denying all the material allegations made in the application for pre-emtion contending inter alia that pre-emptor has no cause of action; that the pre-emptor is not the co-sharer of the disputed holding.

4. Subsequently the case was transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, Saharasti Upazila and was re-numbered as Misc. Case No.5 of 1977.

5. Both parties led evidence before the Assistant Judge, who on consideration of the evidence on record allowed the application for pre-emption Against that judgment and order of the learned Assistant Judge, pre-emptee petitioner filed Misc. Appeal No.91 of 1987 which on transfer was heard by Subordinate Judge, Chandpur, who dismissed the appeal by the judgment and order dated 12.2.90.

6. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order, revisional jurisdiction of this Court was moved and the present Rule was obtained.

7. It is submitted by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner that the learned Subordinate Judge committed error of law occasioning failure of justice in affirming the judgment and order passed by the learned Assistant Judge holding that although the petitioners are co-shares in the disputed holding by gift prior to the transfer sought to be pre-empted, their status are not better than that of a co-sharer which is contrary to the provision contained in sub-Section 10, clause "A" of section96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

8. In order to expose the misconception of law, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee petitioner has relied on sub- section 10 clause 'A' of Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which reads thus:

"10 Nothing in this section shall apply to (a) a transfer to a co-sharer in the tenancy whose interest has accrued otherwise than by purchase; or"

In the instant case pre-emptees petitioners' interest accrued on the, basis of deed of gift dated 10.4.1957 vide Ext A. petitioners who made subsequent purchase a portion of the land appertaining to the same holding on 2.8.76 and this transfer is sought to be pre empted by opposite party no. 1. It is under this circumstances the learned Move for the petitioners having relied on the provision referred to above contends that subsequent transfer sought to be pre-empted is protected, inasmuch as the inter of the accrued in the disputed holding Otherwise than by purchase . In other words, initial interest accrued on the basis of gift. In this connection the learned Advocate has referred to a decision in the case of Mansuruddn Bhuiyan Vs Md. Yeakub Ali Dewan reported in XXI D.L.R. page 556. Fact involved in the cited case is almost identical with the fact involved in the instant case. Their lordships observed in the following language,

"a co-sharer by gift is a co-sharer whose interest has accrued 'otherwise than by purchase' and when such a co-sharer makes a subsequent purchase in respect of a portion of the same holding, he is protected from pre-emption under Section 26F(1) of the Act"

9. In the instant case, petitioners initially acquired interest in the disputed holding on the basis of gift made in their favour by their grandfather Yeakub Ali and that deed of gift vide Ext. 'A' was proved in this case and this gift was made on 10.4.1957 in favour of the petitioners. After some time, petition purchase a portion of the land appertaining to the same holding by registered sale deed dated 2.8.76 and this transfer is sought to be pre-empted by opposite party No. 1.

<u>10. Both the courts below misinterpreted the provision of Sub-section clause 'A' of Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The transfer sought to be pre-empted is view of the cited decision referred above. The cited decision relates to the transferred made under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act but the principle laid down therein is folly applicable to the instant case inasmuch as East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is said to the successor of Bengal Tenancy Act such provides for pre-emption under section 96 of the Act. Exception- has been made by subsection 10 of Section 96 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act with respect to certain transfer by excepting them from operation of pre emption and clause 'A' of sub-section 96 Of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act exempts transfer to co-sharer of the tenancy whose interest has accrued otherwise than by purchase from pre-emption. This provision is similar to the provision of Section 26(FX1) (a) of Bengal Tenancy Act. It is, therefore, obvious that co-sharer in the tenancy whose existing interest has accrued otherwise than by purchase i.e. by way of gift as in the present case is protected from pre-emption.</u>

11. Both the Courts below put a wider meaning on the word "purchase". Thus the policy of law which exempts a co-sharer whose existing interest has accrued otherwise than purchase from pre-emption. The word "purchase" occurring in sub-section 10 clause ('a') of Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act should not be stretched so much in order to include transfer by way of gift in the category of transfer by purchase.

12. Thus, having considered the entire materials on record and facts involved in the instant case, I am of opinion 'that both the Courts committed error in law in interpreting the provision contained in sub-section 10 of clause 'A' of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and as such the judgment and order a not sustainable in law.

13. In the result, the impugned judgment and order passed by the teamed Subordinate Judge, Chandpur, in Misc. Case No. 91 of 1990 is hereby set aside and the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost.

End.

Md. Azhar Hossain ----- Petitioner in writ petition No. 29201 1989
Vs.
The Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Habibur Rahman Khan, J.: Two separate rules were issued, one on 20-2-89 in writ petition No.223 of 1989 filed by Md. Masudul Hussain and another one 12-3-1989 in writ petition No.292 of 1989 filed by Azhar Hossain calling upon the respondent to show cause as to why the notices dated 31-12-88 under section 3 of the Ordinance and 11-2-1989 under section 6 of the Ordinance confirming the Government decision to acquire the petitioners property (Annexures "D" and 'F') should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and propel.

2. Pending hearing of the rule the operation of the impugned order was stayed.

3. Though the parties in the two writ petitions are different and they claimed right, title and interest in respect of different parcels of land on the basis of separate documents the order impugned in the same and the common question of law is involved in both the writ petitions and hence as per orders passed by this court, both the matters are heard simultaneously and disposed of by the same judgment.

4. The short facts of the two writ petitions are given below:

The petitioner in writ petition No.223 of 1989 Md. Masudul Hussain became the owner of. 0.14 acres of land within mouza Kawran being CS. Dag No.71, Khatian No.43 corresponding to S.A. Dag No.108/1054, Khatian No.70 by virtue of purchase vide registered deed of sale bearing No. dated 27-6-6t Subsequent to the purchase the petitioners name was mutated in the revenue records vide Mutation Case no.12089(sh)87 dated 15-7-87 in the office of the Circle Officer (Revenue) Tejgaon, Dhaka. The petitioner had been in ex elusive and peaceful possession of the aforesaid property ever since his purchase and had been enjoying the same without any let or hindrance from any quarter on payment of rents and taxes regularly.

5. The petitioner in writ petition No. 292 of 1989 Azher Hossain purchased the land from Dr. Md. Aftabuddin Ahmed measuring 0.1050 acre in Mouza, Kawran being C.S. Dag No.71, Khatian No.43, corresponding to S.A. Dag No.108, Khatian No.70 vide registered sale deed bearing No.10574 on 27-6-68 and since the date of purchase he has been possessing the land on mutation of his name in the revenue records vide Mutation Case no. 5033(sh)81 dated 23-3-1981 and had been enjoying the land without any let or hindrance from any quarter on payment of rents and taxes regularly.

6. The land of both the petitioners lies on the southern side of the newly built road, Pantha Path which has connected the Sonargaon Hotel with Green Road.

7. On 31-12-88 the Respondent No.2 the land acquisition officer, Dhaka caused a notice served in L.A. Case. No.8/88-89 by virtue of section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 stating that the land mentioned in the schedule to the said notice was required or likely to be required for public purpose for setting up a three-star Hotel. An objection was also invited from the persons interested in the said land, it is submitted that the notice  was not published at convenient places or near the property sought to be acquired as in required under the provision of the Ordinance and as such the petitioners were absolutely in dark about the notice of requisition. Having come to know from the neighbouring people that some portion of the land around Sundarban Hotel was going to be acquired the petitioners went to the office of the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and to their utter surprise and dismey found that the land of the petitioners mentioned in the schedule of the notice under section 3 of the Ordinance along with some other properties were purported to have been requisitioned and acquired. Immediately they met the respondent No. 2 and intimated him that the notice appearing in the board was never published on or near the land. On being advised the petitioners raised objection and produced the documents before the respondent No.2 who after hearing the petitioners and examining the documents of title seemed to have been convinced about the genuineness of the claim of the petitioners in respect of the land in question but did nothing so as to exclude the same from acquisition. In spite of the objections raised the petitioners was served with another notice on 11.2.1989 under section 6 of the Ordinance wherein it was stated that, the Government has decided to acquire the property mentioned in the schedule to the notice for the purpose of setting up a 3-Star Hotel therein. The owners and occupiers of the land were also directed to appear before the respondent No on 28-2-1989 in connection with the assessment of compensation to be paid to the affected persons. The petitioners being in distress consulted their lawyers and on their instructions got the notices served upon the respondents calling upon them to withdraw and rescind the order of requisition. Having not received any reply the petitioners moved this court and obtained the present rule.

8. In both the writ petitions it is stated that the self same land was sought to be acquired in L.A. Case No. 122/60-61 and subsequently the L.A. Collector by his notice No. 286 dated 21- 2-1966 announced the de-requisition of the said land whereupon the compensation money paid to the land owners was refunded to the Government and the petitioners were allowed to possess the said land. It is submitted that the area having developed due to the construction of a new road and buildings around, the petitioners have contemplated to build a multi-storied commercial complex upon their respective lands The proposal of certain interested persons offering to buy the land at a nominal price having been turned down they in collusion with the respondents have taken recourse to get the land acquired for their own purpose and personal gain. It is submitted that the scheme of acquiring the land of the petitioners is malafide collusive, arbitrary and has been made in colorable exercise of power by the authority. It is also submitted that the acquisition of land for setting up a 3-Star Hotel cannot be construed as a "public purpose" nor does it meet any of the lawful requirements laid down for acquiring land for public purpose. The acquisition of the land for the purpose of building of 3-Star hotel obviously is not a public purpose nor it is in public interest. For the purpose of establishing a hotel lands could be made available in the city of Dhaka on private negotiation and hence the compulsive acquisition of the petitioners' property is an abuse of the authority as it is not done in the public interest butler the private and commercial gain of some interested person or persons it is further submitted that the original notice under section 3 of the Ordinance was not published in terms of the Ordinance at convenient place on or near the property sought to be acquired. It is further submitted that the initial order being malafide, the subsequent order vide Annexure is also invalid, void and inoperative.

9. In the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 the statements and allegations made in the petition have been controverted. It is stated that the notice under section 3 of the Ordinance Noll of 1982 was duly published on the land under acquisition in L.A. Case No.8/88-89 and also in the notice bard of the Collectorate, Dhaka and other offices on 31-12-88 as required under Rule 4 of the Acquisition of Immovable Property Rules, 1982. It is stated that the notice under section 6 of the Ordinance was duly is sued. The averments made to the effect that the acquisition of land for standard hotels is for a public purpose, as it has been included as one of the service oriented industries in Group-X of the Industrial Investment Schedule for third five years plan (1985-90) for private sector and in order to accelerate the peace of growth of Industries the Government of Bangladesh announced the Industrial Policy in 1986 for the Third five year plan period 1985-90 laying emphasis on private sectors. Two of the objectives are 1) to encourage foreign investment in appropriate sectors, and 2) encourage tourism. The gist of the averment made in the long affidavit sworn by the respondents are that the establishment of the hotel Will pave the way for the investment of foreign capital in our country and in flow of foreign currency of there investment from abroad. The proposed I will serve as a source of encouragement to the tourists and therefore, the acquisition of law for establishing hotel is made for a public purpose and in public interest. The statements and averments made in the affidavit-in-opposition have been also controverted in the affidavit-in-reply filed on behalf of the petitioners.

10. The submissions made by Mr. Ziaur Rahman Khan, the learned council in writ petition No. 223 of 1989 has been adopted by Mr. A.F.M. Ali Asgar, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner in writ petition No. 292 of 1989. Mr. Abdul Mannan Bhuiyan, the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing on behalf of the respondents opposed the rule.

11. Mr. Ziaur Rahman Khan, the learned counsel for the petitioner after taking us through the petition affidavit-in-opposition.affidavit-in-reply and Annexures challenged the order of requisition on various grounds. Mr. Khan submitted that under Article 42 of the Constitution of Bangladesh every citizen has the right to acquire, hold, transfer or otherwise dispose of properly, and no property shall be compulsorily acquired, nationalised or requisitioned save by authority of law and this right of the citizen shall be exercised only subject to restrictions which has been imposed under sub-article (2) of the Constitution. Mr. Khan submitted that the law of acquisition as provided under the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 empowers the Deputy Commissioner to acquire property under certain conditions when the property is needed or likely to be needed for the public purpose or in the public interest and for that purpose the notice is to be published at convenient place or near the property proposed to be acquired in the prescribed form. But the specific provision of section 3 of the Ordinance has not been adheared to and for such violation the order for acquiring the property of the petitioners is liable to be struck down. By way of elaborating his argument the learned counsel for the petitioners has drawn our attention to Annexure-D' and submitted that the notice was issued under the signature of the land acquisition Officer but the Ordinance provides that the Deputy Commissioner shaft cause the notice to be published. The word Deputy Commissioner as defined under section 2(b) includes an Additional Deputy Commissioner and any other officer authorised by the Deputy Commissioner. Mr. Ziaur Rahman Khan submitted that there is nothing to show that the land acquisition officer under whose signature the notice is purported to have been issued was duly authorised by the Deputy Commissioner. On perusal of the notice under section 3 it also appears that the land sought to be acquired on the ground that it is necessary for the construction of 3 Star Hotel and also that it is likely to be needed for the construction of the said hotel. Mr. Khan submitted that the property may be needed for the public purpose or it is likely to be needed but while was property the Deputy Commissioner cannot manage to keep both the alternatives in his locket and choose between the two at his pleasure. The use of both the alternatives in the notice under section 3 displays the lack of application of mind of the acquiring authority.

12. The learned Counsel relied on the case of Sankar Gopal Chatterjee and others Versus The Additional Commissioner, Dhaka Division and others reported in 41 DLR 326 wherein it is held:-

"The law of acquisition gives the Deputy Commissioner the power to acquire property in the likelihood of two situations. First, if the property is needed. Or, the property is likely to be needed. A property is either needed or it is likely to be needed. But while acquiring a property the Deputy Commissioner cannot keep both the alternatives in his pocket. He has to choose between the two. If he keeps both the options open, then he does not know whether the property is needed for immediate use or it is likely to be needed for some future use. The use of both these alternative expressions in the notice under section 3 is indicative of a lack of application of mind and the notice under section 3 is liable to be struck down on that ground as well."

13. In the instant case the notice issued by the land acquisition officer vide Annexure-D does not speak specifically as to whether the land is needed for immediate use or likely to be needed for future. In view of the principle laid down in the above referred to case we hold that the notice under section 3 suffers from lack of application of mind of the requisitioning authority and for that matter it suffers from legal infirmity

14. Mr. Ziaur Rahman Khan then argued that the notice was not served in the place or near about the property as required under section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982. The learned Assistant Attorney General also has not been able to show either from the notice or from the record chat the notice was published at any convenient place on or near the property proposed to be acquired. Rule 4(2) of Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 also provides that notices under section 3 shall be published at a convenient place or near the property sought to be acquired with copies of such notices displayed in the notice board of the Collectorate. The next point the learned counsel for the petitioners urged is that the purpose for which the property of the petitioners sought to be acquired is neither a public purpose nor it is in the interest of the public. The learned counsel further submits that the purported requisition for the establishment of a 3-Star Hotel at the initiative of a particular person or a group of persons is designed for their pecuniary benefit only and not for public purpose. Mr. Abdul Mannan Bhuiya, the learned Assistant Attorney General submitted that the establishment of 3-Stars Hotel in Dhaka City will attract the tourist and it will accelerate the flow of foreign exchange to the country from abroad.

<u>15. The learned counsel for the petitioner referred to the case of SK. Aminuddin and another Versus Deputy Commissioner and others reported in 15 DLR 442 which arose out a case of requisition of land for the establishment of nursing home in a town where there was none or the existing provision was not adequate. While deciding the case as to whether the establishment of nursing home was for a public purpose or not, the learned Judges found.</u>

<u>"While the meaning of the expression public purpose is flexible and must be interpreted with reference to the circumstances prevailing at a particular time, such a purpose can only be established if it is shown that the purpose is to benefit the public directly and not incidentally, If the purpose is, however, to benefit an individual or a group of individuals directly and the benefit to the public or to a section of it is only prospective or remote or incidental, the purpose is private."</u>

<u>Public purpose as defined on Willoughby's Constitution of the United States, Volume 3 at page 1740 as quoted in the 15 DLR case is in the following language:</u>

<u>"A public use is one in which the interest of the public is directly and primarily concerned. It may happen, and indeed, it very frequently happens, that in the exercise of the statutes powers, whether of eminent domain, taxation or police regulation, particular individuals or classes of individuals are benefited. If, however, the Section is to be sustained, its aim must be shown to be not merely that this specific result will be reached as a final end, but that the public has itself an interest in securing this benefit to the individual concerned."</u>

<u>16. In this case the property of the petitioner sought to be requisitioned is for establishing a 3-Star Hotel. From the averments made by the respective parties it appears that the hotel is sought to be established at the initiative of an individual and it is a private enterprise. There is absolutely no material to show that either the Government has direct financial involvement or that the public has interest in the establishment of the hotel. It appears that it is a commercial concern in which some people might have interest and, therefore, such purpose cannot be said to be a public purpose by any stretch of imagination and, therefore, the land of the petitioners cannot be taken for the use and enjoyment of some depriving the owner from using and utilising their own land as guaranteed under the Constitution.</u>

17. In the case of Abdus Sobhan Sowdagor and another -Versus- Province of East Pakistan and others reported in 14 DLR at page 496 the learned Judge observed:

"Every grocery which exists in any country serves a public interest, but such a grocery is not primarily and directly concerned with such public purpose."

<u>18. In the situation as presented in the case, we feel incliend to accept the averments made on behalf of the petitioners that the purpose for which the land sought to be acquired is purely for private benefit and, therefore, placing reliance on the principle laid down in the earlier cases we hold that the contemplated acquisition is not for a public purpose. It has been laid down in several decisions of this Court that the requisitioning authority must "strike a balance between the demand made by the requiring body and the suffering of the expropriated land owner and come to a conclusion of its own after independent application of mind as to the area necessary for the purpose for which the requisition is sought to be made. On a perusal a of the record produced before us, we are of the view that there has been no application of mind of the authority in making the impugned order. As the establishment of 3-Star hotel does not fall within the category of public purpose, we are of the view that the proposed acquisition of the property of the petitioners is not for public purpose, rather it is for the benefit of a group of individuals directly and the benefit of the public or to a section of it is only prospective or remote or incidental. In taking this view we get our support from the principle laid down in the case of Abdus Sobhan Sowdagor and another Versus- Province of East Pakistan and others reported in 14 DLR 486 wherein it is observed:-</u>

<u>"In the first place, the expression public purpose must include a purpose, that is, an object or aim, in which the general interest of the community as opposed to the particular interest of an individual is concerned. Secondly, such interest must be directly connected with the order that is being made and must be vitally concerned with the said order.</u>

<u>There will be no public purpose in any undertaking or venture in which the public interest is served indirectly and in a circuitious way. Every grocery which exists in any country serves a public interest, but such grocery is not primarily and directly concerned with such public purpose."</u>

<u>19. The same principle was laid down in the case reported in 11 DLR at page 222 and 411 wherein it is held that the Government is not empowered to give the property of a private individual to another private individual. The Supreme Court of India in the case reported in AIR 1961 (S.C) 343 laid down the principle that for a decision as to whether the purpose is public purpose or not it is to be seen whether the compensation money is to be paid for acquisition comes from the private individual of public exchequer. Referring to section 15 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance the learned counsel for the petitioners submitted that the provision of the said section has not been complied with. In the present case there is no material to show that the person for whom the property was sought to be acquired entered into an agreement with the Government before issuing the notice under section 3 an agreement with the Government and requiring body is sine quo non for the exercise of such power.</u>

20. The learned Assistant Attorney General Mr. Abdul Mannan Bhuiya, finally opposed the Rule arguing that having regard to the facts that the Divisional Commissioner having made a decision for acquisition of property under section 5(1) considering the reports submitted before him under Section 4(3) about the acquisition of the property such decision of the Divisional Commissioner shall be final and conclusive evidence that the property is needed for a public purpose or in public interest. In this regard the learned Assistant Attorney General referred to the case of Province of East Pakistan -Versus- Dr. Azizul Islam reported in P 1963 (SC) page 296 wherein it was held:

"Presumption that official act of requisition had been regularly and properly performed—Onus would then be upon the person seeking to challenge the correctness of the recital to show the contrary."

21. In the said case the property was requisitioned for the purpose of rehabilitation of displaced person and therefore on the very face of it assumed the character of the public purpose. The learned Assistant Attorney General then referred to the decision reported in 8 DLR(1956) 210 and submitted that whether the property is required for public purpose cannot be questioned in a court of law. With the pas sage of time and change in the law relating to the requisition and acquisition of the property the superior courts have consistently laid down the principle that if the order of requisition and acquisition is made without following the prescribed procedures it is not outside the scope of the superior court to see whether it is for public purpose or for collateral purpose or for the benefit of an individual or a group of individuals.

22. In the Case of Md. Mansur Rahman and others -Versus- Province of East Pakistan reported in 14 DLR at page 604 it is found that the purpose for which the acquisition is subject to the scrutiny of the court and the court is entitled to enquire whether the authority seeking to take the property of an individual is required to take it for public purpose or that the purpose for which the land sought to be acquired is at all a public purpose or not.

23. In this case there is absolutely no material to show that the public has an interest in the 3-star hotel so as to guarantee that the public benefit will be secured. The 3-star hotel, as it appears from the materials, will be a commercial institution for the purpose of accommodation of the boarders on payment of charges but it can never be for the common benefit of all or a greater number of people and such interest of a few is not sufficient to held that the acquisition is for a public purpose.

24. In view of the above, we are of the view that the order for acquiring the property of the petitioners suffers from legal infirmities as the procedure laid down under section 3, 5, 6 and 7 have not been complied with and, therefore, we are unable to accept the submission of the learned Assistant Attorney General that whatever order has been passed by the authority is deemed to be conclusive. On the contrary we find from the record that there are enough material to show that the purpose for which the property is sought to be acquired is not a public purpose and in that view of the matter we hold that the order for the acquisition of the property as evidenced vide Annexure-'D' and 'F' have been passed without any lawful authority and are of no legal effect.

25. In the result both the Rules are made absolute without any order as to costs.

End.
