<u>19. Now I would like to consider the legal aspect of the case. It appears from the trend of the earlier judicial pronouncements that in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff is to prove exclusive, possession of the suit land and incidentally a prima fade title to the suit land. If these two requirements are fulfilled by the plaintiff, only then he is entitled to get a permanent injunction. If we look to section 110 of the Evidence Act we find that this section embodies the well known principle of Roman Law that possession is prima facie proof of owner ship and when, therefore, a person is in possession of a property the presumption of ownership is highly in his favour and under s 110 the onus of proving that he is not the owner is on the person who asserts that he is not the owner.</u>

<u>20. Similarly, section 9 of the Specific Relief Act also protects the possessory right of a person. Title cannot be pleaded in bar of a suit of this nature and the Court does not adjudicate upon the title of the parties in a suit under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, It is thus, clear that even a trespasser can recover his possession if he is dispossessed from an immovable property without his consent. If that be so, then why a person already in possession of an immovable property claiming to b6 the owner will be requited to prove his title to the property in order to protect his possession? In my opinion, the correct legal position is that in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff need not prove his title to the property as a condition precedent to succeed in an action for permanent injunction. It is sufficient if the plaintiff can prove his prior and present possession of the suit land i.e. in a suit for permanent injunction possession is of paramount consideration and the fate of the suit veers round the proof of possession by the plaintiff. From a review of the judicial pronouncements of the Superior Courts of this sub-continent it appears that earlier trend was that in order to succeed in an action for permanent injunction the plaintiff bad to prove both possession and prima fade title. The said trend has undergone a change. Now the superior Courts emphasis on the possession and not on the title. It is now well settled that if a man has a long continuous possession in the suit land he is entitled to protect his tight by way of permanent injunction. It has been held in IV B.L.D. at page U7 that a person in long possession can be evicted only in due course of law. Even the rightful owner cannot evict him with force. If he cannot be evicted with force he continues to be in possession and he can resist invasion of his possession by everyone, including the rightful owner, If the rightful owner threatened his possession he can pray for an equitable relief of injunction to protect his possession, and the remedy of the rightful owner lies in bringing an appropriate suit for establishing his right and for recovery of possession. Our Appellate Division in the case of Manindra Nath Sen Sarma Vs Bangladesh reported in IV B.L.D. (AD) 285 held that if the plaintiff fails to prove his title in a suit for permanent injunction that will not disentitle him to an order of permanent injunction. So, it is crystal clear that suits for permanent injunction are merely concerned with the fact of possession, and not with the nature or the character of the possession or the capacity of the possession. If the plaintiff is found to be in possession, he is entitled to the injunction. If he is not in possession, he is not entitled to the injunction. The principle of a Division Bench ruling of the Kerala High Court of Velu Pilli and Krishna Moorthy, JJ in Kuttan Narayan V. Thomman Mathai (1966 KER. 199), also seems to support the view, namely, that a person in possession,  even if wrongful is entitled to maintain his possession even against the true owner, till evicted by due process of law. So, the recent trend of the judicial pronouncements in this regard is that in a suit for permanent injunction the question of title is of no significance. If in a properly framed suit the plaintiff can prove his exclusive possession of the suit land there is no doubt that he is entitled to protect his possession by way of permanent injunction against the whole world, including the real owner. In that view of the matter also the observations made by the lower appellate court about title of the suit land is of no significance.</u>

<u>21. Mr. Saha while arguing in support of the rule submitted that the judgment of the lower appellate court cannot be termed as a proper judgment of reversal at all because it has utterly failed to comply with the requirement of Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and for this purpose he has relied on the case reported in 14 B.L.D. (AD) 229 wherein it has been held that the appellate court whether reversing or affirming the decision of the trial Court must independently discuss and consider the evidence on record. But in the case of affirming the finding of the trial court, the narration of the entire evidence and reiteration of the reasons are not essential. In such a case expressions of general agreement with those of the trial Court are generally considered sufficient. But in the case of a reversal of a judgment, the consideration of the evidence, of necessity, has to be thorough and more elaborate.</u>

<u>22. From a perusal of the impugned judgment I find that the appellate court below without adverting to the evidence at all abruptly found that the plaintiff has failed to prove his possession and the appellate court below has also failed to assign reason as to why and how it disagrees with the finding of the trial Court. In the instant case we find that the judgment of the trial court is well reasoned and elaborate and the judgment is amply supported by evidence bothoral and documentary and the learned lower appellate court failed to reverse the findings by cogent reasons.</u>

23. In view of the aforesaid discussion, I find merits in the submissions made by Mr. Saha and I am unable to agree with the submissions made by Dr. Rahman. 24. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The judgment and decree dated 9.6.90 (decree signed on 17.9.90) passed by the learned Additional District. Judge, Kishoregonj in Other Appeal No. 87 of 1984 are set aside and the judgment and decree dated 5.9.84 (decree signed on 13.9.84) passed by the Musnif, Katiadi in other Suit No. 322011983) is restored. However, there will be no order as to cost.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Shafique Ahmed with Mr. Fazlur Rahman Khan, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner
Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan with Mr. S.K. Sinha and Ms. Umme Kulsum Rekha, Advocates ------ For Respondent No. 2
parties:
Advocate Mohammad Abdul Hamid ------ Petitioner
Vs.
The Chief Election Commissioner, Bangladesh Election Commission and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Mohammad Fazlul Karim, J: This rule was issued calling upon the Respondent to show cause as to why the order dated 30.3.98 signed on 5.2.98 passed by Election Commissioner on behalf of respondent (Annexure-A) shall not he declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effects. In an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh the petitioner stated, inter alia, that the petitioner has filed the petition under Article 54(1) of the Representation of the People Order 1972 alleging inter-alia that while the petitioner was the President of the Advocates Bar Association of Kishoregonj the Divisional Election Tribunal. Dhaka was a Additional District and Sessions Judge in the said station and the petitioner as its President had to mediate between the members of the Association and the said Court over certain problems whereupon he became the cause of mental sufferings of the tribunal whereby the learned Judge had been maintaining grudge against the members of the said Bar. From the Order of the Tribunal prior to 12.3.98 the petitioner has a bonafide apprehension in his mind that he may not get impartial trial before the said Tribunal. The Election Commissioner heard the petition on 16.3.98 and called for record fixing on 30.3.98 for hearing of the admission matter and stayed the further proceeding of the Election Tribunal Case No. 2 of 1997. The petition was heard on 30.3.98 and rejected by the impugned order on the same date signed on 5.4.98 by the Election Commissioner. The petitioner has further alleged in the application that one Md. Fazlur Rahman had challenged the election of the petitioner, a returned Candidate of the Constituency No. 169 Kishoregonj-5 held on 12th June, 1996 by an Election petition filed on 30th July, 1996. Upon prayer for transfer, the Election case was withdrawn from the Judge's Court Kishoregonj and transferred to Dhaka for trial. Ultimately the case was transferred by the Election commissioner to the Divisional Election Tribunal. Dhaka for trial of election case and 3.7.1997 was fixed for tadbir for serving notices upon the opposite parties including the petitioner and the process was issued fixing 13.7.97 for return on 4.8.97 the petitioner appeared and submitted application for dismissal of the election case which having been heard was rejected on 5.10.97 fixing 19.10.97 for filling written statement the petitioner filed Civil Revision before the High Court Division which was summarily rejected on 19.11.97. Ultimately the petitioner prayed for 30 daystime for filling written statement but mean while the petitioner moved the Appellate Division on 23.11.97 and the further proceeding of the election case was stayed till 8.2.98. Ultimately the Civil Petition and on the date the petition moved the Tribunal for time to file written statement which was allowed fixing 25.2.98. Petitioner thereafter filed another application for rejecting the election petition on the ground of change of nature and character of the case by a alleged amendment which was fixed for hearing on 4.3.98 and on that date another application for adjournment was rejected. So reading the mind of the Tribunal the petitioner preferred Writ petition No. 649 of 1998 on 8.3.1998 challenging the legality of the Election on Petition No. 2 of 1997 and on 12.3.1998 sought for 15 days adjournment in the Tribunal case but said prayer was rejected by the Tribunal fixing 18.3.98 for filing written statement by the opposite party, failing which the Election case would be disposed of Ex-parte the said Writ Petition No. 649 of 1998 was however rejected as not pressed on 15.3.98. The petitioner further stated that the learned Judge of the Tribunal was the Additional District and Sessions Judge of Kishoregonj for long 2 years and during that time the petitioner was the President of Kishoregonj Bar Association and had to meet up many unpleasent matters that arose in between the said  Judge and the members of the Bar Association for which the learned Judge is maintaining grudge against .the petitioner which is also apparent from the fact that although the process in the case in respect of the opposite party Nos. 2.4.5.6.8.9 and 10 remained un-served, the case has been fixed for ex-parte disposal illegally and even no time is allowed to obtain any order in Writ Petition No. 498 of 1998 by the learned Tribunal and as such the petitioner prayed for withdrawal of the case from the Court of Divisional Election Tribunal. Dhaka and to transfer it to any order Tribunal of competent jurisdiction The Rule has been contested by Respondent No.2 filing affidavit-in-opposition stating inter-alia that false allegations have been made for transfer of the case from the Divisional Election Tribunal. Dhaka and the said plea of the animosity between the petitioner and Tribunal Judge was belated and concocted one. The amendment of Election petition was allowed as the same was relating to clarification of the statement made in the Election petition and had nothing to do with the change in the nature of character of the election case. The respondent further stated that the petitioner knowing fully well that the Tribunal Judge who the Additional Judge at. Kishoregonj entered appearance in the case but made no allegation of any such animosity and maintaining grudge or that he shall not get any fair and impartial trial from the Election Tribunal at the earliest opportunity. The notices upon the petitioner could not be served in normal course but the service of notice of the case was effected through special messenger and consequently the petitioner appeared on 23.7.97 but adopted various delatory tactics in filing written statement on this plea or other and ultimately filed application for transfer of the case on some concocted and false allegation. The Election Commissioner having been dissatisfied with the ground for transfer rejected the said application. The petitioner had no grievance against the Election Tribunal until 12.3.98 by which date the Tribunal rejected his repeated applications for rejecting the Election Petition as not maintainable and has come out with the application for transfer at the belated stage solely to delay disposal of the case.

2. The petitioner filed an affidavit-in-reply denying the allegations in the affidavit-in-opposition of the Respondent No. 2 and asserted inter alia that respondent. No. 1 illegally rejected the transfer petition on misconception of Article 53(1)(2) and 54(1) of the Representation of the People Order, 1972.

3. The petitioner has however by way of supplementary affidavit to the affidavit-in-reply stated inter-alia that the petitioner for transfer was not filed earlier as a mark of respect for the tribunal. The learned Judge of the Divisional Election Tribunal. Dhaka while engaged as an Additional District and Sessions Judge of Kishoregonj the petitioner was the President of the Advocates Bar Association and had to take some lawful steps against the conduct of the said Judge. for which the latter has been maintaining grudge against the petitioner and in order to harass the petitioner the Tribunal fixed 8.2.98 and 15.2.98 for written statement when the matter was pending before the Appellate Division as to the maintainability of the Election case and that a resolution was taken against the said Tribunal while he was an Additional District and Sessions Judge at Kishoregonj in a meeting dated 16.2.96 in which the petitioner as the President of the Kishoregonj Bar Association presided and had to take several 'steps against the Judge of the Tribunal condemning the anti-judicial sentiment of the said Judge demanding his immediate withdrawal and that the Judge would not be invited to any of the functions of the Association annexing a copy of the extract of the said resolution as 'C'.

4. In the course of hearing of the rule the petitioner has came out with a affidavit though his authorised power of attorney stating that he on behalf of the petitioner do hereby undertake to make all legal co-operation for completion of the trial of the Election case in the Election Tribunal within 6(six) months of the receipt of the Election Case No. 2 of 1997 by the Tribunal.

5. Mr. Shafique Ahmed the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner has submitted with reference to be resolution dated 18.2.96 (Annexure-C) of Kishoregonj District Advocates Association which was taken in a meeting of the members held under the President ship of the petitioner that the said meeting condemned the then Additional District and Sessions Judge, Kishoregonj now the learned Judge of the Divisional Election Tribunal. Dhaka for this anti-Judicial sentiment arid demanded immediate withdrawal from the said station, further resolving not to invite the said Judge in any function of the Association submitted that in spite of the ground having been taken in the transfer petition before the Election Commissioner being Ground No. 1 the Election Commission acted illegally in not at all considering the said ground while rejecting the application for transfer. The learned Council further submitted that the observation of the Election Commission that the appointment of a new Tribunal from among the District and Sessions Judge would further delay disposal of the case and the permission of the Supreme Court is necessary in this regard has no legal bearing in view of the provision of Article 53 of the Representation of the People Order No. 155 of 1972 which empowered the Election Commission to set up as many Election Tribunal as may be necessary and the Tribunal shall consist of a person who is or has been a District and Sessions Judge or an Additional District and Sessions Judge to dispose of the Election case. The learned Counsel with reference to the said resolution (Annexure-C) to this supplementary affidavit and the ground taken in the Election petition and the ill feeling and likelihood of maintaining of grudge by the Tribunal submitted that it is just and proper to transfer the Election Case to any other Tribunal as there is bonafide apprehension in the mind of the petitioner that he may not get just and impartial trial before the present Election Tribunal and the Commission should have transferred the case from the Divisional Election Tribunal Dhaka to any other competent Tribunal.

6. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel appearing for the Respondent No. 2 has submitted that the case record would show that the notice of the case would not be served upon the petitioner in the normal course because the petitioner evaded service thereof, for which upon an order for special messenger for the purpose. the service of notices was effected on 30.7.97 and in spite of his appearance before the Tribunal on 4.8.97 no written statement has been filed untill 15.3.98 and meanwhile the petitioner adopted dilatory tactics on this plea or others even coming to this Court with writ application and moving the Appellate Division. The learned Counsel further submitted that the plea of alleged resolution was taken at a much belated stage which did never struck the mind of the petitioner at earliest opportunity and such application at the belated stage was designed to prolong and delay disposal of the case inasmuch as no such resolution was produced before the Election Commission.

7. From the record it appears that notices on the petitioner was served by special messenger. The petitioner though appeared in the case on 23.7.97 but until 15.3.98 the written statement was not filed in the case. The petitioner has however filed the application for transfer before the Election Commission with allegation that be may not get fair and impartial trial before the Divisional Election Tribunal as there was animosity between the learned Judge and the petitioner as the President and a member of the Kishoregonj Bar Association. The petitioner has produced a copy of the extract of the resolution dated 18.2.96 which go to show that the Bar Association condemned the anti-judicial sentiment of the Tribunal Judge who was the Additional District and Sessions Judge and demanded his immediate removal from the said station and even decision was taken not to invite him in any function of the Association. Though the petitioner explained the delay as mark of respect to the Tribunal but should have taken this plea for transfer of the case at the earliest opportunity but had spent time adopting other steps in the case. We are of the view that the resolution itself cannot be ignored or cannot be brushed aside as the litigant's mind is always susceptible to doubts and naturally a bonafide apprehension may arise in the mind of the petitioner that he may not get any fair or impartial trial before the Election Tribunal against which he was party to the resolution while the latter was an Additional District and Sessions Judge in the recent post.

8. From the impugned order it also appears that the mind of the Election Commissioner has also worked towards an order of transfer as is apparent from his observation that the "learned Advocate for the petitioner wants it to be transferred to any Court at Dhaka, District Judge. Dhaka is very busy with his own Court and Additional District Judge are not appointed tribunal. If any Additional District Judge is to be appointed Tribunal approval of the Hon'ble Chief Justice will be necessary, which will take more time".

<u>9. Article 53 of the People's Order No. 155 of 1972 provide that the Commission shall appoint as many Election Tribunal as may be necessary for trial of the Election petition and a Tribunal shall consist of person who is or has been a District and Sessions Judge or an Additional District and Sessions Judge.</u>

<u>10. In the facts and circumstances above, we are of the view that a bonafide apprehension may arise in the mind of the petitioner that he may not get any fair and impartial trial in the hand of the Divisional Election Tribunal, Dhaka. In view of the above, ends of justice would be best served if the Election Tribunal Case No. 2 of 1997 be transferred from the Divisional Election Tribunal, Dhaka to any other Court of competent Jurisdiction at Dhaka.</u>

11. Upon transfer of the case, the District Judge or Additional District and Sessions Judge as the newly appointed Election Tribunal shall only hear and dispose of this case in accordance in law and as such upon appointment by the Commission for this case only, the newly appointed Tribunal shall dispose of the Election case with its all existing logistic support available to it to hear and dispose of the case of its normal Jurisdiction.

12. In view of the above the impugned order of the Election Commission is not sustainable in law and the same is set aside and the Election Tribunal Case No. 2 of 1997 now pending before Divisional Election Tribunal, Dhaka is transferred to the Court of any Additional District and Sessions Judge. Dhaka to be appointed by the Election Commission for disposal for this Election Case No. 2 of 1997 only with its available logistic support of the said newly appointed court and the Election Commissioner shall accordingly issue an appropriate notification appointing one of the Additional District and Sessions Judge, Dhaka within 15 days receipt of this order obtaining permission, if any from the Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh and shall forthwith transmit the record of the case of the said Tribunal preferably within a week for trial.

<u>13. Article 57(6) provides that the Tribunal shall try an Election petition as expeditiously as possible and shall endeavour to conclude the trial within six months from the date on which the election petition is referred to it for trial. This Election Case was filed on 13.8.96 and the Election Tribunal received the record on 2.11.96 and although the notice of the case was served on 23.7.97 but the petitioner filed written statement on 15.3.98 and in the process the case could not be heard as yet. The petitioner has given a solemn undertaking in this Court that he would co-operate for disposal of the case within six months from the date of receipt of the record by the Tribunal. This is a solemn promise given by the petitioner who obtained the love and admiration from the people's to be elected as the Deputy Speaker of the Parliament. In view of the provision of law and the undertaking as above, we direct that the Additional District and Sessions Judge. Dhaka to be appointed by the Election Commission as the Election Tribunal for this case alone, shall endeavour to complete the hearing and dispose of the case on priority basis within six months from the date of receipt of the record of the case and it is hoped that the parties shall co-operate with the Tribunal in the disposal of the case within the time fixed.</u>

14. The newly appointed Tribunal on receipt of the record of the case shall forthwith issue notices of the case to the parties and also allow the respondent No. 2 effect the service of notices upon the petitioner and other opposite parties to the Election Petition, if necessary though special messenger to help disposal of the case at the earliest.

15. In the result this Rule made absolute but without any order as to costs. Let the record of the Tribunal Case No. 2 of 1997 along with the copy of this order be transmitted to the Election Commission for taking appropriate action in the light of this order at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. M.K. Rahman with Mr. Idrisur Rahman, Advocates for the petitioner
Mr. Abdul Quiyum, Advocate for the opposite party
parties:
Syed A. Jalil ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Mahbub Alam (Babul) and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md. Nurul Islam, J: This Rule was is-sued at the instance of the petitioner directing the opposite party No. I to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 29.11.1994 passed by the learned District Judge, Patuakhali in Election Appeal No. 6 of 1993 affirming the Judgment and order dated 16.9.1993 passed by the learned Election Tribunal, Patuakhali in Election Petition Case No. 9 of 1992 declaring opposite party No. 1 as Chairman of No. 12 Bauphal Union Parishad should not be set aside.

2. The fact of the case, in short, is that the petitioner filed an Election Petition before the Assistant Judge and Election Tribunal being Election Petition Case No. 9 of 1992 against the opposite party No. 1 stating, inter alia, that the opposite party no. 1 and other candidates contested the election for the post of Chairman of Bauphal Union Parishad and the said election was held on 29.1.1992 and 27.2.1992. The symbol of the petitioner was 'duck' and opposite party No 1 symbol was 'deer', and the other candidates had their other symbols. The election centers were at Goshinga Government Primary School, Bibilash Government Primary School (No. 2) No. 1 Bibilash Government Primary School, Bauphal Degree College, Jouta Primary School and Bilbilash Olipura Salehia Dakhil Madrasha. In the said election the petitioner secured the highest votes from his nearest rival opposite party no. 1 and according to the result of the election, the name of the petitioner was published as Chairman of the aforesaid Union Parishad in the official Gazette dated 11.4.1992. Thereafter the petitioner took oath as Chairman of the aforesaid Union Parishad and since then he has been performing his functions of the office of the Chairman as Chairmen of the said Union Parishad. The opposite party no.1 filed a Election Petition before the Senior Assistant Judge and Election Tribunal, Patuakhali Challenging the election stating that the votes were not held justly and fairly in Goshinga Government Primary School Centre and Jouta Primary School Centre and in other four polling centres vote were held peacefully but counting of ballots in all the centres were not done fairly and malpractices were adopted there. For this he filed this election petition for declaration that the declaration of the petitioner as elected Chairman of Bauphal Union Parishad according to the election held on 29.1.1992 and 27.2.1992 respectively is illegal, unlawful and void and feat the opposite party No. 1 is elected Chairman of the said Union Parishad.

3. The petitioner who is the opposite party no. 1 in the election petition contested the case by filing written objection denying all material allegations stated in the election petition and stated inter alia that the election and counting of votes were held properly and in presence of all the agents of contesting candidates and he got highest votes and declared as Chairman of the said election. During the course of trial the tribunal made in order dated 26.4.1993 for recounting of ballots of the said election. Being aggrieved at and dissatisfied with the order dated 26.4.1993 the petitioner filed a Writ Petition being No. 749 of 1993 before this Court and the said Writ Petition was rejected of 12.5.1993. Against that order dated 12.5.1993 the petitioner moved Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 208 of 1993 before the Appellate Division of this Court and their Lordship by their judgment dismissed the petition on 4.7.1993 after giving some directions to the tribunal for disposal of the petition. According to the observations and direction of the Appellate Division the tribunal examined 6 Presiding Officers of all 6 polling centres and the Returning Officer as prosecution witnesses and tribunal recounted the ballot papers on 21.7.1993 and 24.8.1993 and found that the petitioner got 2694 instead of 2729 votes secured originally and the opposite party no. 1 i.e. the present petitioner secured 2697 votes including challenged votes. Ext. 2 (Gha) and in place of 2726 votes he secured in original counting. The Election Tribunal after recruiting the votes all after perusal of the record allowed the election petition on 16.9.1993 and declared opposite party No. 1 as Chairman of Bauphal Union Parishad, is illegal and void and the petitioner is declared as Chairman of the said Union Parishad. The opposite party preferred an appeal against the aforesaid order before the appellate tribunal and the said appeal is numbered as Election Appeal No. 6 of 1993. The appellate tribunal by its Judgment and order dated 29.11.94 dismissed the appeal and upheld the order of election tribunal. Being aggrieved at and dissatisfied with the aforesaid order the petitioner preferred this application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

4. Mr. M.K. Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submitted that at the time of rejection the leave petition by the Appellate Division their Lordships made some observation to be followed by the tribunal. But at the time of recounting the votes the tribunal did into comply with these observations into and did not discuss the deposition of P.Ws. 1-8. Although those de-position were taken as per observation of the Appellate Division and therefore the tribunal failed to arrive at a correct decision. In the order of the leave petition their Lordships observed as follows:-

“However, in the matter of recounting of ballot paper, the tribunal must take adequate precaution against any malpractices; the tribunal must see whether the ballot box was kept in proper custody from the time of its despatch by the presiding officer till its destination and whether the sealed bag containing the ballot packets, as well as the sealed ballot packets are intact, in that connection evidence of competent witnesses including the presiding officer concerned should be recorded".

<u>5. It is stated above that the tribunal examined 8 P.Ws. after this observation and they are presiding officers and returning officers of the election centres. The learned Advocate further submitted that the trial court did not discuss anything about the deposit ones of those p.ws. in its judgment. But the learned Advocate for the opposite party submitted that the Appellate Tribunal discussed evidences of those witnesses in its judgment. A question before us is that the Appellate Division directed the tribunal to comply with its observation and not to the appellate tribunal. In this respect the learned Advocate for the opposite party draw our attention to the orders no. 26-37 stating that but those are not election tribunal complied with the observation of the Appellate Division. I have gone through all the orders. Only orders no. 26 speaks about recounting of the votes but in that order the learned Assistant Judge did not discussed the evidence of P.Ws. 1-6 specially whether the bags contained the ballot papers are intact according to the direction of the Appellate Division. The learned Advocate for the petitioner pointed out some portion of deposition of P.Ws. 1-6 which is stated in the petition in paragraph 13 about 'gala seal' torn gunny bags and signature of the agent of the candidates on the paper of the bag. The learned tribunal Judge did not discuss these evidences and discard those by giving reasons. The appellate court in the last partition of para 7 of the judgment made a summarily discussion of the evidences of P.Ws. and case to a finding that the seals of gunny bags and ballot papers were intact and in proper order at the time of re-opening the gunny bags for recounting the ballot papers. I have gone through the evidences of P.Ws. only to see whether the tribunal considered the evidences of P.Ws. in accordance with the observation of the Appellate Division. P.W. 1 Md. Daliluddin said that he was presiding officer of Bauphal Degree College centre and he sealed the bag and sent it to the Returning officer, In cross-examination he said that the seal over the bag is broken and the paper was lost. Similarly P.W. 2 who was presiding officer of Goshinga Government primary school centre said in cross-examination that he did not take signature of the agent of any parties of the paper at the time of giving seal and that the paper which is on the bag is not posted by him. P.W. 3 A.K.M. Fazlul Huq who was presiding officer of Goshinga Government primary school centre said in his cross-examination that with the ballot paper gunny bag he found seals are tagged with which he did not tag with the bag. P.W. 5 Ayub Ali said in his cross examination that there is a hole under the bag which contains the ballot. P.W. 6 who was presiding officer of Bilbilash (1) Government primary school centre said in his cross examination that the polithin beg which contain the original seal of the election was not under gala seal and the paper over the bag was without any writing and was torn. All the aforesaid P.Ws. said that they send the bags of ballot papers to the Assistant Returning Officer. But P.W.7 the Returning Officer of the election, said that he received those bags from the presiding officers and all were kept within a room of the Thana Nirbahi Officers office and thereafter these were kept at the Agrani Bank on the order of the T.N.O. In cross-examination he said that his duty was to sent the those bag to T.N.O. but he did not deposit those to T.N.O. and no written order was obtained from T.N.O. to give those bags in the custody of Agrani Bank. In support of his submission the learned Advocate for the petitioner referred a case reported in 15 BLD 651 (Md. Mostakin Ali Vs. Abdul Matlib and others) where in his Lordship Mr. Bimalendu Bikash Roy Chowdhury, J observed.</u>

<u>"Rules 40(1)(4)and 42 of the Union Parishads (Election) Rules, 1993 provides that these rules provide for proper sealing of the packets containing ballot papers and also the gunny bags so as to ensure that nothing is removeable therefrom without breaking the seal. The object of those rules is to secure not only the secrecy of the ballot but also to eliminate chances of post election tampering of the election materials"</u>

<u>According to above discussion of these evidences of p.ws. some discrepancies are found that is about the bag of original seals which was found open and tagged with a gunny bag of ballot paper although those were sent within a separate polithin bag and also about proper custody of these ballot paper gunny bags and also about condition of those bags. These facts have not been discussed by the tribunal or the appellate tribunal in their judgments. The learned Advocates for the opposite party submitted that the custody of the ballot paper, bagged, allegations of tampering of ballot papers condition of gunny bags and original seals etc. are question of fact and this court has no jurisdiction to decide those in its revisional jurisdiction. Against these the learned Advocate for the petitioner relied on a decision reported in 16 B.L.D. (AD) 21 (Government of Bangladesh Vs. Md. Jalil and others) wherein their Lordership in a case, under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh, a case about the decision of the Court of Settlement observed that</u>

<u>"The High Court Division was not a court of appeal required to make determination of facts on its his own. It could interfere with the findings of a tribunal of fact under the extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution only if it could be shown that the tribunal had acted without jurisdiction or made any finding upon no evidence or without considering any material evidence/facts causing prejudice to the complaining party or that it had acted malafide or in violation of any principle of natural justice. In the absence of any of these conditions the interference by the High Court Division will itself be an act without jurisdiction."</u>

<u>The principle is applicable in the case of above nature but it cannot be taken into consideration in the present case which is not under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh. Here in the instant case the Appellate Division directed the Tribunal to decide some facts and for arriving at a proper decision. The tribunal examined some P.W.s and recorded their deposition but the tribunal did not consider those deposition in arriving at a correct decision and thereby the tribunal did not only comply with the observations made by the Appellate Division but it acted in violation of the above observations. Similarly the Appellate Tribunal did not comply with the observation of the Appellate Division in deciding the case and made no remark in its judgment about non compliance of such observation by the tribunal. The observation of superior court is binding on and guiding principle of the lower court or tribunal. It is not understood whether non-compliance of superior court is a wilful negligence or of carelessness of the tribunals. However, the lower court or tribunal must be careful to comply with the observation of the superior court. As regards gunny bag the learned Advocate for the opposite party submitted that if there be any hole in gunny bag containing the ballot papers and if there is no allegation of malpractice committed either increase or decrease of ballots from each side the question of recounting of ballot papers of the gunny bag do not arise. But in the instant case the Appellate Division gave specific direction for recounting of the ballot papers.</u>

<u>But it is found that the tribunal failed to comply with the observation before recounting of the ballot papers. In view of the above discussion I find substances in the submission made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner.</u>

<u>6. About delay in recounting the ballot papers he submitted that in a case reported in 15 B.L.D. 651 it is observed that the delay in re-counting the ballot papers after nine months is considered not justified. In the instant case election was held on 29.1.1992 and 27.2.92 and the Gazette Notification took place on 11.4.1992 and the election petition was filed on 10.5.1992 and recounting of ballot papers took place on 21.7.1993 and 24.8.93 i.e. about 1½ years after the election. Moreover it is found that the election materials specially the gunny bags of ballot papers were under the custody of Thana Nirbahi Officer instead of the Deputy Commissioner or according to Rules 40 and 42 of the Union Parishad Rules 1983. From whose custody the ballot papers, bags were brought back to the tribunal has not been ascertained and the tribunal did not give any finding about proper custody of ballot paper. It is not the duty of the tribunal to recount ballot papers which did not come from the proper custody and found not properly gala sealed at the time of opening the bags of the ballot for recounting. So the recounting of the ballot papers by the tribunal, in the instant case, cannot be considered as properly and legally done. Considering the above discussion of the facts and circumstances of the case I find substance in the application.</u>

7. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order of the Appellate Tribunal is set aside. Send down the lower Court's record immediately.

End.

Vs.

with
Idu Mia and others
Vs.

full_judgment:
S. K. Shiha, J: These rules arise between the same parties over the same subject matter, against decisions of two distinct  suits of distinct in nature, are taken up for analogous hearing for, the convenience of the parties. Therefore, this judgment would govern both the rules. Rule in Civil Revision no.3475 of 1998 is directed against the judgment and decree dated 6.8.98 of the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in title appeal no.150 of 1988 reversing those dated 30.6.88 of the learned Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in title suit no.37 of 1985. Rule in Civil Revision No.803 of 1987 is directed against the judgment and decree dated 29.8.87 of the Small Causes Court, Dhaka, in S.C.C. Suit no.180 of 1985. In title suit no. 37 of 1985, the plaintiffs are the defendants in S.C.C. Suit no.180 of 1985 and the defendants are the plaintiffs in S.C.C. suit no.180 of 1985.

2. Plaintiffs instituted the suit for declaration of title and for further declaration that they are not tenants under the defendants. Defendants instituted S.C.C. Suit No.180 of 1985 for eviction of tenants claiming the plaintiffs in title suit no.37 of 1985 as their tenants in respect of the suit land.

3. Plaintiffs' case in title suit no.37 of 1985 is that Abdul Gani Khalifa was the original owner of the suit land on whose death, Sk. Jummon, Mohiuddin, Idu, Karim, Joygun Bibi and Belaton Bibi became the owners of the suit land. The said Abdul Gani Khalifa settled the suit land in favour of Abdul Hakim, the predecessor of the plaintiffs on yearly rental basis, who constructed a dwelling house on the suit land. After the death of Abdul Gani Khalifa, Abdul Hakim executed a kabuliyat in Chaitra, 1348 B.S. in favour of said Sk. Jummon and others for a period of 11 years. Abdul Hakim mutated his name in the Municipal holding, paid rent to the Municipality and also paid rent to the Government and continued such possession till the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, came into operation. In 1955 Abdul Hakim died and the plaintiffs continue such possession as of right. On 8.2.84, the defendants served a. notice upon them under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act demanding them to vacate possession of the suit land, which cast cloud in their title in the suit land.

4. Defendants contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying all material allegations made in the plaint and asserted that Abdul Hakim took lease of the suit land with a measurement of 13 cubits X 10 cubits by executing a kabuliyat for 11 years at a yearly rental of Tk.3/-. Subsequently Abdul Hakitn surrendered the land in favour of the landlord and he was granted lease of 12X5½  cubits of land at a fixed rent to be paid on yearly basis. After the death of Abdul Hakim, the plaintiffs have no right to continue as tenants in the suit land, who are trespassers and therefore, they are liable to be evicted. Their further case is that they have already instituted S.C.C. Suit No.180 of 1985 for eviction of the plaintiffs on the ground that they were trespassers in the suit land.

5. The defence case of the defendants in title suit no. 37 of 1985 is the plaint case in S.C.C. Suit no. 180 of 1985 and the plaint case in title suit no. 37 of 1985 is the defence case in S.C.C. Suit no. 180 of 1985. As such in order to avoid repetition I need not to reiterate the plaint case and the defence case in S.C.C. Suit no. 180 of 1985.

6. The learned Assistant Judge by judgment and order dated 30.6.88 decreed title suit no.37 of 1985. Defendants being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree, preferred title appeal no.150 of 1988. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka who heard the said appeal, by judgment and decree dated 6.8.98, allowed the appeal and set aside those of the learned Assistant Judge. Plaintiffs being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the court of appeal below, obtained rule in Civil Revision no.3475 of 1998. On the other hand, the learned S.C.C. Judge by judgment and decree dated 27.4.87, dismissed the S.C.C. Suit No.180 of 1985 holding that complicated questions of title is involved in the stilt. Defendants being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree, preferred a revisional application under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act and rule in Civil Revision No.803 of 1987 arises out of the said judgment.

7. Mr. A. B. Roy Chowdhury, learned Advocate for the petitioners in Civil Revision No. 3475 of 1998 submits that the court of appeal below on misconception of law held that the plaintiffs have acquired no right, title and interest in the suit land.

8. It is admitted by the parties that Abdul Gani Khalifa was the original owner of the suit land who granted settlement of the suit land in favour of Abdul Hakim. It is also admitted fact that after the death of Abdul Gani Khalifa, Abdul Hakim executed a registered kabuliyat on 8th Chaitra, 1348 B. S. in favour of Sk. Jummon and others binding himself as tenant to pay yearly rent of Tk.3/= for 11 years in respect of the suit land. In the plaint there is positive averments that Abdul Hakim took settlement of the suit land and .thereafter he raised constructions in the suit land. In the written statement, the defendants have not denied the said facts, rather in paragraph 13(kha), they have admitted that Abdul Hakim gave lease of the land and not the premises with land. In such admitted position of the case, there is no dispute that Abdul Gani Khalifa gave lease of non-agricultural land to Abdul Hakim and the plaintiffs Predecessor Abdul Hakim was non-agricultural tenant within the meaning of Sub-section(5) of Section 2 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, which provides:

"Non-agricultural tenant" means a person who holds non-agricultural land under another person with consent of that person and is, or but for a special contract would be, liable to pay rent to such person for that land and also includes the successors-in-interest of the former but does not include any person who holds any such land on which any premises occupied by such person are situated if such premises have been erected, or are owned by the person to whom such occupier is, or but for a special contract would be liable to pay rent for such occupation:".

"Explanation- In this clause "premises" mean any building such as a house, manufactory, warehouse, stable, shop or but whether constructed of masonry, bricks, concrete, wood, mud, metal or any other material whatsoever and includes any land appertaining to such building."

9. It appears that the kabuliyat Ext. 2 is an admitted document executed on 8th Chaitra, 1348 B.S. corresponding to 22.3.42 for a period of 11 years. The said deed has been described as “মিরাশী স্বত্ব ভুমির ১১ বৎসরের মেয়াদী কবুলিয়াত"।In the said deed, it has been recited that মিরাশী ভুমিমিরাশ বন্দোবস্ত লইয়া ও মালিক দখল থাকিয়া। This expression মিরাশ according to Glossary of settlement and vernacular terms means,

"From war as to inherit, it signifies an ancestral tenure. In practical use it implies a, tenure at a fixed rent and is heritable and transferable."

In the plaint there is clear averment to the effect that the land was settled in favour of Abdul Hakim by Abdul Gani Khalifa. On a perusal of the said Kabuliyat ext 2, there is no dispute that the plaintiffs' predecessor was given "Miras settlement" of non-agricultural land for 11 years from before 22.3.42. Before the expiry of said period of 11 years, the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 came into force on 20th October 1949. It is an admitted fact that the "Miras settlement" of the suit land was granted at an annual rental of Tk.3/-.

10. The tenancy of Abdul Hakim was created under the provisions of the Bengal Non Agricultural Tenancy (Temporary Provisions) Act 1940, which tenancy was neither heritable nor transferable. The said Act, 1940 was repealed on 20.10.49 and the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 came into force on and from that date. Though the defendants claim that the plaintiffs surrendered possession, but they failed to prove such claim, rather it has been established from the pleadings as well as from the evidence on record that from before the date of execution of the kubutiyat, ext-2. Abdul Hakim had been in possession of the suit land in the same capacity for more than 12 years. Rights of a tenant of Non-Agricultural land were recognised under section 7 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, the relevant provision runs thus:-

"7. INCIDENTS OF CERTAIN TENANCIES.-Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or, in any contract-....

(1)......

(2) if the non-agricultural land comprised in any tenancy which has been or is created after the commencement of the Transfer of Property Act; 1882 (IV of 1882), has been held for a period of not less than twelve years without any lease in writing, or

(3) ......

(4) ......

(5) if the landlord has allowed pucca structures to he erected on any non-agricultural landheld  under a lease in writing for a period specified therein, whether such  structures have been erected

(a) before the expiration of the said period, or

(b) where such non-agricultural land .continues to be held with the express or implied consent of the landlord after the expiration of the said period during the period such non-agricultural land so continues to be held,

then-

(i) the tenant holding the non-agricultural land comprised in such tenancy shall not be ejected by his landlord from such land except on the ground that he has used such land in a manner which renders it unfit for use for any of the purposes specified in section 4;

(ii) subject to the provisions of section 91 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, (E.B. Act XXVIII of 1951), the interest of the tenant in the non-agricultural land comprised in such tenancy shall, in the case where such tenant dies intestate in respect of such interest, be transmitted by inheritance in the same manner as his other immovable property.

Under this section certain classes of tenants holding non-agricultural land were given non-ejectable and heritable right if such tenants are in continuous occupation of the tenanted land by raising pucca structures for over 12 years did bring them within the category of "Non-Agricultural Tenant" and the tenants shall get protection under section 7 of the said Act.

<u>11. In view of the nature of settlement as given to Abdul Hakim "Mirash Bandubasta" of the suit land, followed by continuous possession over 12 years, by raising constructions such settlement, falls into one such class under section 7(2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. The tenancy in question was created prior to 22.3.42 which continued on 20.10.49 when Act XXIII of 1949 came into force and in view of section 89A of the said Act, the plaintiffs acquired an interest to continue such possession as of right which is protected from eviction. The interest of Abdul Hakim in the suit land in such tenancy has been transmitted by inheritance to the plaintiffs on the death of Abdul Hakim under clause (II) of sub-section (5) of Section 7.</u>

12. It is admitted fact that after the death of Abdul Hakim, the plaintiffs are continuing in possession without any interruption till 8.2.84 on which date, they received a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act directing them to vacate possession in favour of the defendants which constituted the cause of action for instituting the suit.

13. The Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act was amended by Ordinance No. IX of 1967, wherein certain chapters and sections of the said Act were repealed and section 26A was inserted prohibiting sub-letting of tenancy, which provides:-

"26A(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, no non-agricultural tenant shall sub-let the whole or any part of his tenancy on any terms or conditions whatsoever.

(2) If any tenancy or any part of a tenancy is sub-let, in contravention of the provision of sub-section(1), the interest of the non-agricultural tenant in the tenancy or in that part of the tenancy, as the case may be, shall be extinguished, and the tenancy or the part of the tenancy shall vest in the Government from the date of such sub-letting free from all encumbrances.

" This provision is almost similar to section 75A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. The intention of the legislature in inserting this provision and deletion of certain provisions is clear. The rights of the landlord of non-agricultural land which they had, even after the acquisition of rent receiving interest has been curtailed, on and from the date of promulgation of ordinance No. IX of 1967. There cannot be any new lease of non-agricultural land from the date of promulgation of the said ordinance. The expression "subletting" connotes the creation of a sub-ordinate tenancy or under raiyat, under which the sub-lessee would but for a special contract be liable to pay rent for that land to a person other than the Government. The purpose of inserting this section appears to be that since after the acquisition of the interest of rent receivers by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, the rent receivers were themselves to retain certain classes of retainable khas land as tenants directly under the Government, they should not be allowed to create further sub-tenancies under them. I am therefore, of the view that the plaintiffs status became tenants under th6 Government after section 26A, came into force. Considering this aspect of the matter, Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan finds difficult to oppose the rule. He however, feebly argues that the court of appeal below was justified in dismissing the suit.

<u>14. Plaintiffs in support of their claim of title in the suit land, filed ext. 1 series, the payment of holding tax to the pourashava, the mutation of the name of Abdul Hakim in the Municipal holding, exts. 4 and the payment of rent to the government ext.3 series, besides ext.2 the kabuliyat. This payment of rent by the plaintiffs in respect of the suit land shows that the plaintiffs have been recognised as tenants under the government. The trial court has considered these documentary evidence and held that the plaintiffs have acquired title in the suit land, since they are in possession for more than 12 years.</u>

15. The court of appeal below misconstrued Ext. 2, the kabuliyat and held that the said deed being an unilateral deed," Abdul Hakim was a lessee under the defendants and not tenant in the suit land and that as no bilateral lease deed was executed, the said kabuliyat is hit by section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act. The court of appeal below further held that Abdul Hakim was not a yearly tenant, who acquired no status as "tenant" under the Non-agricultural Tenancy Act. The court of appeal below totally misread ext.2 wherein there is specific recitals to the effect that the tenancy would be heritable, which was created at a yearly rental of Tk.3/=. The court of appeal below also did not consider section 7 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, under which provision if the landlord allows the tenant to erect pucca structures in the tenanted land such tenancy will be heritable. It may be pointed out here that Abdul Hakim raised construction in the suit land is not disputed by the defendants. In view of such facts, though the suit land was recorded in the name of the defendants, I am of the opinion that such record will not stand on the way in getting a decree by the plaintiffs in the suit since the plaintiffs have acquired a heritable, non-eject able right in the suit land particularly when the said S.A. record which was prepared after 1960, after the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 came into force. I am further of the view that the plaintiffs have acquired a right which cannot be said anything less than title in the suit land. The court of appeal below upon misconstruction of Ext. 2, the Kabuliyat held that Abdul Hakim was given lease of the suit land by Kabuliyat ext.2 which is hit by section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act. This decision of the court of appeal below is an error occasioning failure of justice In that view of the matter, the learned Assistant Judge was justified in finding title of the plaintiffs in the suit land and has rightly decreed the suit.

16. As I find above that Abdul Hakim was granted settlement of non-agricultural land, where Abdul Hakim raised construction, the S.C.C suit No. 180 of 1985 instituted by the defendants under the provisions of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance was a misconceived one. Further, as plaintiffs have acquired title in the suit land; this suit for eviction is not legally maintainable. The learned S.C.C. Judge has rightly dismissed the suit holding that the suit is not maintainable. In view of the above, I find substance in the rule in Civil Revision no. 3475 of 1998 and I find no substance in the Rule in Civil Revision no. 803 of 1987.

17. In the result, the Rule in Civil Revision no. 3475 of 1998 is made absolute without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree dated 6.8.98 of the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in title appeal no.150 of 1988 reversing those dated 30.6.88 of the learned Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, in title suit no.37 of 1985 are set aside and restored those of the learned Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka. The rule in Civil Revision no.803 of 1987 is discharged without any order as to costs.

Send the lower court records.

End.

case_source: (arising out of Writ Petition No. 2328 and 2329 of 1998)
full_judgment:
Qazi Shafiuddin, J: These two review applications being Review Application Nos. 15 and 16 of 1998 arises out of Writ Petition Nos. 2328 and 2329 of 1998 respectively have been heard together and will now be disposed of by this common judgment as the same arise out of the order dated 14.12.97 passed by the President and Member, Customs Excise and VAT Tribunal in CEVT/Case(Kas) no. 148/97.

2. In these two applications the judgment and order dated 9.8.98 passed in writ petition nos. 2328 and 2329 of 1998 have sought to be reviewed on the ground stated in the applications. In these petitions it is stated that the Appellate Tribunal did not consider the petitioners declaration form and further the petitioners were heard by a Special Bench not duly constituted and hence it is said that the impugned order is corum non-judice. Being aggrieved with the order dated 9.8.98 the petitioners sought that the same should be reviewed.

3. In the original writ petitions under Article 102 of the Constitution the judgment and order dated 14.12.97 passed by the President and Member, Customs Excise and VAT Tribunal in CEVT/Case (Kas) no. 148/97 affirming the order dated 14.5.97 passed by the Commissioner, Customs House, Dhaka were called in question.

4. The review petitioner Md. Omar Faruk (Review Petition No. 15/98) filed W.P. No. 2328/98. It is stated in the writ petition that the petitioner returned to Zia International Airport, Dhaka from Singapore. He carried with him 170 tolas of gold in 17 bars and 4 Kg. silver in two separate polythine covered packets and also other miscellaneous articles. It is stated that the petitioner made a declaration before the Inspector about the goods including 170 tolas of gold in 17 bars and 4 Kg. silver in two separate polythine covered packets. It is stated that he also signed the declaration form on the same date. It is further stated that the Customs Authority seized the goods on 12.5.97 including 170 tolas of gold and 4 Kg silver and other miscellaneous articles and made a seizure list. An appeal was preferred against the order dated 12.5.97 before the Commissioner, Customs House, Kurmitola, Dhaka but the appeal was dismissed. Thereafter the petitioner preferred an appeal on 17.8.97 before the President, Appellate Tribunal, Customs Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal affirmed the judgment and order of the Commissioner, Customs, Dhaka by its order dated 14.12.97 and dismissed the appeal. Thereafter he filed a review application before the Tribunal but the Tribunal rejected the review petition and lastly he filed an application under Article 102 of the Constitution before this Court and this Court by order dated 9.8.98 summarily rejected the application. Against the aforesaid order the review application being Review Application No. 15/98 has been filed.

5. Petitioner Ashraf in Review Petition No. 16/98 also filed an application under Article 102 of the Constitution being W.P. No. 2329/98 challenging the judgment and order as aforesaid. In that application it is stated that the petitioner returned to Zia International Airport, Dhaka on 10.5.98 from Singapore and carried 130 tolas of gold in 13 bars and 4 Kg silver in two separate polythine covered packets. He kept those goods on the table of the Excise Inspector for payment of taxes. He made a self-declaration before the Inspector about the gold and silver carried by him. The petitioner did not sign the declaration form on 10.5.97. It is alleged that the Inspector did not return the goods of the petitioner without showing any reasonable ground. The goods were seized. Thereafter the petitioner filed a petition before the Commissioner of Customs for releasing the seized goods and the Commissioner of Customs passed the order on 14.5.97. The petitioner did not make any declaration as to the goods. Order dated 14.5.97 was passed forfeiting 130 tolas of gold and 4 Kg silver. He filed an appeal on 17.8.97 before the Appellate Tribunal. The Appellate Tribunal passed the judgment and order on 14.12.97. Thereafter a review petition was filed before the Tribunal but the same was rejected and thereafter he filed a writ petition before this Court and this Court by order dated 9.8.98 summarily rejected the writ petition. Against the aforesaid order dated 9.8.98 this review application has been filed.

6. In these two review applications it is stated that the Appellate Tribunal did not consider the declaration form and further the Special Bench so constituted was not formed in accordance with law who heard the appeal as such the order passed by the Tribunal is a corum-non-judice. On these two grounds these review applications have been filed. These two grounds were not stated in the writ petitions and there is no explanation whatsoever that these two grounds are new and important grounds which escaped the notice of the petitioner as such the judgment and order complained of should be reviewed. It is admitted by the petitioners that the Tribunal so constituted was well within their knowledge and they appeared before the Tribunal and further they filed a review petition before the Tribunal. So improper constitution of the Tribunal cannot be agitated at this stage by way of submission that this constitutes a new and important ground which they came to know after the passing of the judgment. The petitioners were well aware about the constitution of the Tribunal and the same was not at all agitated before this Court at the time of hearing of the writ petitions.

7. The order sought to be reviewed is dated 9.8.98 passed by this Court. These review applications were filed on 27.8.98 long after the statutory period of limitation. Article 103 of the Constitution provides:-

"103. (1) The Appellate Division shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine appeals from judgments, decrees, orders or sentences of the High Court Division.

(2) An appeal to the Appellate Division from a judgment, decree, order or sentence of the High Court Division shall lie as of right were the High Court Division—

(a) Certifies that the case involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of this constitution; or

(b) Has sentenced a person to death or to (imprisonment) for life; or

(c) Has imposed punishment on a person for contempt of that division; and in such other cases as may be provided for by Act or Parliament.

(3) An appeal to the Appellate Division from a judgment, decree, order or sentence of the High Court Division in a case to which clause (2) does not apply shall lie only if the Appellate Division grants leave to appeal.

(4) Parliament may be law declares that the provisions of this article shall apply in relation to any other court or tribunal as they apply in relation to the High Court Division."

It is to be noted that the petitioners did not file any appeal before the Appellate Division against the order dated 9.8.98 and now they have filed these two review applications which is out of time. The Constitution does not provide for any review of the judgments, decree, order etc. passed by the High Court Division, Article 105 of the Constitution sets out:

"The Appellate Division shall have power, subject to the provisions of any Act of Parliament and of any rules made by that division to review any judgment pronounced or order made by it".

Only the Appellate Division by the power subject to the provision of an Act of Parliament and any rules made by it, the Appellate Division may review its own judgment or order.

<u>8. Jurisdiction is a creature of statute or law. If the statute does not expressly confer jurisdiction upon any Court, the order passed by the Court becomes corum non-judice. As we have observed that the power of review have been provided in Article 105 of the Constitution only to the Appellate Division and the Appellate Division may review the judgment and order and the same is exercised in two ways (1) changing the decision of a case by reviewing the judgment originally delivered in that case and (II) overruling a principle of law enunciated in a previous case. In a leading case Kaikaus, J observed—</u>

<u>"On a proper consideration it will be found that the principles underlying the limitations mentioned in Order XLVII, Rule 1, Civil Procedure Code, are implicit in the nature of review jurisdiction. While I would prefer not to accept those limitations as if they placed any technical obstruction in the exercise of the review jurisdiction of this Court I would accept that they would embody the principles on which this Court would act in the exercise of such jurisdiction. It is not because a conclusion is wrong but because something obvious has been overlooked. Some important aspect of the matter has not been considered, that a review petition will lie. It is a remedy to be used only in exceptional circumstances."</u>

<u>Order 47 Rule 1 C.P.C. also provides for review by person considering himself aggrieved:</u>

<u>"(a) by a decree or order 'from which an appeal is allowed, but from which no appeal has been preferred,</u>

<u>(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is allowed, or</u>

<u>(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of Small Causes,"</u>

<u>In these review applications the petitioners does not say that they have discovered a new ground which escaped their notice earlier but simply they have said that the Tribunal so constituted was not a proper Tribunal as per law and hence the order passed by it is a corum non-judice. As we have already observed that the Tribunal as constituted is well within their knowledge. They filed appeal and review application before that Tribunal. As to the constitution of the Tribunal they cannot now say that the Tribunal is corum non-judice and furthermore they did not make any grievance about the constitution of the Tribunal earlier. There is no such explanation for not urging the point before this Court 1st the time of hearing the writ petition. Therefore, neither the ingredients of Order 47 Rule 1 C.P.C. nor the Appellate Division Rules apply in this case. Furthermore we have already observed that he jurisdiction is the creature of the statute. Since the Constitution is silent we feel that we have no jurisdiction to tear these review applications.</u>

9. Furthermore the review sought for n reviewing the judgment and order fated 9.8.98 is time-barred. In writ jurisdiction we do find any jurisdiction created or vested by any statute. As such he review applications filed by the petitioners are to the rejected.

Accordingly these two review applications being Review Applications Nos. 5 and 16 of 1998 are rejected.

End.
