In respectful agreement with my learned brother Mr. Md. Mozammel Hoঙue, J that the First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 44 of 1999 stand allowed and First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 67 of 1999 is dismissed, in view of importance of tow points, I would add the following:

36. The general election of the member of Seventh Parliament was held on June 12, 1996 wherein appellant of First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 44 of 1999, and respondent in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 67 of 1999, Md. Emdadul Huq Bhuiyan was sponsored by Bangladesh Awami League while respondent No. 1 if First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 44 of 1999 and appellant in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 67 of 1999. Md. Ataur Rahman Khan was fielded by Bangladesh Nationalist Party as candidates from constituency No. 203, Narayanganj-2. Besides, there were other candidates from other political parties. The election symbol of Bangladesh Awami League candidate was Boat (নৌকা) and the symbol of Bangladesh Nationalist Party candidate was Sheaf of Paddy (ধানের শীষ).

37. On June 12, 1996 election was held peacefully in 63 polling stations and in view of disturbance, polls in 6 polling stations stood adjourned. In the election held on June 12, 1996 candidate of Bangladesh Awami League secured 49,802 votes and candidate of Bangladesh Nationalist Party got 53,251votes. Fresh poll in the 6 adjourned polling stations was held on 19.06.1996. In the adjourned polls held on that date Bangladesh Awami League candidate obtained 9145 votes and Bangladesh Nationalist Party candidate secured 5137 votes. On consolidation of total votes candidate of Bangladesh Awami League secured 58,947 votes and candidate of Bangladesh Nationalist Party got 58,388 votes and candidate of Bangladesh Awami League had been declared to have been elected as a member of the Parliament by a margin of 559 votes than the candidate of Bangladesh Nationalist Party. The elected candidate and the defeated candidate shall be described, hereinafter, as the returned candidate and the unsuccessful candidate respectively.

38. The validity of the election of the re-turned candidate has been challenged by the unsuccessful candidate on presentation of an election petition before the Election Tribunal under Article 49 of the Representation of the People Order 1972 (P.O. No. 155 of 1972) hereinafter referred to as order figuring himself as petitioner and impleading the returned candidate as respondent for declaring the election of the returned candidate void and the petitioner (unsuccessful candidate) to have been duly elected Member of the Parliament or in the alternative declaring the election of the returned candidate to be void and directing fresh poll in 4 polling stations. Main at-tack launched or the main case projected before the Election Tribunal against the returned candidate is that he had indulged in the commission of corrupt practices of booth capturing and strapping of votes by himself and through his men in getting himself elected as member of the Parliament.

39. The returned candidate keenly resisted the election petition by specifically traversing all adverse allegations leveled against him. He specifically denied to have committed any corrupt or illegal practice or illegal act by himself, his agents or men.

40. The Election Tribunal found that there had been corrupt practice committed by returned candidate in the election. The Tribunal on reopening the ballot boxes recounted votes of two polling stations, namely, Shambupur High School polling station and Domar' Char Government Primary School Polling Station, hereinafter, referred to as Shambupurৃ polling station and Domarchar polling station, excluded 1411 votes from total votes secured by the returned candidate and declared the unsuccessful candidate as the elected member of the Parliament by showing a margin of 852 votes.

41. Aggrieved of the above adjudication, the returned candidate and the unsuccessful candidate presented the above stated two First Miscellaneous  Appeals.

42. The controversy in the case in hand seems to revolve on the answer to two question which are:

i) Whether the statutory requirement of election law as mandated in Article 51 of the Order had been complied with in presenting election petition before the Election Tribunal and whether alleged corruptor illegal practice or illegal act allegedly committed by the returned candidate or his agent or his men could be proved by unimpeachable evidence and whether the Tribunal was well founded in recording the finding that there had been corrupt practices committed by the returned candidate in getting himself declared as the successful candidate in getting himself declared as the successful candidate in the election.

ii) Whether recounting of the ballot papers on reopening the ballot boxes was a material issue before the Tribunal and whether sufficient foundation for recounting ballot papers had been all laid by the unsuccessful candidate and also whether the Tribunal was satisfied on the materials produced before it regarding the truth of the allegations made for recount and came to the conclusion that the order to grant prayer for recounting it was imperatively necessary to decide the dispute and to do complete and effectual justice between the parties.

43. In answering to the first question it would be profitable to notice relevant portion of Article 51, 58 and 63 of the Order. 43. An election petition is presented in terms of Article 51 of the Order. Article 51(a) and (b) demonstrates that every election petition shall contain a precise statement of the material facts on which the petitioner relies, full particulars of any corrupt or illegal practice or other illegal act alleged to have been committed, including as full a statement as possible of the names of the parties alleged to have committed such corrupt or illegal practice or illegal act and the date and place of the commission of such practice or act.

44. Article 58(a) enjoins that the Tribunal shall dismiss an election petition, if the provisions of Article 50 or Article 51 have not been complied with.

45. Article 63 (I)(d) manifests that the Tribunal shall declare the election of the returned candidate to be void if it is satisfied that a corrupt or illegal practice has been committed by the returned candidate or his election agent.

47. Article 63(1)(a) provides that the election of a returned candidate shall not be declared void on the ground that any corrupt, or illegal practice has been committed if the Tribunal is satisfied that it was not committed by. or with consent or connivance of that candidate or his election agent and that the candidate and the election agent took all reasonable precaution to prevent its commission.

48. The essence of Article 58 (a) is that in the event of failure on the part of the election petitioner to comply with the statutory requirement of law enshrined in Article 51(1)(a) and (b) of the Order, the tribunal shall dismiss the election petition. From the language used in Article 58(a) it is evidently clear that the world "shall" is mandatory and not a mere directory.

49. Again on a perusal of the language used in Article 63(1)(d) it is manifestly clear that the election of a returned candidate is liable to be declared void if the Tribunal is satsfied that a corrupt or illegal practice has been committed by the returned candidate or his election agent or any other person with the connivance of the candidate or his election agent. A reading of Article 63(2)(a) evidently shows that the election of a returned candidate shall not be declared void if the Tribunal is satisfied that corrupt or illegal practice has not been committed by the returned candidate or with his consent or connivance of his agent or his election agent.

50. It will be pertinent to notice here that both in sub-article (1)(d) and 2 (a) of Article 63 the words "illegal act" as coined in Article 51(1)(b) are not stated. The election of a returned candidate, this, can be declared void if the returned candidate is charged with the commission of corrupt or illegal practice but not for illegal act and for the commission of illegal act his election cannot be declared void.

51. The election law, therefore, insists that to unseat a returned candidate, the full particulars of corrupt or illegal practice or other illegal acts alleged to have been committed including full statement disclosing the names of the parties alleged to have committed such corrupt or illegal practice or illegal act must be specifically pleaded and alleged. The statutory requirements of election law are to be strictly observed because the election contest is not an action at law or a suit in equity but it is purely a statutory proceeding unknown to common law.

52. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in Mir Nabi Baksh Khan Vs. The Election Petitioner and Tribunal, Government of West Pakistan and others, PLD 1957 SC 301 stated:

"An election contest is not an action in law but a statutory proceeding as is, therefore, necessary that the statute which confers jurisdiction on it should be strictly observed."

53. In Jagan Nath Vs. Jaswant Singh and others 1954 SCR 892, 895 = AIR 1954 SC 210, the Supreme Court of India expressed similar views.

Mahajan, C.J. Spoke for the court thus:

"The general rule is well settled that the statutory requirements of election law must be strictly observed and that an election law must be strictly observed and that an election contest is not an action at law or a suit in equity but is a purely statutory proceeding unknown to the common law and that the court possesses no common law power".

54. The said court in Jamuna Prasad Vs. Lachchi Ram, AIR 1954 SC 686 observed thus:

"The right to stand as a candidate and contest an election is not a common law right. It a special right created by the statute and can only be exercised on conditions laid down by the statute."

55. The Supreme Court of India in Joyti Basu Vs. Devi Ghosal, (1982)SCR 318(1982) 1 SCC 691=AIR 1982 SC 983 reiterated the position by saying:

"A right to elect, fundamental though it is to democracy is anomalously enough, neither a fundamental right nor a common law right. It is pure and simple, a statutory right. So is the right to be elected. So is the right to dispute an election. Outside of statute, there is no right to elect, no right to be elected and no right to dispute and election. Statutory creations they are, and therefore, subject to statutory limitation. An election petition is not an action at common law, nor in equity. It is a statutory proceeding to which neither the common law nor the principles of equity apply but only those rules which the statute makes and applies. It is a special jurisdiction, and a special jurisdiction has always to be exercised in accordance with the statute creating it. Concepts familiar to common law and equity must remain strangers to election law unless statutorily embodied. A court has no right to resort to them on considerations of alleged policy because policy in such matters as those, relating to the trial of election disputes, is what the statute lays down. In the trial of election disputes, court is put in a strait-jacket."

56. The Representation of the People Order, 1972 is a complete Code in itself for challenging an election and an election must be called in question only in the manner provided for by the said Order. Article 51(1)(a)(b) is mandatory. It requires first a concise statement of the material facts on which the petitioner relies and then the full particulars of the alleged corrupt or illegal practice or illegal act alleged to have been committed and a full statement of the names of the persons alleged to have committed such corrupt or illegal practice or illegal act, so as to present a full picture of the cause of action. An election petition levelling a charge of corrupt or illegal practice is required, by law to be verified and the election petitioner is also obliged to disclose his source of information in respect of the commission of the corrupt practice. Since, pleadings play an important role in an election petition, the legislature has mandated that the allegation of corrupt practice, material facts and particulars must be properly alleged and pleaded so as to disclose a complete cause of action.

57. In the election petition, the petitioner (unsuccessful candidate) did not state full particulars of corrupt or illegal practice or illegal acts alleged to have been committed including full statement of the names of the parties who were alleged to have committed such corrupt or illegal practice or illegal acts. No reliable dates had been supplied in the election petition. The allegations suffered from vagueness. This vagueness would vitiate the election petition.

58. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in Mr. Nabi Baksh Khan Vs. The Election Petitioner and Tribunal, Government of West Pakistan (supra) held that

"The election petition shall contain a statement in concise from of the material facts on which the petitioner relies and shall be accompanied by a list setting forth the particulars of corrupt practice which the petitioner alleges and if those are not complied with the Government can dismiss the petition."

59. The Supreme Court of India in Samant N Balakrishna ETC Vs. George Fernandez and others, ETC (1969) 3 SCR 603 = (1969)3 SCC 238 = AIR1969 SC 1201 observed:

"The election petition must contain a concise statement of the material facts on which the petitioner relies and the fullest possible particulars of the corrupt practice alleged. The foundation of the particulars is to present as full a picture of the cause of action as to make the opposite party understand the case he will have to meet."

60. The said court recently in Gajanan Krishnaji Bapat Vs. Dattaji Reghobaji Meghe, (1995) 5 SCC 347 reiterated the same by stating that:

"A petition levelling a charge of corrupt practice is required, by law, to be supported by an affidavit and the election petitioner is also obliged to disclose his source of information in respect of the commission of the corrupt practice. This becomes necessary to bind the election petitioner to the charge levelled by him and to prevent any filing or recording enquiry and to prevent the returned candidate from being taken by surprise."

61. Regarded being had to the above stated position of law it manifestly appears that the requirements of law as enshrined in Article 51(1) of the Articles have not been complied with in presenting the election petition before the Tribunal and the election petition was liable to be dismissed under Article 58 of the Order. The Election Tribunal missed the true import of the election law in this regard and committed a patent illegality in not dismissing the election petition.

62. In the case of an election petition, based on allegation of commission of corrupt or illegal practice or illegal acts such as capturing of booths, rigging and strapping of votes, the burden of proof is on the election petitioner and that burden does never shift. A charge of corrupt and illegal practice are regarded as quasi-criminal in character and the standard of proof required for establishment of corrupt practice is the same as is required to establish a criminal offence. Strict proof is demanded from the person bringing the charge to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt.

63. The allegation of corrupt or illegal practice or illegal act requires strict proof as because the consequence are not only very serious but also penal in nature. On proof of any corrupt practice it is not only the election of the returned candidate which is declared to be void and set aside but the candidate himself or his agent or any other person, if found to have committed the offence of the commission of corrupt practice, may be punished with imprisonment. It is for this reason strict proof of such allegation of corrupt practice is insisted and not mere preponderance of probabilities as in civil action. Suspicion, however strong, cannot take the plea of proof.

64. Evidence led in support of the corrupt practice, must therefore, not only be cogent and definite but if the election petitioner is to succeed he must establish definitely and to the satisfaction of the court the charge of corrupt practice which he brings against the returned candidate. Support for the proposition of law stated in the foregoing paragraphs are sought to be drawn from a catena of authorities of Indian jurisdiction notably amongst others are Mohan Singhs Vs. Bhanwarlal, (1964) 5 SCR 12= AIR 1964 SC 1366, Guriji Shrihar Balirum Jivatode vs. Vithalrao, (1969) 2 SCR 766= (1969) 1 SCC 82, Nihal Singh Vs. Rao Birendra Singh and another, (1970) 3 SCC  239, Smt. Om Prabha Jain Vs. Charan Dass and another, (1975) 4 SCC 849. Daulat Ram Chauhan Vs. Ananda Shama, (1984) 2 SCC 64 = (1984) 2SCR 619, Surinder Singh Vs. Mardial Singh and others, (1985) I SCC 91 = AIR 1985 SC 89, S. Marcharan Singh Vs. S. Saijan Singh and others, (1985) 1 SCC 370 = AIR 1985 SC 236, Quamrul Islam Vs. S.K. Kanta, 1994 Supp (3) SCC 5; Gajanan Krishnaji Bapat Vs. Dattaji Raghobaji Meghe. (1995) 5 SCC 347, Balder Singh Mann Vs. Gurcharan Singh (MLA) and others. (1996) 9 SCC 351.

65. In an election case where the election petitioner seeks the election of a returned candidate to be declared void on the ground of corrupt practice, before the Tribunal can be satisfied that but for the votes obtained by the returned candidate by corrupt practice. the unsuccessful candidate would have obtained a majority of votes, it is necessary for the unsuccessful candidate to furnish reliable oats from which the Tribunal can reasonably come to a clear conclusion that the returned candidate had obtained by corrupt practice by margin votes by which the candidate was declared elected and something more which should be deducted from his total number of votes.

66. Through the testimonies of PW. 1, the election petitioner (unsuccessful candidate), P.W. 2.the Polling Agent of Domarchar Polling Station, P.W. 4, Polling Agent of Shambupura Polling Station and P.W.6, the Polling Agent of Satgram Government Polling Station, a faint attempt was made for proof of commission of corrupt practices such as capturing of polling booths by the supporters of the returned candidate but the testimonies of the PWs were totally demolished by the testimonies of the RWs who through their convincing, reliable and satisfactory testimonies could successfully prove that the polling was peaceful RW. 1 the returned candidate, RW. 2. the principal election agent of returned candidate, RW 3, a voter. RW 4.Chairman of Union Parishad for two terms.RW 5.RW 6.RW 7.RW 8, RW 9 all voters. RW 10 an ex-member of the Parliament from Bangladesh Nationalist Party. RW 12. polling agent of the returned candidate, RW 13, a voter and Union Parishad Member, RW 14. the Headmaster of a High School and Presiding Officer of Domarchar polling station, RW 15. Professor of Government Sadat Ali College and Presiding Officer Shambupura polling station. RW 18, Magistrate, RW 19, Professor of Government Sadat Ali College and Presiding Officer Satgram Government Primary School polling station testified that polling in Shambupura polling station, Domarchar polling station and Satgram polling station had been although peaceful and no untoward incident took place. The testimonies are consistent and inspire confidence.

<u>67. Dealing with the controversy it will be worthy to notice here that on the conclusion of the poll in Shambupura polling station and Domarchar polling station on 12.06.1996 no complaint no allegation whatsoever as to the commission of any corrupt or illegal practices or illegal acts like booth capturing or rigging was made by the unsuccessful candidate to the Presiding Officer. Returning Officer and Election Commission and other authorities. No complaint was ever made to the Police Personnel's who were on election duty at the above stated polling stations. There was not even a whisper about the allegations leveled against the returned candidate to Bangladesh Rifles (BDR) Personnels, who according to election petitioners (unsuccessful candidate) own evidence, was very much present outside the polling stations to maintain law and order. There are no contemporaneous materials or any record to indicate that the unsuccessful candidate, his agent, or any one on his behalf had raised even a finger on any of the alleged incidents to the Returning Officer, Assistant Returning Officer, Presiding Officer. Superintendent of Police, Bangladesh Rifles (BDR) Personnels who were available to entertain complaint if the returned candidate, his election agents or his supporters had committed corrupt or illegal practices or illegal acts.</u>

<u>68. In election matters the evidence about corrupt practice must be of such unimpeachable character that it will lead to only one conclusion that the corrupt practice has been committed and if any other inference is also possible, benefit must go to the returned candidate and the Tribunal should resist from recording any decision of corrupt practice and also he slow to interfere with the verdict of the electorate.</u>

<u>69. In the light of the pleadings and evidence and materials brought on record it is seen that the election petitioner (unsuccessful candidate) failed to adduce any cogent satisfactory or reliable evidence to bring home the charge of corrupt or illegal practice against the returned candidate and miserably failed to discharge the onus of proving the charges levelled by him against the successful candidate. The decision rendered by the Election Tribunal was not at all warranted by law and the same does not stand to any reason. I am of this positive view that the said finding was pureeing speculative and is not a conclusion which any reasonable mind could judicially reach. It is emphasised here that reason is the soul of law.</u>

70. This brings me in answered the second question which is recounting of ballot papers on reopening the ballot boxes. Under the Representation of the People Order 1972 power to recount votes or ballot papers on reopening the ballot boxes has been given to the Presiding Officer under sub-article 36 of the Order and the Presiding Officer may re-count the votes, (a) of his own motion if he considers it necessary. (b) upon tree request of a contesting candidate or an election agent if in his opinion, the request is not unreasonable. Nowhere in the four corners of the order and the rules framed thereunder, power is given to the Election Tribunal to recount the ballot papers on reopening the ballot boxes. This power to recount votes on reopening ballot boxes has been given to the Election Tribunal by judicial authorities which are Judge made law empowering the Tribunal to recount the ballot papers.

71. Ballot papers carry special sanctity of their own and their secrecy should not be infrienged by reopening the sealed packets unless recounting becomes a material issue before the Tribunal and the same becomes indispensably necessary to resolve the controversy. In view of the importance of maintaining secrecy of the ballot papers, scrutiny and recounting of the ballot papers can only be ordered if the election petition contains an adequate statements of the materials faces on which the election petitioner relies in support of his case. The election petition must contain an adequate statement of all material facts on which the allegation of illegality in counting are founded vague or general allegations that invalid votes were improperly accepted or valid votes were illegally rejected will not serve the purpose. Moreover, there must be clinching and unimpeachable evidence adduced from the side of the election petitioner affording a good ground for reopening ballot boxes and recount ballot papers and a foundation must be sufficiently laid. In the absence of any foundation no order for re-counting can be recorded by the Tribunal. Order for recounting of the ballot papers can be made only when the tribunal is satisfied that making of such order is imperatively necessary to decide the dispute and to do complete and effectual justice between the parties. Recounting must not be ordered on the prayer of an unsuccessful candidate whose sole effort is directed to unseat the returned candidate. Recounting should not be made lightly or as a matter or course and also on the sweet wishes of the unsuccessful candidate. Prayer for re-counting if not made by the defeated candidate or his agent of any person on his behalf before the Presiding Officer on conclusion of counting at the polling station as embodied in Article 36(5)(b) or before the Returning Officer as contained in Article 37(5), the foundation for recounting of ballot papers cannot be said to have been laid.

72. Our election law is a pattern on the basis of English Election Law. In Halsbury’s Laws of England, Volume-I4 at page 310, paragraph 559 it is stated:

"Recount is not granted as of right, but on evidence of good ground for believing that there has been a mistake on the part of the Returning Officers."

73. Similarly, Fraser in his Law of Parliamentary Elections and Election Petitions at page 222 observed thus:

"A strong case must be made on affidavit before an order can be obtained for inspection of ballot papers or counterfoils."

74. The importance of maintaining the secrecy of ballot papers and the circumstances under which that secrecy can be violated and recounting of ballot papers on reopening ballot boxes can be made has been considered in various judicial authorities of foreign jurisdiction as well as our jurisdiction.

75. On the question of recount as far back as in the case of Ram Sweak Vs. Mussain Kamil, (1964) 6 SCR 238 = AIR 1964 SC 1249 the Supreme Court of India pointed out that an order for inspection could not be granted as a matter of routine but only under special circumstances and observed as follows:

"An order for inspection may not be granted as a matter of course: having regard to the insistence upon the secrecy of the ballot papers, the Court would be justified in granting an older for inspection provided two conditions are fulfilled

i) that the petition for setting aside an election contains an adequate statement of the material facts on which the petitioner relies in support of his case; and

ii) The Tribunal is prima facie satisfied that in order to decide the dispute and to do complete justice between the parties inspection of the ballot papers is necessary.

But an order for inspection of ballot papers cannot be granted to support vague pleas made in the petition not supported by material facts. To establish a case so pleaded an order for inspection may undoubtedly, if the interests of justice require, be granted. But a mere allegation that the petitioner suspects or believes that there has been an improper reception, refusal or rejection of votes will not be sufficient to support an order for inspection."

76. To the same effect is a latter decision of the said Court in the case of Dr. Jagjit Singh Vs. Giani Kartar Singh, AIR 1966 SC 773 wherein it is stated:

"An application made for the inspection of ballot boxes must give material facts which would enable the Tribunal to consider whether in the interests of justice, the ballot boxes should be inspected or not. In dealing with this question, the importance of the secrecy of the ballot papers cannot be ignored and it is always to be borne in mind that the statutory rules framed under the Act are intended to provide adequate safeguard for the examination of the validity or invalidity of votes and for their proper counting. It may be that in some cases, the ends of justice would make it necessary for the Tribunal to allow a party to inspect the ballot boxes and consider his objections about the improper acceptance or improper rejection of votes tendered by voters at any given election; but in considering the requirements of justice, care must be taken to see that election petitioners do not get a chance to make a roving or fishing enquiry in the ballot boxes so as to justify their claim that the returned candidate's election is void."

77. In Jitendra Bahadur Singh Vs. Krishna Behari, (1970)1 SCR852-19692 SCC 438 the order of the election Judge granting inspection of the ballot papers was reversed by the Supreme Court on the ground that the learned Judge had not followed the essential conditions laid down before granting the prayer for inspection of the ballot papers. In that case court held that the allegations were vague and indefinite and no material fact was pleaded. Megde, J. speaking for the Court laid down the following principles:

i) that the petition for setting aside the election must contain an adequate statement of the material facts on which the petitioner relies in support of his case; and

ii) the Tribunal must be prima facie satisfied that in order to decide the dispute and to do complete justice between the parties, inspection of the ballot papers is necessary.

The case of Ram Sewak Yadav and Dr. Jagjit Singh (supra) were referred to and relied upon by Megde, J. in his judgment.

78. In the case of Sumitra Devi Vs. Shri Sheo Shankar Prasad Yadav, (1973) 2 SCR 920, Mathew, J. after reviewing the various authorities of the Court held as follows:

"In the case at hand, the allegations in the election petition were vague and the petition did not contain an adequate statement of the material facts. The evidence adduced by the appellant to prove the allegations was found unreliable. No definite particulars were also given in the application for inspection as to the illegalities alleged to have been committed in the counting of the ballot papers. A recount will not be granted as a matter of right but only on the basis of evidence of good grounds for believing that there has been a mistake in the counting. It has to be decided in each case whether a prima facie ground has been made out for ordering an inspection.

79. In the case of Baldev Singh vs. Teja Singh Swatantar (dead), (1973) 3 SCR 381 — (1975) 4 SCC 406 Krishna Ayer, J. remarked as follows:

"Disingenuous averments do not promote prospects of judicial recount and will be dismissed as devices to comply with re-quirements suggested in some ruling or other.

80. Similarly, in the case of Chanda Singh Vs. Coudhury Shiv Ram Venna, AIR 1975 SC 403 the observation of the Court is counted in the following language: "A democracy runs smooth on the wheels of periodic and pure elections. The verdict at the polls announced by the Returning Officers lead to the formation of Governments. A certain amount of stability in the electoral process is essential. If the counting of the ballots are interfered with by too frequent and flippant recounts by courts a new system is introduced through the judicial instrument. Moreover, the secrecy of the ballot which is sacrosanct becomes exposed to deleterious praying, if recount of votes is made easy. The general reaction, if there is judicial relaxation on this issue, may well be a fresh pressure on luckless candidates, particularly when the winning margin is only of a few hundred votes as here, to ask for a recount. Micawberishly looking for numerical good fortune or windfall of chance discovery of illegal rejection or reception of ballots. This may tend to a dangerous disorientation which invades the democratic order by injecting widespread scope for reopening of declared returns, unless the Court restricts recourse to recount to cases of genuine apprehension of miscount or illegality or other compulsions of justice necessitating such a drastic step."

81. In the case of Beliram Bhalaik Vs. Jai Beharilal Khachi, (1975) 4 SCC 417 the same principles had been again reiterated in the following words:

"A whimsical and bald statement of the candidate that he is not satisfied with the counting is not tantamount to a statement of the "grounds" within the contemplation of Rule 63 (2). The application was thus not a proper application in the eye of law. It was not supplemented even by an antecedent or contemporaneous oral statement of the author or any of his agents with regard to any irregularities in the counting. It was liable to be rejected summarily under sub-rule (3) of Rule 63 also. Since an order for a recount touches upon the secrecy of the ballot, it should not be made rightly or as a matter of course.

Although no cast-iron rule of universal application can be or has been laid down, yet from a beadroll of the decisions of this Court two broad guidelines are discernible; that the Court would be justified in ordering a recount or permitting inspection of the ballot papers only where (I) all the material facts on which the allegations of irregularity or illegality in counting are founded, are pleaded adequately in the election petition, and (ii) the Court / Tribunal trying the petition is prima facie satisfied that the making of such an order is imperatively necessary to decide the dispute and to do complete and effectual justice between the parties."

82. In Suresh Prasad Yadav Vs. Tai Prakash Mishra, (1975) 4 SCC 822, while summarising the principles laid down by the Court from time to time in granting prayer for inspection of ballot papers, the court adumbrated the circumstances in which a prayer for inspection of ballot papers could be considered and observed is follows:

"Before dealing with these contentions, we may recall, what this court has repeatedly said, that an order for inspection and recount of the ballot papers cannot be made as a matter of course. The reason is twofold. Firstly such an order affects the secrecy of the ballot which under the law is not to be lightly disturbed. Secondly, the Rules provide an elaborate procedure contains so many statutory checks and effective safeguards against trickery, mistakes and fraud in counting, that it can be called almost foolproof. Although no hard and fast rule can be laid down, yet the broad guidelines, as discernible from the decisions of this court, may be indicated thus:

The Court would be justified in ordering a recount of the ballot papers, only where:

1) The election petition contains and adequate statement of all the material facts on which the allegations of irregularity or illegality in counting arc founded;

2) On the basis of evidence adduced such allegations are prima facie established, affording a good ground for believing that there has been a mistake in counting; and

3) The court trying the petition is prima facie satisfied that the making of such an order is imperatively necessary to decide the dispute and to do complete and effectual justice between the par-ties.

83. Finally, the entire case law on the subject regarding the circumstances under which recount could be ordered was fully summarised and catalogued by the Supreme Court of India in the case of Bhabhi Vs. Sheo Govind and others (1976) I SCC 687 which are extracted thus:

"Thus on a close and careful consideration of the various authorities of this Court from time to time it is manifest that the following conditions are imperative before a court can grant inspection, or for that matter sample inspection, of the ballot papers:

1. That it is important to maintain the secrecy of the ballot which is sacrosanct and should not be allowed to he violated on frivolous, vague and in-definite allegations;

2. That before inspection is allowed, the allegations made against the elected candidate must be clear and specific and must be supported by adequate statements of material facts.

3. The court must be prima facie satisfied on the materials produced before the Court regarding the truth of the allegations made for a recount;

4. That the Court must come to the conclusion that in order to grant prayer for inspection it is necessary and imperative to do full justice between the parties;

5. That the discretion conferred on the Court should not be exercised in such a way so as to enable the applicant to indulge in a roving inquiry with a view to fish materials for declaring the election to be void; and

6. That on the special facts of a given case sample inspection may be ordered to lend further assurance to the prima facie satisfaction of the Court regarding the truth of the allegations made for a recount, and not for the purpose of fishing out materials."

84. Coming to authorities of our jurisdiction in Azimuddin Ahmed vs. Election Tribunal, Narayanganj and others, 27DLR(HCD) 594 a Division Bench of the High Court Division observed as follows:

"The Election Rules do not provide for recounting ballot papers by the tribunal and the power to recount ballot papers has been given under rule 41 to the Presiding Officer only. But if recounting of ballot papers is a material issue before the Tribunal and the election petition cannot be determined without such recounting, only then the Tribunal has got power to reopen the ballot boxes and recount the ballot papers in presence of parties. Before doing so it must come to a finding by evidence on oath that this recounting is indispensably necessary."

85. In Nurul Islam Talukder Vs. Munsif of the 4th Court at Sadar, Chittagong acting as Election Tribunal and 10 others, 28 DLR HCD 375 a Division Bench of the High Court Division laid down the manner in which the evidence of Election Officer is to be weighed, the affect of not lodging any complaint with the relevant authorities alleging irregularity in the counting of votes etc. In the said case it was stated thus:

"When the election was held in a peaceful atmosphere and scrutiny and counting of ballot papers where made in an orderly manner, without any objection from any quarter, reports of the Presiding Officers as to due performance of their duties must be accepted. Otherwise, there will be no sanctity of a free election which is a must for running democratic institutions."

86. In Afzal Vs. Election Tribunal and Munsif, 3rd Court, Comilla another, 1980 BSCR 69 = 32DLRAD 186, the Appellate Division held as correct the following views of the High Court Division :

"a) that the counting was not asked for before the presiding officer.

b) Foundation for the exercise of jurisdiction of the Tribunal merely for recounting was not laid.

The further observation of the Appellate Division is couched in the following terms:

Normally mere counting of votes may not be a sole issue before any Election Tribunal unless sufficient foundation for such exercise is laid by evidence. In the present case no allegation was made before the Returning Officer specifically regarding the error in counting but this was raised before Tribunal along with the allegation of corrupt practice

Further observation is as follows:

The jurisdiction of counting eminently lies elsewhere and even the Election Tribunal cannot count the ballot papers, unless the recounting becomes a necessary part of the case itself which has been brought on the basis of contain allegations of corrupt and illegal practices. It is well settled that if recounting of ballot papers is material issue before the Tribunal in connection with an election petition which cannot be determined without such recounting, then only the Tribunal has got power to reopen the ballot boxes and re-count the ballot papers provided sufficient foundation has been laid to come to the finding that the recounting is indispensably necessary for adjudication of the election petition."

87. In Md. Shajahan Vs. Md. Sadeq & another, 38 DLR AD 275 in paragraph 13 the observation of the Appellate Division is extracted hereunder:

"In Election cases, it is often found that a defeated candidate brings a number of allegations including vague charges of his opponent influencing the presiding officer, but ultimately fails to prove, or abandons, all the allegations and insists on only recounting of the ballot-papers. On recounting, it is found that the result has gone in his favour by some mysterious means. That is why recounting of the ballot papers by a Tribunal long after the election should not be resorted to simply on mere asking by an interested party. Ballot papers have special sanctity of their own and their secrecy should not be infringed by reopening the sealed packet unless the recounting becomes indispensably necessary to determine the dispute. When recounting would become so necessary depends on circumstances in each case. In the absence of clear justifications, no recounting should be ordered or made. Some finality must attach to counting of votes. Ground work for recounting must be prepared; recounting should be refused if no prayer for recounting had been made to the Presiding Officer who is alone empowered to recount on the spot either on his own motion or on requests of any candidate. Recounting of ballot-papers by the Tribunal is not specifically provided in the Election Rules, but it falls within the inherent powers of the Tribunal to decide the election dispute. In the instant case, the appellant or his representative did not request the Presiding Officer for recounting the ballot-papers. The Tribunal found that the election was held and the ballot papers were counted in an orderly manner all-through and no objection was raised on the spot before the Presiding officer as to the counting of the ballot pa-pers. In the circumstances, the learned single Judge rightly relied upon the decision in the case of Nurul Islam V. Munsif, Election Tribunal 28 DLR (Dhaka) 375. In that decision it was observed, among other things, that a ballot-box containing ballot papers must be regarded as a sacred thing whose secrecy should not be disturbed on a mere prayer of a defeated candidate when he has failed to prove any of its allegations of mal-practices against his opponent or the election officials."

88: In view of the above discussion and the principles of law propounded in the above stated authorities I am now to approach the controversy of recounting of ballot papers on reopening the ballot boxes.

89. On 12.06.1996 polls in Shambupura polling station and Domarchar polling station were held and the election was held peacefully. Election of the above stated two polling stations was not adjourned as adjourned including Satgram polling station. No allegation, no complaint was ever made to Presiding Officer, Assistant Returning Officer, Superintendment of Police, the Magistrate and also to Chief Election Commissioner as to the Commission of any corrupt or illegal practice or illegal act allegedly committed by the returned candidate, his agent or any other per-son or his supporters. No complaint, no allegation was ever laid with respect to rigging, capturing of booths and strapping of votes, proper and illegal acceptance of invalid ballot papers as valid ballot papers in favour of the returned candidate by the Presiding Officer and the other officers who were on election duty. There is no contemporaneous papers, documents and materials manifesting that on the conclusion of poll at Shambupura polling station and Domarchar polling stations on 12.06.1996, the unsuccessful candidate made any prayer even an approach to the Presiding Officer and the Returning Officer to recount ballot papers which were very much permitted under Article 36(5)(b) and 37(5)(a) of the Order. The election petitioner (unsuccessful candidate) on the conclusion of the poll held at 6 adjourned polling stations on 19.06.1996 by laying an application before the Returning Officer brought allegations against the successful candidate and his supporters in commission of illegal acts and corrupt practice only in respect of Satgram polling station and in the application also no allegations had been launched with respect to any illegal acts or corrupt practices allegedly committed by the returned candidate and improper acceptance of invalid votes as valid votes in favour of the returned candidate by the Presiding Officer and other election officials at Shambupura and Domarchar polling stations. In the event of any commission of illegal acts or corrupt practices by the returned candidate his agents, and supporters and improper and illegal counting of invalid votes as valid votes in favour of the returned candidate by the Presiding Officer and other election officials, then the unsuccessful candidate would have definitely brought allegations to the election officials and other authorities. Non launching of allegations with respect to commission of illegal acts, corrupt practices and improper reception of invalid votes as valid votes in favour of the returned candidate. The unsuccessful candidate in the election petition, for the first time, brought vague allegations of the alleged commission of illegal acts and corrupt or illegal practices and improper counting of invalid votes as valid votes by the Presiding Officer in favour of the returned candidate without supplying full particulars and reliable data's. It is well settled that full particulars must be supplied and in support of those particulars there must be strict proof by which the Tribunal would come to a decision whether the foundation had been at all laid for recounting of ballot papers on reopening ballot boxes. Care must be taken to see that the election petitioner (unsuccessful candidate) do not get a chance to make a roving or fishing inquiry into the ballot boxes.

90. Though a faint attempt had been made from the side of the unsuccessful candidate to show through the testimonies of PW 2 and PW.4, election agents of the unsuccessful candidate that there had been improper counting of invalid votes as valid votes in favour of the returned candidate in Shambupura polling station and Domarchar polling stations but the evidentiary value of the testimonies of PW 2 and 4 was totally demolished by the convincing and credible testimonies of RW Nos. 2,3,4,5,6,7,8,10,14 and 15. Of the witness RW 14 and 15 were the Presiding Officers of Domarchar and Shambupura polling stations. All the witnesses testified that there had been no disturbance, illegal acts and corrupt practices committed by the returned candidate and the counting was fair. The testimony of the Presiding Officers as to the due performance of their duties as to the proper counting of votes must be accepted. The election petitioner had failed to show through le-gal evidence that there had been booth capturing and strapping of votes by the returned candidate or his supporters and therefore the question of the recounting of ballot papers on reopening ballot boxes are packets of counter-foil did not arise at all in the case in hand. There were no satisfactory materials before the Tribunal by which the Tribunal could be satisfied in the matter of taking the course of recounting of ballot papers.

91. Before taking the course of recounting ballot papers on reopening ballot boxes the Election Tribunal must be prima facie satisfied on the basis of the statements made in the election petition and the legal evidence adduced and other materials on record that the scrutiny and the recounting of ballot papers has become a material issue and is imperatively necessary to resolve the controversy and to do complete and effectual justice between the parties. An Election Tribunal can be satisfied not on the basis of mere allegation unsupported by substantial evidence but only on the basis of proof to the hilt beyond all reasonable doubt. The Tribunal if so satisfied, is required to record reasons as to how it came to be satisfied. Every judicial decision must he based on reasons and the reasons must be disclosed in the judgment itself. From the order No. 77 dated 9.12.1998 calling the ballot papers and other election materials and the judgment itself it appears that the Election Tribunal made no attempt at all to give finding whether he was prima facie satisfied regarding the credibility of the evidence adduced before it and other materials on record that recounting became imperative to decide the controversy. Mere decision that to secure ends of justice recounting of ballot papers are necessary will not do. The learned Tribunal without recording any reason simply stated that for ends of justice, recounting was necessary. A Judge can be satisfied on the basis of proof and not on the basis of mere vague allegation. There is absolutely no proof in this case to support the allegations on the basis of which the scrutiny and recounting of ballot papers can be made.

92. On conspectus I am of this considered view that on the prayer of the election petitioner (unsuccessful candidate) there could not be any recounting of ballot papers when he failed to bring home the allegation of corrupt or illegal practice against the returned candidate and when no foundation of recounting had been laid. The election of the returned candidate was not to be interfered with at the sweet wishes of the defeated candidate and the Tribunal was not to brush aside the success for the duly elected member of the Parliament on an election petition founded on vague, indefinite, frivolous and flimsy grounds. The learned Tribunal committed a patent illegality and flagrant error of law in recounting ballot papers by opening scaled packets containing ballot papers.

End.
